countermeasures.limitations: Hardening buys delay, not denial — a sufficiently equipped or numerous actor can defeat a single portal given time; effectiveness depends on guard vigilance and on lockdown being triggered before the breach completes

countermeasures.measure: Deploy hostile-vehicle and forced-entry detection — perimeter intrusion sensing, ANPR and behavioral watch for hostile approach vectors, and panic alarms tied to automatic lockdown and immediate law-enforcement notification
countermeasures.limitations: Warning time from detection to impact can be seconds for a ramming vehicle; value depends on pre-planned automatic responses (barrier activation, lockdown) since human decision cycles are too slow to interdict a committed approach

response_protocols.trigger: Vehicle ram into the site, or a forced entry overpowering staff, observed in progress
response_protocols.action: Treat as an active life-safety attack. Initiate immediate lockdown and mass-notification, direct occupants away from the vehicle path or breach point using run-hide-fight guidance, trigger duress alarms, and summon law enforcement and EMS with a mass-casualty declaration. Preserve the scene for a possible ram-then-dismount or breach-then-advance and account for secondary hazards. Do not stand down until law enforcement confirms the scene is clear.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Casualties present, the actor dismounts to continue on foot, a follow-on device or second attacker appears, or the breach opens the way to the occupied interior
response_protocols.legal_notes: Life-safety response is within facility authority; use-of-force by the guard force must remain within lawful defense-of-others limits, and scene preservation should support the subsequent criminal investigation. Document decisions and timings contemporaneously.

response_protocols.trigger: Hostile vehicle approach vector detected, or an attempted forced entry against a controlled point, before impact or breach completes
response_protocols.action: Interdict and deny. Raise active barriers and close vehicle gates, channel occupants away from the approach corridor and lock down exposed entrances, alert the guard force to hold the entry point, and notify law enforcement of an attack in progress. Prepare to transition to full life-safety response the instant impact or breach occurs.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: The vehicle continues past initial barriers, the forced entry defeats the controlled point, or occupants come within the approach path
response_protocols.legal_notes: Barrier activation and access denial are within facility authority; ensure emergency egress remains available to occupants during lockdown to avoid entrapment, and document the threat basis for the interdiction.

tactics.field_notes: Forced entry and vehicle ram are the two ways an actor buys past a facility's standoff and access controls with raw kinetic force, and at the scene they read fast: the tell is not the vehicle or the tool but the trajectory. A deliberate ram accelerates, tracks the crowd or the doorway, and does not brake — an accident brakes and swerves. A hostile forced entry drives toward the occupied core and presses past the first obstacle; a benign one recovers a lockout and stops. The hardest minutes are the first seconds, because a committed ramming approach gives too little warning for a human decision cycle — which is why the countermeasures that matter are the ones that fire automatically, rated barriers that arrest the vehicle whether or not anyone reacts. When force is applied to people — a ram into a queue, a breach that overpowers the guard — it is the attack itself, scored at the casualty floor, and the immediate question shifts from assessment to whether it is a single act or the opening of a complex one.
observed_contexts: vehicle deliberately accelerated into a pedestrian queue at an occupied entrance during peak hours, tracking the crowd with no braking before impact
forced entry in which the actor overpowered a lone reception guard to breach a controlled lobby and advance into the occupied interior
heavy vehicle rammed a perimeter gate and bollard line to defeat standoff, followed by dismounted attackers moving toward the building
[literature: CISA-HVM-2024 / ASTM-F2656-2020 pattern — hostile-vehicle attacks on unprotected pedestrian frontages defeating inadequate or absent standoff barriers]

tactics.name: Occupation & Blockade
tactics.notes: Seizing, occupying, or blockading the targeted facility to deny its use — sit-ins, lock-ons, human chains, barricaded doors, perimeter or access-point blockades, and sustained siege postures that hold the site against its normal operation. The objective is denial of use rather than destruction: the place is taken and held. Distinct from Forced Entry / Vehicle Ram (which breaches to enter or damage) in that the defining act is holding and denying, not breaching. Most occupations are disruptive rather than lethal, but any occupation with occupants or bystanders present carries a life-safety dimension — blocked egress, a barricaded crowd, or the physical seizure of occupants can convert a denial-of-use event into a casualty event.
tactics.cpn_notes: Occupations and blockades are increasingly organized, live-streamed, and sustained through online coordination — mobilization calls, real-time logistics, and shared tactics for lock-ons and barricades that let a group seize and hold a facility faster than on-site security can respond.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, persistence over time, and recoverable evidence that a group intends to seize and hold the facility rather than protest lawfully outside it. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when a lawful assembly with no intent to occupy or blockade was never ruled out.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — mobilization calls, staging of lock-on or barricade materiel, and physical massing at the site within overlapping timeframes.
Temporal persistence — a stated intent to occupy or blockade observed building across days, not a single remark.
Material evidence — recovered lock-on devices, chains, barricade materials, occupation supplies, or logistics plans naming the site.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who observed the massing, the blocking of an entrance, or the refusal to disperse, with high-resolution reporting of what was done and when.
Behavioral specificity — the group named the specific facility, entrance, or access point it intended to hold, not a vague category.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — trained on-site reporter or security operator through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip, reporter cannot be re-contacted.
Content-specificity weakness — a vague call to 'shut it down' that could fit any lawful demonstration.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one-time remark with no massing, staging, or follow-through.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to embellish (labor dispute, counter-protest rivalry, litigation).
Unrebutted lawful explanation — the activity admits a benign reading (permitted picket, lawful assembly on public ground) that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that a routine demonstration is retrofitted to an occupation narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the group can seize and hold the facility — coordinated numbers, lock-on and barricade hardware, logistics to sustain a siege, and the discipline to defeat dispersal. Capability falls with small disorganized numbers, no holding materiel, and a posture that dissolves on first contact with security or law enforcement.
high_signal_anchors: Holding materiel on hand — lock-on devices, chains, sleeping dragons, barricade stock, or vehicles positioned to block access points.
Coordinated numbers and roles — a crowd large enough to hold multiple entrances, with assigned blockade, supply, and communications functions.
Sustainment logistics — food, water, shelter, medical, and shift rotation staged to hold the site through multiple operational periods.
Access achieved into an occupiable space — the group has reached a lobby, floor, or chokepoint it can physically hold, not just the public perimeter.
Counter-dispersal discipline — the group anticipates and defeats extraction (locking together, going limp, re-forming), and does not break on first challenge.
Demonstrated tactical literacy — organizers reason about which chokepoint denies the most use for the least force, and pre-position accordingly.
low_signal_anchors: Small disorganized presence — a handful of individuals with no capacity to hold an entrance.
No holding materiel — bodies only, no lock-ons, barricades, or vehicles, so the blockade is trivially cleared.
No sustainment — no supplies or rotation; the presence cannot outlast a single shift.
Perimeter-only reach — the group is confined to public ground outside the controlled boundary and cannot occupy an interior space.
Dissolution on contact — the group disperses immediately when challenged by security or law enforcement.
Single-modality mobilization — an online call with no observable staging, materiel, or physical massing behind it.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the conduct progresses from lawful assembly toward denial of use — blocking egress, refusing lawful dispersal orders, fortifying against extraction, and escalating from symbolic presence toward physical control of occupants or the site. Intent falls with lawful, orderly protest that keeps access open and disperses on request.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression from assembly to denial — an observable shift from standing outside to physically blocking ingress and egress.
Egress obstruction — doors chained, exits barricaded, or a crowd positioned so occupants cannot freely leave; a life-safety line has been crossed.
Refusal of lawful dispersal — the group is ordered to clear and instead fortifies, locks on, or re-forms.
Sustained denial of use — the site's normal operation is halted and the group acts to keep it halted rather than making a point and leaving.
Escalation toward occupants — the group moves from holding space to controlling, confining, or confronting the people inside.

Hostile framing paired with holding conduct — the group has expressed a demand to shut the facility down AND is observed physically holding it; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
low_signal_anchors: Lawful orderly assembly — presence that keeps entrances and exits clear and does not deny use.
One-time symbolic action without holding — a brief demonstration that ends without occupation or blockade.
Compliance with dispersal — the group clears when lawfully directed.
No egress interference — access and exit remain open throughout.
Ambiguous objective — a demonstration whose aim is expression, with no observed move to seize or hold the site.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the group can reach and hold the facility — an unhardened entrance, occupied hours that maximize disruption and hostage value, thin on-site security, and a chokepoint whose seizure denies the most use. Opportunity falls with hardened access, controlled ingress, robust extraction capacity, and standoff that keeps a blockade at the public boundary; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: Unimpeded reach to a holdable space — the group entered a lobby, corridor, or chokepoint without being stopped at a controlled boundary.
Occupied-hours timing — the seizure coincides with peak occupancy, maximizing both disruption and the number of people inside the held space.
Thin on-site response capacity — security or law-enforcement presence cannot clear the held space before it is fortified.
Chokepoint leverage — the group holds a single point (main entrance, loading dock, utility corridor) whose denial halts the whole site.
Insider facilitation — an identified employee, contractor, or member who props a door, disables a lock, or guides the group past controls.
Sustainment and re-supply access — the held position can be resupplied, letting the occupation outlast the defender's patience.
low_signal_anchors: Blocked at a hardened boundary — controlled ingress, mantraps, or secured entrances kept the group outside the occupiable envelope. Durable signal: sticky unless the group adapts.
Rapid extraction capacity on hand — sufficient security or law-enforcement presence to clear the space before it is held.
Perimeter standoff — barriers and setback keep any blockade at the public edge, away from the operational chokepoints.
Dispersal without adaptation — the group left when challenged and did not re-form or fortify. Transient: may flip if it adapts.
Institutional rule-out of insider facilitation — access audits or process actively cleared the possibility of internal help.
Posture change created barriers — locked-down access, added guards, or closed hours block the group's known approach; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Lawful protest and ordinary business activity resemble occupation on the surface — a permitted picket outside a building looks similar to a blockade forming; a crowded lobby at opening looks similar to a massing occupation. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the conduct keeps ingress and egress open, has lawful authority or a permit behind it, and disperses on lawful request rather than moving to deny use.
contexts: Lawful assembly — permitted pickets, rallies, and demonstrations on public ground that keep entrances and exits clear.
Legal authority — labor actions within lawful bounds; authorized inspections, drills, or evacuations that temporarily restrict access with facility consent.
Ordinary congestion — normal crowding at openings, events, deliveries, or shift changes with no intent to hold or deny use.
Emergency and service activity — first responders, utility crews, or contractors who legitimately stage vehicles or block an access point for a job.
Expressive but non-obstructive action — a brief symbolic gathering, vigil, or press event that does not barricade, lock on, or refuse to clear.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: An occupation or blockade in progress is a life-safety event whenever occupants or bystanders are present: obstruction of egress, barricading of a crowded space, or any move to physically seize, confine, or harm an occupant warrants immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier, and captive-taking warrants immediate law-enforcement and crisis-negotiation coordination. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: whether egress and life-safety are compromised, the group's holding capability, and its refusal of lawful dispersal. A lawful assembly keeping access open sits at the monitoring tier. A forming blockade that begins to obstruct ingress sits at the investigation tier. An active occupation denying use with occupants present sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as an in-progress facility attack. An occupation that has barricaded egress, fortified against extraction, or moved to control occupants sits at the committed-actor tier and warrants an immediate life-safety response. Multiple lower-tier signals correlating in time — a mobilization call plus staged lock-on materiel plus massing at a chokepoint — may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers logging and liaison; investigation triggers on-site assessment and access control review; elevation triggers civil-disturbance response activation and law-enforcement coordination; the committed-actor tier triggers a life-safety response with priority on protecting and extracting occupants.

indicators.behavior: Threat actors enter the targeted facility and refuse to leave, staging a sit-in or occupation that halts the site's normal operation during occupied hours
Threat actors barricade or chain entrances and exits, or lock themselves onto doors and fixtures with devices, obstructing egress from an occupied space
Threat actors blockade the facility's access points with bodies, vehicles, or lock-on devices at the perimeter, denying ingress and egress to the site
Threat actors physically seize, confine, or restrain occupants or staff within the held facility, taking them captive or blocking their movement by force
Threat actors fortify and entrench the held position with supplies and materiel, refusing lawful dispersal orders and defeating extraction to sustain the siege

countermeasures.measure: Enforce controlled ingress at staffed and access-controlled entrances so a group cannot reach and seize an interior chokepoint, keeping any massing at the public boundary rather than inside the operational envelope
countermeasures.limitations: Controlled ingress slows a seizure but cannot stop a large coordinated crowd at a public-facing lobby; balances against legitimate visitor and patron access

countermeasures.measure: Protect and monitor emergency egress — anti-barricade hardware, tamper-alarmed fire exits, and maintained unobstructed exit routes — so an occupation cannot trap occupants behind blocked doors
countermeasures.limitations: Protects life-safety egress but does not by itself end the occupation; determined actors may still barricade primary entrances even where fire exits are held clear

countermeasures.measure: Maintain a civil-disturbance and occupation response plan with pre-established law-enforcement liaison, trained de-escalation, and lawful negotiated-dispersal procedures rehearsed with facility staff
countermeasures.limitations: Effectiveness depends on law-enforcement response time and the group's willingness to negotiate; a fortified lock-on occupation can outlast an unrehearsed response

countermeasures.measure: Deploy perimeter and lobby surveillance with duress alarms and crowd-massing detection to flag a forming blockade or occupation early enough to lock down access and summon response before the site is held
countermeasures.limitations: Provides early warning but not intervention; value depends on a staffed response that can act on the alert before the group reaches a holdable chokepoint

response_protocols.trigger: An occupation or blockade is in progress — a group has entered and refuses to leave, is obstructing ingress or egress, or has barricaded a space with occupants present
response_protocols.action: Activate the occupation response plan with life-safety first: (a) account for and protect occupants, keeping at least one monitored egress route clear, (b) lock down further access to contain the held area, (c) establish law-enforcement liaison and a single point of contact for negotiation, (d) preserve CCTV and access-log evidence and document the timeline. Do not attempt unilateral extraction of locked-on actors.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Egress becomes fully obstructed with occupants inside, the group fortifies against extraction, or actors move to seize or confine occupants
response_protocols.legal_notes: Response must respect lawful-assembly and free-speech protections until conduct crosses into unlawful obstruction or confinement; coordinate use-of-force and dispersal decisions with law enforcement and counsel, and document the basis for each escalation.

response_protocols.trigger: Occupation escalates to captive-taking or confinement — actors physically seize, restrain, or block the movement of occupants or staff within the held facility
response_protocols.action: Treat as a barricade/hostage life-safety emergency. Transfer tactical lead to law enforcement, activate crisis negotiation, and establish a controlled inner and outer perimeter. Provide responders with facility schematics, occupant counts and locations, camera feeds, and utility controls. Manage communications to avoid inflaming the situation and support affected occupants and families.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Weapons are displayed, injury occurs, or negotiation breaks down
response_protocols.legal_notes: Captive-taking is a criminal act triggering law-enforcement primacy; facility personnel support but do not lead tactical response. Preserve evidence and document all decisions and communications for subsequent investigation and prosecution.

tactics.field_notes: Occupation and blockade is the one execution tactic where the point is to hold rather than destroy, and that changes the whole response calculus. Most occupations are disruptive and non-lethal — a sit-in, a chained door, a human chain across a driveway — and the pressure is to treat them as a public-order problem. The line that matters for a threat program is egress: the moment a barricaded door or a massed crowd means occupants cannot freely leave, a denial-of-use event has become a life-safety event, and blocked exits turn deadly the instant anything else goes wrong inside. The other line is the person — an occupation that moves from holding space to holding people is a hostage situation and belongs to law enforcement immediately. The hard part is that lawful assembly and unlawful occupation look identical until the group refuses to clear or blocks a way out, so the assessment hinges on holding capability, egress status, and response to a lawful dispersal order, not on the presence of a crowd.
observed_contexts: clinic occupation where activists chained themselves across the entrance and blocked patient and staff access during operating hours
corporate-lobby sit-in where a group barricaded the doors and refused dispersal orders, holding the space over multiple days with staged supplies
blockade of a facility's loading dock and access points by vehicles and lock-on devices that denied use of the whole site
[literature: FBI-HOBAS-2024 / NAF-CLINICVIOLENCE-2024 pattern — barricade and occupation incidents at clinics and public facilities escalating from denial-of-use to confinement of occupants]

tactics.name: Vandalism & Defacement
tactics.notes: Deliberate damage, defacement, or symbolic marking of the targeted facility's fabric, fixtures, or surfaces — spray-painted messaging and graffiti, broken windows and lighting, slashed or etched surfaces, adhesive-fouled locks, toppled signage, and destroyed monuments, plaques, or memorials. The objective is to deface, degrade, or communicate through the place rather than to injure occupants; incidents typically occur when the site is unoccupied or on its exterior, so no persons are directly involved. Distinct from Structural Sabotage (which attacks load-bearing integrity to damage or collapse) and from Incendiary and Explosive Attack (which apply destructive force with mass-casualty potential). Vandalism is property-first, but symbolic and hate-motivated marking of a place — a slur or extremist symbol on a house of worship, a defaced memorial — carries community-terror weight disproportionate to the repair cost and is frequently a precursor to escalation against the same site.
tactics.cpn_notes: Defacement is increasingly staged for online audiences — the mark itself is photographed and posted, hashtags and manifestos accompany the image, and the act is coordinated or claimed through social channels. Public building-condition reporting apps, streetview imagery, and social posts of prior damage also let an actor pre-select vulnerable, unmonitored, or symbolically resonant surfaces before approaching the site.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, persistence over time, and recoverable evidence backing first-hand reports that the actor damaged or defaced the specific facility. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when a plausible non-hostile explanation — accidental damage, unaffiliated tagging, weathering — was never ruled out.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — recovered imagery of the mark, CCTV of the act, and a claim or grievance post against the same site within overlapping timeframes.
Temporal persistence — repeated defacement of the place across weeks to months, not a single isolated mark.
Material evidence — spray cans, stencils, etching tools, or matching paint recovered and physically tied to the actor and the site.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who saw the actor mark or damage the facility; high-resolution reporting of the act, content, and timing.
Content specificity — the mark names or targets the specific facility, its tenant, or the group it represents rather than generic tagging.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — facility staff or a trained observer reporting through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip, reporter cannot be re-contacted.
Content-specificity weakness — generic graffiti or tagging that could fit any wall in the district.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one-time mark with no follow-through or pattern against the site.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to embellish (property dispute, tenant rivalry, insurance interest).
Unrebutted benign explanation — the damage admits an accidental, weathering, or unaffiliated-tagger reading that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that the target and intent may be retrofitted to a threat narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the defacement shows preparation and discipline — pre-staged materials, target-surface selection to maximize visibility or symbolic wound, timing to the site's unmonitored windows, and defeat of the facility's observation. Capability falls with impulsive, conspicuous, or low-effort marking that leaves the actor exposed and the damage trivially reversible.
high_signal_anchors: Pre-staged materials — stencils, pre-mixed paint, cutting or etching tools brought to the site rather than improvised on scene.
Surface and placement selection — the mark is placed for maximum visibility, symbolic resonance, or permanence (etched glass, masonry, a monument face) rather than an incidental wall.
Timing to unmonitored windows — the act is executed during the facility's low-observation periods, showing pattern-of-life knowledge.
Counter-surveillance behaviors — the actor obscures identity, disables or avoids cameras, and departs without an observable return pattern.
Coordinated or claimed action — the defacement is documented and disseminated with messaging, indicating an organized rather than opportunistic act.
Escalation literacy — the marking is paired with reconnaissance-type behavior or method-durability choices that read as a step toward heavier damage.
low_signal_anchors: Impulsive execution — improvised marking with materials found on scene, no evident planning.
Conspicuous posture — marking in the open during monitored hours, indifferent to cameras or witnesses.
Low-effort reversibility — chalk, removable stickers, or washable marker that the facility can clear within hours.
No concealment — the actor made no attempt to obscure identity or defeat observation.
Single-surface, single-instance — one incidental mark with no target-selection logic evident.
Attribution to unaffiliated tagging — the style, placement, and content match generic graffiti rather than targeted defacement of the site.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the defacement is targeted at what the facility represents, when the content carries threat or hate messaging, when the actor claims or disseminates the act, and when marking repeats or escalates against the same site. Intent falls with generic, apolitical, or opportunistic tagging that is not fixed to the place as an objective.
high_signal_anchors: Targeted symbolic content — slurs, extremist symbols, or threat messaging aimed at the facility's tenant, faith, or function rather than generic tags.
Facility-specific fixation — attention concentrates on the named site, its signage, or its most symbolically loaded surfaces.
Claim or dissemination — the actor photographs, posts, or claims the defacement, framing the place as the objective.
Repetition and escalation — the same site is marked repeatedly, or the damage escalates in permanence or severity over time.

Grievance paired with the act — the actor has expressed hostility toward the facility or what it represents AND is observed defacing it; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
Threat-forward messaging — the mark communicates a future intention (countdown, 'you're next,' target-list references) beyond the damage itself.
low_signal_anchors: Generic tagging — apolitical graffiti or a personal tag not tied to the facility's identity or function.
Opportunistic damage — breakage or marking incidental to trespass, theft, or shelter-seeking, not aimed at the place as an objective.
One-time act without escalation — a single mark that does not repeat or intensify.
Verifiable non-hostile purpose — sanctioned mural, permitted signage change, or an unrelated dispute surfaces and checks out.
Target ambiguity — the same style appears across many unrelated sites, indicating a roaming tagger rather than site fixation.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can reach and mark the facility freely — exposed and unmonitored exterior surfaces, low-observation windows, proximity to the site, and an absence of cameras, lighting, or barrier hardening around the marked area. Opportunity falls with hardened surfaces, active observation, and defensive friction the actor did not adapt to; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: No defensive friction encountered — the actor marked and departed unimpeded despite the facility's posture.
Exposed unmonitored surfaces — the marked area lacks cameras, lighting, or anti-graffiti hardening and sits outside patrol coverage.
Pattern-of-life mastery — the actor reliably knows the site's low-observation periods and after-hours windows.
Proximity — the actor lives, works, or routinely transits near the facility and is present during its vulnerable windows.
Repeatable access to the same surface — the actor returns to the identical surface, indicating a stable and exploited access pathway.
Coverage gap knowledge — the actor knows which approaches, blind spots, or fence lines allow undetected marking of the site.
low_signal_anchors: Approach defeated by hardened posture — anti-graffiti coatings, lighting, or active surveillance blocked or rapidly reversed the actor's marking. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor materially adapts or the posture drops.
Surface hardening in place — protective film, sacrificial coatings, or barrier setback denies durable marking of the targeted surface.
Structural access degradation — the actor's prior approach pathway was closed (fencing, sealed access, relocation).
Defensive friction without adaptation — the actor left after being observed or challenged and did not return or adapt. Transient: may flip if the actor adapts.
Geographic distance not closed — the actor is remote and reaching the surface requires an investment not yet made.
Posture change created barriers — new cameras, lighting, or patrol emphasis blocks the actor's known marking approach; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Much surface change on a facility resembles hostile defacement on first look — a sanctioned mural resembles graffiti, storm or accident damage resembles deliberate breakage, and an unaffiliated tagger's mark resembles targeted defacement. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the change has a verifiable authorization, an accidental or environmental cause, or content that is generic rather than aimed at the site's identity.
contexts: Authorized work — permitted murals, commissioned art, sanctioned signage changes, and maintenance or renovation that alters surfaces with facility consent.
Accidental and environmental damage — vehicle strikes, storm and hail damage, settling and weathering, or wildlife that mimics deliberate breakage.
Unaffiliated tagging — roaming graffiti writers whose apolitical tags appear across many sites with no fixation on this facility.
Sanctioned protest expression — lawful, temporary, removable demonstration materials (chalk, banners, adhesive-free signage) placed with or without objection but without property damage.
Prior-incident residue — old, already-documented marks re-reported as new, or contractor test patches and primer mistaken for defacement.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Defacement findings correlating with heavier facility execution behaviors — accelerant staging, forced-entry attempts, threat messaging naming a date or method, or marks that function as target designation for a later attack — warrant immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: the credibility of the attribution, the symbolic or threat weight of the content, and persistence against the same site. A single low-credibility, generic mark with an available benign explanation sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility incident with targeted hate or threat content sits at the investigation tier. Cross-modal corroboration — grievance plus repeated targeted marking plus a claim against the same site — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as a coordinated campaign against the facility. Defacement persisting despite implemented countermeasures, or escalating in permanence and severity, sits at the committed-actor tier and suggests progression toward heavier damage. Multiple lower-priority incidents correlating temporally or by content may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single mark warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers documentation, preservation, and pattern-detection; investigation triggers actor-identification and a surface-vulnerability review; elevation triggers hardening and surveillance of the targeted surfaces plus community notification where hate-motivated; the committed-actor tier triggers a defensive-posture upgrade; a confirmed actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination and hate-crime reporting where the content applies.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor is observed actively defacing the facility — spray-painting or applying graffiti, breaking windows or lighting, or fouling locks and entrances — while the act is in progress
Threat actor applies hate-motivated or symbolic marking to the facility — a slur, extremist symbol, or threat message on a house of worship, cultural site, or the tenant's identifying signage

Facility staff discover covert overnight property destruction — slashed or etched surfaces, adhesive-fouled locks, cut wiring to non-critical fixtures, or smashed exterior glass — after the fact with the actor gone

Threat actor conducts a repeated, escalating defacement campaign against the same facility — the site is marked again after cleanup, or the damage intensifies in permanence, placement, or content over successive incidents
Threat actor destroys or topples a symbolic fixture of the facility — a monument, memorial, plaque, statue, flag, or identifying sign — targeting what the object represents

countermeasures.measure: Harden exposed and symbolically loaded surfaces with anti-graffiti coatings, sacrificial films, protective glazing, and durable materials that make marking reversible and destruction difficult on the facility's most-targeted faces
countermeasures.limitations: Coatings and glazing raise the effort and reduce permanence but do not stop a determined actor; monuments, ornamental fixtures, and heritage surfaces often cannot be coated without altering their character

countermeasures.measure: Deploy exterior lighting, cameras, and motion detection focused on the facility's exposed surfaces, signage, and symbolic fixtures, with alerting on after-hours approach to those areas
countermeasures.limitations: Cameras record but do not prevent a fast, masked defacement; coverage gaps, glare, and blind spots persist, and attribution from footage is often incomplete

countermeasures.measure: Adopt a rapid-removal and evidence-preservation protocol — photograph and document each incident, report hate-motivated marks to law enforcement, then remove within hours to deny the actor the publicized result and reduce copycat effect
countermeasures.limitations: Fast removal can erase evidence if documentation is skipped, and rapid cleanup does not deter an actor motivated by the act itself rather than its persistence

countermeasures.measure: Establish community and staff reporting channels and liaison with peer facilities and fusion centers to flag targeted or hate-motivated defacement trends and identify repeat actors against the facility class
countermeasures.limitations: Depends on reporting discipline and cross-facility information sharing; roaming or opportunistic vandals may never be identified, and trend warning may lag the first incident

response_protocols.trigger: Targeted or hate-motivated defacement of the facility discovered or observed (slur, extremist symbol, threat message, or destruction of a symbolic fixture)
response_protocols.action: Open or update the facility threat case. Within 24 hours: (a) photograph and preserve the mark and any physical evidence before removal, (b) pull CCTV and access logs for the incident window and attempt actor identification, (c) assess whether content constitutes a hate crime or threat requiring law-enforcement referral, (d) brief facility and tenant leadership and, where the content targets a community, coordinate notification. Remove the mark promptly after documentation. Record all sourcing.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Marking recurs against the same site, content names a date or method, or the defacement correlates with heavier execution behaviors (accelerant staging, forced-entry attempts) by the same actor
response_protocols.legal_notes: Hate-motivated defacement may trigger mandatory reporting and hate-crime statutes that vary by jurisdiction; preserve chain of custody for evidence and consult counsel before publicizing content or attribution.

response_protocols.trigger: Repeated or escalating defacement against the facility despite cleanup, or a targeting trend against the facility class without a named actor
response_protocols.action: Elevate posture for the targeted surfaces: add or reposition lighting and cameras, apply protective coatings or glazing, increase patrol emphasis during identified low-observation windows, and coordinate with local law enforcement and peer facilities on the pattern. Track incidents as a linked campaign and reassess after each event.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Escalation in permanence or severity of damage, threat-forward content, or attribution to a known threat-actor profile
response_protocols.legal_notes: Posture changes are within facility authority; document the incident history to support resource requests and to defend proportionality of any surveillance or access changes.

tactics.field_notes: Vandalism reads as the lowest-consequence facility attack until you weigh what the mark says and whether it repeats. A generic tag on a loading dock is a maintenance ticket; a slur or extremist symbol on a house of worship is community terror with a repair cost attached, and the two demand very different responses. The diagnostic questions are content, targeting, and persistence: does the mark aim at what the place represents, does it name the site or its people, and does it come back after cleanup? Repeat targeted defacement is the tell that matters most — it signals fixation on the site and frequently precedes heavier damage, so the same wall marked three times deserves more concern than three different walls marked once. Rapid removal is the right instinct for denying the actor a publicized result, but photograph and preserve first: fast cleanup that destroys the evidence trades a short-term win for a lost case. The act itself is usually overt and discoverable — the challenge is attribution and reading which marks are noise and which are a campaign opening.
observed_contexts: house of worship repeatedly marked with extremist symbols over successive weekends before an attempted arson against the same site
cultural-center signage defaced with threatening messaging that was photographed and posted by the actor to claim the act
clinic exterior subjected to recurring overnight glass breakage and lock-fouling as part of a sustained intimidation campaign
[literature: FBI-HATECRIME-2024 / CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 pattern — targeted defacement and symbolic marking as community intimidation and a precursor to escalation against the site]

tactics.name: Contamination
tactics.notes: Introduction of a hazardous chemical, biological, or radiological substance into a facility or the shared systems that serve it — the potable-water supply, the air-handling and HVAC circuit, food-service or common consumables, or other distribution paths that carry the contaminant to occupants. This tactic captures the act of contamination as a defender observes it: a substance being placed into a system that serves people, tampering at the access point that feeds such a system, or the downstream signs that a release is underway. Distinct from Systems Sabotage (TF0304), which disables or weaponizes building systems for their mechanical effect; here the system is the delivery path and persons are exposed to the contaminant itself. When the facility is occupied, contamination of its air or water applies direct physical force to everyone the system serves.
tactics.cpn_notes: Contamination targeting is increasingly informed by publicly exposed facility engineering detail — permitting records, mechanical drawings, water-utility schematics, and building-automation portals that reveal where a facility draws air and water, where intakes and access points sit, and which zones a single injection point would reach.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, physical evidence of a substance or tampering at a system that serves occupants, and recoverable reporting that ties the actor to the access point. Credibility falls when the signal is a single uncorroborated report, when the observed material admits a benign maintenance explanation, and when no exposure pathway to persons was ever established.
high_signal_anchors: Physical evidence at the delivery point — a foreign container, residue, or introduced substance recovered at a water intake, HVAC air intake, mechanical room, or food-service line that serves the facility's occupants.
Cross-modal corroboration — tampering evidence, an actor placed at the access point on CCTV, and a stated hazardous-materials grievance within overlapping timeframes.
Downstream confirmation — laboratory or sensor confirmation of an out-of-range contaminant in the water, air, or consumables the facility distributes.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who saw the actor at a restricted utility or mechanical access point and reported it through a formal channel with time and location.
Behavioral specificity — the actor's interest concentrated on the specific system that reaches occupants (which intake, which zone, when the building is full) rather than a vague hazard reference.
Material acquisition consistent with the pathway — evidence the actor obtained access credentials, keys, or protective equipment appropriate to reaching a served system.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip about 'something in the water' that cannot be re-contacted or corroborated.
Benign-material ambiguity — a residue or container at a mechanical space that plausibly belongs to routine maintenance, cleaning, or water treatment and was never chemically characterized.
No established exposure pathway — the observed activity does not connect to any system that actually reaches occupants.
Temporal-pattern weakness — a one-time presence near a utility area with no recurrence and no accompanying signal.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a dispute with facilities staff, a vendor rivalry, or a tenant grievance that supplies a reason to embellish.
Reconstructive memory — a long reporting delay during which an ordinary odor or illness was retrofitted to a contamination narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the actor demonstrates the access, materials, and technical literacy to place a hazardous substance into a system that reaches occupants — restricted access to intakes or mechanical spaces, handling that suggests a genuinely harmful agent, and understanding of how a facility's distribution carries a contaminant. Capability falls with no path to a served system, conspicuous behavior at the access point, and materials that pose no real exposure hazard.
high_signal_anchors: Restricted-system access — the actor reaches a water intake, HVAC air-handling unit, mechanical room, chemical-feed system, or food-service area that is not open to the public.
Insider or credentialed access being used — an employee, contractor, or vendor role gives the actor legitimate reach to the served system, defeating access controls.
Handling discipline consistent with a real hazard — the actor uses protective equipment, containment, or careful transfer behavior appropriate to a genuinely dangerous agent.
Demonstrated system literacy — the actor reasons correctly about which injection point reaches which occupied zone and about occupancy timing that maximizes exposure.
Covert introduction tradecraft — the substance is introduced without disrupting normal system operation, so the delivery path keeps carrying it undetected.
Counter-detection behavior — the actor times introduction to defeat routine water testing, filter changes, or air-quality monitoring windows.
low_signal_anchors: No path to a served system — the actor reached only public areas with no connection to air, water, or consumables that distribute to occupants.
Conspicuous access attempt — obvious forcing of a mechanical door or lingering at an intake in the open, immediately recognizable as unusual.
Non-hazardous material — the introduced or referenced substance poses no meaningful exposure risk (dye, nuisance odorant, inert powder).
No system literacy — the actor's chosen point does not actually reach occupants, revealing a misunderstanding of the distribution path.
Single-point, single-attempt behavior — one clumsy attempt with no concealment and no understanding of testing or filtration.
Access defeated at first contact — controls, seals, or staff challenge stopped the actor before any served system was reached.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the actor's engagement progresses from interest in facility systems toward the specific act of placing a harmful substance where it reaches people, when occupancy timing is chosen to maximize exposure, and when the behavior pairs with a stated grievance about the facility, its water, its air, or its function. Intent falls with generic hazardous-materials interest, activity that does not connect to a served system, and a verifiable legitimate purpose at the mechanical space.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression toward the delivery act — an observable move from studying facility systems to positioning at, or introducing material into, the point that reaches occupants.
Occupancy-timed action — the actor acts when the building is full or when the served zone is most heavily used, revealing exposure of persons as the objective.
Concentration on the served pathway — attention fixed on the specific intake, zone, or consumable line that distributes to people, not on mechanical damage for its own sake.

Hostile attribution paired with system access — the actor has voiced grievance toward the facility, its occupants, or what it represents AND is observed reaching or tampering with a system that serves them; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
Concealment of the introduction — steps taken so the release continues undetected imply intent to expose occupants over time rather than to make a statement.
Retention of pathway intelligence — saved schematics, intake photos, or notes on occupancy and testing windows, suggesting a planned delivery rather than idle interest.
low_signal_anchors: Generic hazard interest — broad curiosity about chemicals or water safety not pinned to introducing a substance into this facility's served systems.
No connection to occupants — activity touches systems that do not distribute to people, or an empty, decommissioned pathway.
One-time encounter without escalation — presence near a mechanical space surfaced once with no follow-through or pattern.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — water-treatment, HVAC-maintenance, pest-control, or inspection role surfaces and checks out.
No retention behavior — system information viewed casually but not saved, organized, or paired with timing intelligence.
Statement without means — expressed desire to 'poison' the place with no observed access to any served system.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can reach a system that distributes to occupants — combining access to intakes or mechanical spaces, knowledge of which point reaches which zone, mastery of occupancy and testing windows, and exploited insider access. Opportunity falls with hardened and monitored access points, backflow and filtration barriers not defeated, and testing regimes the actor cannot evade; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: Unimpeded reach to a served system — the actor accesses a water intake, air-handling unit, or consumables line without encountering effective barriers.

Insider connection being exploited — an identified employee, contractor, or vendor relationship the actor is actively leveraging for access to mechanical or distribution systems. The exploitation pattern, not a dormant credential, is the high-signal element.
Distribution-path mastery — the actor reliably knows which injection point reaches which occupied zone, and how far and fast the contaminant would carry.
Occupancy- and testing-window knowledge — the actor knows when the building is full and when water testing, filter changes, or air monitoring occur, and can time introduction to the gap.
Physical proximity during vulnerable windows — the actor is present at the facility during service, delivery, or low-oversight periods that expose the access point.
Direct system access through a legitimate role — the actor has unsupervised access to intakes, mechanical rooms, or food service as part of an authorized function.
low_signal_anchors: Hardened, monitored access points — secured, sealed, and alarmed intakes and mechanical spaces actively blocked the actor's reach. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor materially adapts or the posture drops.
Barrier not defeated — backflow prevention, filtration, treatment, or tamper-evident sealing stopped or would neutralize the introduction, and the actor has not overcome it.
Institutional rule-out of insider access — access audits or process actively cleared the credentialed-access possibility, not merely failed to find it.
Testing regime the actor cannot evade — continuous or frequent water and air monitoring would detect an introduction before meaningful exposure, and the actor has no way around it.
Structural access degradation — the actor's prior access pathway terminated (role ended, contract lapsed, area re-secured).
Defensive friction encountered without adaptation — the actor was challenged at a mechanical space and left without returning or adapting. Transient: may flip if the actor adapts.

false_positive_context.criteria: Many legitimate activities resemble contamination on the surface — a water-treatment technician adding chemicals to a feed system looks similar to an actor injecting a contaminant; a maintenance worker at a rooftop air handler looks similar to tampering. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the person has a verifiable legitimate purpose, an accountable identity behind the access, and the substances and behaviors are consistent with authorized facility operations.
contexts: Authorized building-systems work — water-treatment operators, HVAC and mechanical technicians, plumbers, and pest-control professionals performing scheduled or on-call service with proper credentials and work orders.

Utility and regulatory activity — municipal water and utility crews, public-health inspectors, and environmental samplers conducting authorized testing, flushing, or maintenance at intakes and distribution points.
Food-service operations — catering, cafeteria, and vending personnel handling and stocking consumables as part of normal facility service.
Emergency and remediation response — hazmat, restoration, mold-remediation, and industrial-hygiene contractors working a known incident with documented authorization.
Ordinary anomalies — chlorination odor, new-filter smell, discolored water after main work, or seasonal illness clusters that mimic exposure signs but resolve to benign causes on assessment.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Any indicator that a hazardous substance has been introduced into an occupied facility's air, water, or consumables warrants immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier — contamination applies force to everyone the system serves, and the exposure window closes only when the pathway is isolated. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: whether an exposure pathway to occupants is established, the credibility of the tampering or release signal, and confirmation of the substance. A vague report near a mechanical space with no established pathway sits at the monitoring tier. Observed tampering at a served system's access point without confirmed release sits at the investigation-and-precaution tier and warrants isolating and sampling the pathway. A confirmed foreign substance at a water intake, air handler, or consumables line, or downstream sensor or symptom indications, sits at the immediate-response tier: isolate the system, shut down or divert the pathway, protect and evacuate or shelter occupants, and coordinate hazmat, EMS, and public health. Multiple lower-priority indicators correlating temporally or modally — a grievance about the facility's occupants, an actor placed at an intake, and an unexplained odor — may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers logging and pathway review; investigation triggers actor-identification, access-point inspection, and precautionary sampling; immediate-response triggers system isolation, occupant protection, and integrated hazmat and public-health coordination; a confirmed release in an occupied facility warrants urgent law-enforcement and public-health notification at any tier.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor introduces a hazardous substance into the facility's potable-water supply or a water system that distributes to occupants, exposing everyone the system serves
Threat actor introduces a hazardous substance into the facility's air-handling or HVAC system, dispersing the contaminant through occupied zones served by the circuit

Threat actor is observed tampering at a served-system access point — a water intake, HVAC outdoor-air intake, mechanical room, or chemical-feed system — with an unexplained substance, container, or residue present but no confirmed release
Threat actor introduces a hazardous substance into food-service stock, a cafeteria line, or common consumables in the occupied facility, exposing persons who consume them

Occupants exhibit acute symptoms consistent with an airborne or waterborne exposure, or an unexplained odor, discoloration, or residue appears at a distribution point, indicating a contaminant release is underway in the occupied facility

countermeasures.measure: Deploy continuous water-quality monitoring (residual, turbidity, and contaminant sensing) with backflow prevention on the facility's potable and distributed water systems, alarmed to security and facilities operations
countermeasures.limitations: Sensors cover known contaminants and sampling points; a novel agent or an injection downstream of the monitored point may reach occupants before detection, and alarms require a staffed response to be actionable

countermeasures.measure: Harden and control access to served-system points — secure, seal, and alarm water intakes, outdoor-air intakes, mechanical rooms, and chemical-feed systems, with tamper-evident measures and logged entry
countermeasures.limitations: Raises the effort to reach a delivery point but does not stop a credentialed insider or authorized contractor; roof and grounds intakes are difficult to fully enclose without impairing operation

countermeasures.measure: Protect the air-handling circuit — elevate and screen outdoor-air intakes, add filtration appropriate to the threat, install air monitoring, and provide an emergency HVAC shutdown and zone-isolation capability accessible to responders
countermeasures.limitations: Filtration and elevated intakes reduce but do not eliminate exposure; internal introduction downstream of filtration bypasses these controls, and rapid shutdown depends on early recognition of a release

countermeasures.measure: Maintain a chemical-biological-radiological incident response plan integrating system isolation, shelter-or-evacuate decision criteria, decontamination, and pre-established coordination with EMS, hazmat, and public health, exercised periodically
countermeasures.limitations: A plan governs response speed and coordination but cannot prevent introduction; effectiveness depends on early recognition of exposure and on staff and partners executing under uncertainty

response_protocols.trigger: Confirmed or strongly indicated introduction of a hazardous substance into an occupied facility's air, water, or consumables — a foreign substance at a distribution point, sensor alarm, or occupants showing acute exposure symptoms
response_protocols.action: Activate the CBR incident response immediately. Isolate the affected system: shut down or divert HVAC and isolate the served zones, close or bypass the affected water segment, and pull suspect consumables from service. Protect occupants per the exposure pathway — shelter or evacuate away from the release. Summon EMS and hazmat, notify public health and law enforcement, and preserve the scene and any container or residue for characterization. Do not clear the pathway for reuse until sampling confirms it is safe.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Confirmation of a genuinely hazardous agent, multiple exposed occupants, or a second distribution point implicated
response_protocols.legal_notes: A contaminant release is a mass-casualty and public-health emergency; public-health and law-enforcement notification obligations attach. Preserve evidence and chain of custody while prioritizing life safety; document decontamination and exposure records for responder and occupant health follow-up.

response_protocols.trigger: Observed tampering, or discovery of an unexplained substance or container, at a served-system access point without a confirmed release (water intake, air handler, mechanical room, food-service line)
response_protocols.action: Isolate and preserve the access point without disturbing the material. Precautionarily take the served pathway out of use — divert or stop the affected water segment, isolate the HVAC zone, or hold suspect consumables — and restrict the area. Arrange sampling and hazmat assessment before any resumption, and evacuate or shelter the potentially affected zone as a precaution pending characterization. Review access logs and CCTV to identify the actor and any prior approaches.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Sampling confirms a hazardous substance, a served pathway is confirmed contaminated, or occupants begin reporting symptoms
response_protocols.legal_notes: Precautionary shutdown of building systems is within facility authority; document the threat basis to support the disruption and any resumption decision. Coordinate with counsel and public health before communicating exposure risk to occupants.

tactics.field_notes: Contamination is the facility tactic that turns the building's own systems against the people inside it — the air and water that serve occupants become the delivery path. The defining move is introducing a hazardous substance where the distribution carries it to persons, which is why the same act reads as force applied to everyone the system serves when the building is occupied. The hardest problem is recognition: a covert introduction may leave no immediate sign, so the first indicator is often downstream — an odor, discolored water, or a cluster of occupants with acute symptoms — by which point exposure is already underway. That drives the emphasis on monitoring at the distribution points and on hardening the small number of access points, intakes, and mechanical spaces that reach the whole population. Insider and credentialed access is the recurring enabler, because the people authorized to service water, air, and food systems are precisely the people positioned to contaminate them. Most legitimate activity at these systems is routine maintenance, so the discriminators are an established exposure pathway to occupants, a substance that is actually hazardous, and behavior timed to reach people rather than to service the equipment.
observed_contexts: actor with contractor access observed at a rooftop air-handling unit outside any scheduled work window, later tied to a grievance against the building's occupants
unexplained container and residue discovered at a potable-water intake serving an occupied building, prompting precautionary shutdown and sampling
cluster of occupants reporting acute symptoms consistent with a waterborne exposure, isolating the served zone before the pathway was characterized
[literature: NIOSH-BLDG-CBR-2002 / FEMA-426-2011 pattern — introduction of a CBR agent into building air or water systems to expose occupants through the facility's own distribution]

tactics.name: Response Suppression
tactics.notes: Deliberate defeat or delay of the emergency and security response during an attack on a facility, so that the primary act — fire, explosion, armed assault, structural or systems sabotage — runs longer and reaches more people before help arrives. Observable forms include blocking, chaining, barricading, or locking emergency exits to trap occupants; disabling or sabotaging fire alarms and suppression systems; jamming, cutting, or degrading emergency communications and duress alarms; emplacing secondary devices or hazards positioned to strike arriving responders; and overpowering or neutralizing on-site security. Distinct from Systems Sabotage (TF0304), which weaponizes or disables building systems as the attack itself; here the disablement is in service of a concurrent attack, aimed at the response rather than at the structure. Response suppression is force-multiplying: it converts a survivable event into a mass-casualty one by attacking the site's ability to protect and evacuate.
tactics.cpn_notes: Response suppression is increasingly informed by online reconnaissance — published fire-evacuation and life-safety plans, permitting records exposing alarm and suppression layouts, vendor and monitoring-service disclosures, and open discussion of local emergency response times — all of which let an actor plan which exits to block, which systems to disable, and how long a delay their method needs before any physical presence at the site.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, persistence over time, and recoverable evidence that the actor's engagement with the facility is oriented toward defeating its response — not merely reaching or damaging it. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when a plausible operational, maintenance, or life-safety-testing explanation for interest in exits, alarms, or suppression was never ruled out.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — statements about trapping occupants or delaying help, research into the site's alarms and response times, and physical interest in exits and system panels within overlapping timeframes.
Temporal persistence — attention to the facility's response posture observed across weeks to months, not a single remark or visit.
Material evidence — saved evacuation plans, annotated exit maps, notes on alarm or suppression locations, or communications naming how the response would be delayed.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who heard the actor describe blocking exits, killing the alarms, or hitting responders, with high-resolution reporting of statement, context, and timing.
Behavioral specificity — the actor identified specific egress doors, specific panels or systems, or specific response units rather than a vague intent to 'stop them getting out.'
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — trained reporter through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip, reporter cannot be re-contacted.
Content-specificity weakness — a vague statement that 'no one should get out' with no reference to any specific exit, system, or method.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one-time remark with no follow-through or corroborating behavior.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to embellish (labor dispute, tenant rivalry, litigation over the facility's safety).

Unrebutted legitimate explanation — interest in exits, alarms, or suppression admits a benign reading (facilities staff, fire-safety contractor, inspector, tenant drill) that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that details may be retrofitted to a threat narrative after an unrelated scare.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the actor's engagement shows the technical literacy and access to actually defeat a response — knowing where suppression risers and alarm panels sit, how to chain or defeat egress hardware, how to degrade the site's communications, and how responders will approach. Capability falls with conspicuous, uninformed behavior, OSINT-only reach, and methods that any supervised life-safety system would catch on first attempt.
high_signal_anchors: Life-safety system literacy — the actor reasons correctly about which alarm, suppression, or notification path to disable and in what order to maximize delay.
Egress-defeat knowledge — familiarity with exit hardware, door-position monitoring, and which doors are load-bearing for evacuation of an occupied space.
Restricted-material acquisition — the actor obtains non-public evacuation plans, alarm and suppression schematics, or monitoring-service detail for the facility.
Responder-model awareness — the actor understands local response times and ingress routes and positions to exploit them, indicating secondary-hazard capability.
Communications-degradation means — evidence the actor can jam, cut, or spoof the site's radio, cellular, landline, or duress paths.
Insider or vendor access — the actor holds or exploits a role (facilities, security, fire-service contractor) giving hands-on reach to the very systems that would sound the alarm.
low_signal_anchors: Conspicuous posture — obvious tampering with exits or panels in the open, with no concealment or pretext.
System-naive behavior — the actor targets the wrong hardware or misunderstands how the alarm or suppression is supervised.
Pretext failure on initial contact — staff immediately recognized interest in exits or systems as unusual.
OSINT-only reach — all knowledge of the site's response posture is from public sources; no operational reach to the hardware.
Single-modality engagement — only digital research or only physical loitering; no coordination toward a suppression method.
No means of degradation — intent to 'block the exits' or 'cut the alarms' with no observed tools, access, or technical means to do so.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when engagement moves from interest in the facility toward operationally specific attention to its response — which exits, which systems, which responders — and is paired with a concurrent-attack posture or grievance. Intent falls with generic safety curiosity, encounters that do not escalate, and a verifiable legitimate role in the site's life-safety program.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression broad-to-narrow — an observable funnel from general interest in the site toward operational detail about its exits, alarms, suppression, or response timing.
Response-specific behavior — attention concentrates on how occupants would leave and how help would arrive, not just on how to reach or damage the structure.
Operational specificity — asking about or documenting exit locking, alarm silencing, sprinkler shutoff, monitoring-service response, or fire-lane and ingress routes.
Pairing with a concurrent method — response-defeat interest observed alongside accelerant, explosive, weapon, or breaching preparation against the same site.
Retention of acquired materials — evacuation plans archived, panel photos saved, response-time notes maintained, suggesting operational use.

Hostile framing paired with suppression detail — the actor has expressed intent to maximize harm or 'make sure no one gets out' AND is observed researching or handling the site's response systems; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
low_signal_anchors: Generic-safety interest — broad curiosity about fire safety or emergency planning not pinned to defeating a specific site's response.
One-time encounter without escalation — interest surfaced but no follow-through, pairing, or pattern.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — facilities, inspection, drill, or fire-service relationship surfaces and checks out.
No retention behavior — plans or panels observed casually but not saved or organized.
Method ambiguity — interest in the site with no orientation toward its response, exits, or systems.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can actually reach and defeat the response — unsupervised access to exits and system panels during occupied hours, knowledge of monitoring gaps and response times, and the positional ability to be present as the concurrent attack runs. Opportunity falls with supervised life-safety systems, hardened egress, tamper alarms, and rapid mutual-aid response the actor has not adapted to; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: No defensive friction encountered — the actor's access to exits, panels, or communications paths continues unimpeded despite the facility's posture.
Occupancy-window mastery — the actor reliably knows when the site is fullest, so blocking egress or delaying response maximizes exposure. The informational dimension of opportunity.
System- and monitoring-gap knowledge — the actor knows which alarms are supervised, which exits are unmonitored, and how long an off-site monitoring service takes to react.

Insider connection being exploited — an identified employee, contractor, or vendor relationship the actor is actively leveraging for access to exits, panels, or duress systems. Dormant connections are potential, not realized; the exploitation pattern is high-signal.
Geographic-temporal proximity — the actor is present during the site's vulnerable, high-occupancy windows and near responder ingress routes.
Direct system access — the actor has unsupervised, legitimate-role access to the very life-safety and communications systems that must fail for the attack to succeed.
low_signal_anchors: Approach defeated by hardened posture — supervised alarms, tamper-alarmed egress, or resilient communications actively blocked the actor's method. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor materially adapts.
Institutional rule-out of insider access — access audits or process actively cleared reach to exits and system panels, not merely failed to find it.
Structural access degradation — the actor's prior access pathway terminated (role ended, contract lapsed, relocation).
Defensive friction encountered without adaptation — the actor abandoned a tamper attempt after it alarmed and did not return or adapt. Transient: may flip if the actor adapts.
Rapid response not defeasible — mutual-aid and monitoring response is fast and redundant enough that the actor's planned delay is not achievable; transient unless the actor finds a workaround.
Posture change created barriers — supervised systems, changed occupancy schedules, or added egress monitoring block the actor's known methods; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Much legitimate activity resembles response suppression on the surface — a fire-safety contractor takes suppression offline for service; a facilities worker props or secures exits; an inspector photographs alarm panels; a drill temporarily silences alarms. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the underlying activity has a verifiable legitimate purpose, a transparent and accountable identity behind it, and coordination with the site's own life-safety program.
contexts: Authorized life-safety work — fire-alarm and sprinkler contractors, alarm-monitoring technicians, and inspectors servicing, testing, or certifying systems, which routinely takes them briefly offline under a work order.
Facilities and building operations — staff securing, propping, or maintaining exit hardware, door controllers, and egress paths as part of normal operations.
Sanctioned drills and testing — scheduled fire drills, evacuation exercises, and alarm tests that silence alarms or route occupants through specific exits under supervision.
Authorized security operations — guards controlling access and egress during a lawful lockdown, medical event, or police action at the facility.
Utility and communications work — carriers or contractors working on radio, cellular, or landline infrastructure that can transiently degrade site communications.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Response suppression is an execution-phase, life-safety tactic: any credible indication that egress is being blocked, that life-safety systems are being disabled, that a secondary hazard is staged for responders, or that on-site security is being neutralized during a concurrent attack warrants immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier — because the harm it enables is measured in occupant lives and responder lives. Tier-determination for pre-incident findings depends on three factors: credibility of the indicator, breadth across modalities, and pairing with a concurrent attack method. A single low-credibility indicator with an available legitimate explanation (contractor, drill, facilities work) sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility indicator with operational specificity about the site's exits, systems, or response sits at the investigation tier. Response-defeat interest paired with accelerant, explosive, weapon, or breaching preparation against the same site sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as an imminent mass-casualty plot. Indicators persisting despite implemented countermeasures sit at the committed-actor tier. In-progress indicators — exits found chained during an incident, alarms or suppression confirmed disabled, a secondary device reported, communications jammed — are not assessment findings but active mass-casualty conditions and trigger the full emergency response immediately. A confirmed actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor blocks, chains, barricades, or locks the emergency exits of an occupied facility to trap occupants inside during a concurrent attack
Threat actor disables or sabotages the facility's fire alarms or suppression systems (silencing panels, closing sprinkler valves, defeating detectors) ahead of or during an attack on an occupied site
Threat actor emplaces a secondary device or hazard positioned at ingress routes, staging areas, or evacuation paths to strike arriving emergency responders
Threat actor jams, cuts, or degrades the facility's emergency communications — radio, cellular, landline, or duress and panic alarms — to delay notification and response during an attack
Threat actor overpowers, disarms, or neutralizes the facility's on-site security personnel to remove the site's first line of response during the attack

countermeasures.measure: Maintain fire-code-compliant emergency egress that cannot be chained, barricaded, or locked against evacuation, with door-position and tamper monitoring so any attempt to defeat an exit generates an immediate alarm
countermeasures.limitations: Life-safety codes require exits to remain openable from inside, but improvised external blocking (vehicles, chains, debris) can still trap occupants; monitoring detects tampering but does not physically prevent it

countermeasures.measure: Supervise fire alarm, suppression, and detection systems with tamper detection and independent off-site monitoring so that silencing a panel, closing a valve, or defeating a detector triggers an alert rather than a silent failure
countermeasures.limitations: Monitoring shortens the window between disablement and notice but does not restore the disabled function; an insider with legitimate system access may defeat supervision or mask the tamper as routine service

countermeasures.measure: Adopt a secondary-hazard and responder-safety protocol — train security and coordinate with fire, EMS, and law enforcement on secondary-device awareness, staged and controlled ingress, and pre-planned alternate approach routes to occupied areas
countermeasures.limitations: A controlled, staged approach that protects responders can also lengthen time-to-aid for trapped occupants; effectiveness depends on realistic joint exercises and on responders actually recognizing a staged hazard under pressure

countermeasures.measure: Provide redundant, out-of-band emergency communications — cellular, landline, radio, and a manual runner protocol — hardened against jamming or line-cut, so that disabling any single path does not silence the alarm or the call for help
countermeasures.limitations: Redundant paths add cost and maintenance and can drift out of readiness if not exercised; a sufficiently broad jamming or infrastructure attack can degrade several paths at once, leaving only the manual fallback
