response_protocols.trigger: Indication during an incident that emergency egress is being blocked or that fire alarm or suppression systems have been disabled at an occupied facility (exits found chained, panels silenced, sprinklers valved off, or a supervised-system tamper alarm during an active event)
response_protocols.action: Treat as an active mass-casualty condition immediately. Force a full multi-agency emergency response and do not rely on the facility's own alarms or notification. Direct occupants to alternate, verified egress; assign staff or security to clear and hold usable exits; report the specific blocked exits and disabled systems to incoming responders so they can plan rescue and controlled entry. Preserve the scene for investigation once life-safety is secured.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Occupants confirmed trapped, secondary hazard suspected, or the concurrent attack method (fire, explosive, armed assault) confirmed in progress
response_protocols.legal_notes: Overriding locked or secured egress and directing evacuation are within emergency authority; document the life-safety basis and system state observed. Preservation of tampered systems supports later arson, terrorism, or reckless-endangerment prosecution.

response_protocols.trigger: Indication that a secondary device or hazard is staged for responders, that on-site security has been neutralized, or that emergency communications have been jammed or cut during an attack
response_protocols.action: Halt uncontrolled ingress and establish a controlled, staged approach with law-enforcement and bomb-squad/EOD support before committing responders to the affected area. Work around degraded communications using pre-planned redundant and out-of-band paths and a runner protocol. Account for and reinforce any neutralized on-site security. Sweep responder ingress routes and staging areas for secondary hazards before massing personnel.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Secondary device confirmed, responder casualty, or communications loss preventing coordination across responding units
response_protocols.legal_notes: Staged approach and controlled ingress are standard incident-command authority; document the secondary-hazard basis for any delay in reaching occupants to defend proportionality. Coordinate custody of any secondary device or jamming equipment with law enforcement.

tactics.field_notes: Response suppression is what turns a bad day into a massacre, and it is usually the most premeditated part of an attack — you do not chain a fire exit or silence a sprinkler panel on impulse. The clearest tells are physical and in-the-moment: an exit that will not open, an alarm that never sounded, a security officer down before the shooting started, radios that go to static. Backward from the act, the diagnostic signal is interest in the response rather than the target — an actor who asks about how people get out, how fast the fire department arrives, where the panels are, and who is on the desk at night. Blocking exits on an occupied building and staging hazards for responders are the two behaviors that most reliably signal an intent to maximize casualties, and both should be treated as critical the instant they appear. The hard part for defenders is that the same actions look identical to legitimate life-safety work — a contractor takes suppression offline every week under a work order — so the discriminators are accountability, authorization, and whether the activity pairs with any concurrent attack preparation.
observed_contexts: arson case at an occupied premises where the actor chained a rear fire exit before igniting near the only other egress
plot in which an actor mapped the site's alarm-monitoring service and planned to silence the panel so an off-site responder would not be dispatched
attack planning that included a secondary device staged at the parking-area ingress to strike arriving fire and police units
[literature: FEMA-426-2011 / CISA-BOMBTHREAT-2023 pattern — secondary devices and defeated life-safety systems used to extend an attack and target responders]

tactics.name: Withdrawal
tactics.notes: Departure from the site after the act — the actor's movement away from the facility along an escape route, using pre-planned egress, transportation switches, appearance changes, crowd cover, and distance to break the trail and defeat pursuit. Distinct from Evidence Management (which handles what is left at or removed from the scene) and from Cover Reestablishment (which restores a normal legend once clear of the area). Withdrawal is about getting off the X: how the actor leaves, where they go, and how the exit was prepared. The primary harm is already done; withdrawal behaviors determine whether the actor escapes attribution and remains free to act again.
tactics.cpn_notes: Egress is increasingly planned and executed with digital assistance — real-time mapping and traffic apps, police-scanner and emergency-frequency monitoring, and geolocation-aware route selection that avoids license-plate readers and known camera corridors. Counter-tracking discipline (leaving phones behind, disabling location services, cash-only transportation) is likewise informed by publicly circulated tradecraft, and recovered devices or route data often expose a reconnoitered escape path after the fact.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, persistence of a reconstructable escape pattern, and recoverable evidence backing first-hand reports that the actor executed a directed departure rather than a panicked flight. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when a plausible innocent reason for the observed departure — an ordinary evacuee, a passerby leaving the area — was never ruled out.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — camera capture, witness description, and transportation records converging on the same departing individual and vector within overlapping timeframes.
Reconstructable route — the withdrawal path can be traced across multiple fixed points, indicating a deliberate line rather than random dispersal.
Material evidence — recovered mapping, staged or switched vehicles, cached clothing, or device data physically tying the actor to a prepared egress.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who saw the actor move against the flow of evacuation or depart with atypical purpose; high-resolution reporting of the movement, context, and timing.
Behavioral specificity — the departure shows planning artifacts (pre-positioned transportation, appearance change) rather than generic flight.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — trained observer or responder reporting through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip, reporter cannot be re-contacted to clarify the direction or manner of departure.
Content-specificity weakness — a vague account of 'someone running' that could fit any of dozens of evacuees.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one fleeting sighting with no second fixed point to establish a vector.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to embellish (proximity dispute, media incentive, litigation).
Unrebutted legitimate explanation — the departure admits a benign reading (ordinary evacuee, delivery driver leaving) that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that the manner of departure may be retrofitted to a threat narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the withdrawal shows operational discipline — a rehearsed route, transportation switches, appearance changes, counter-tracking measures, and the composure to execute them under post-attack conditions. Capability falls with disorganized flight, reliance on a single traceable conveyance, and departures that collapse the moment they meet friction.
high_signal_anchors: Rehearsed egress execution — the actor moves along a pre-planned route with evident familiarity, not improvisation.
Multi-stage break of the trail — switch vehicle, changed clothing, or transfer to alternate transportation to defeat continuous tracking.
Counter-tracking tradecraft — avoidance of camera corridors and plate readers, phones left behind, location services disabled, cash transportation.
Pre-positioned resources — staged vehicles, cached supplies, or a prepared safe location established before the act.
Composure under duress — the actor maintains a disciplined departure amid alarm, evacuation, and emergency response rather than fleeing conspicuously.
Demonstrated route literacy — the actor exploits terrain, jurisdiction seams, and low-observation corridors, reasoning about pursuit and interdiction.
low_signal_anchors: Conspicuous flight — visible sprinting from the point of act along the most obvious line, drawing attention.
Single-conveyance dependence — one traceable vehicle or transit method with no switch or fallback.
No counter-tracking — the actor carries an active phone, uses traceable payment, and transits monitored corridors.
Route collapse on friction — the departure fails at the first checkpoint, obstacle, or challenge.
Improvised dispersal — no evidence of prior route planning; the actor simply ran in an available direction.
Self-identifying behavior during egress — the actor draws attention through erratic movement, discarded items, or contact with bystanders that fixes identity.

intent.criteria: Intent to escape attribution and preserve freedom of action rises when the departure is planned and deliberate, when the actor invested in egress preparation before the act, and when withdrawal is paired with measures to defeat identification. Intent falls with panicked, unplanned flight, with immediate surrender or self-exposure, and with a verifiable innocent reason for leaving the area.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression prepared-to-executed — an observable link between pre-attack egress reconnaissance and the manner of the actual departure.
Escape-specific behavior — attention and preparation concentrated on getting clear of the site and evading pursuit, not on the act alone.
Operational specificity in egress — staged transportation, reconnoitered routes, timed to evacuation or response windows, cross-jurisdiction planning.
Sustained evasion posture — the actor continues to break the trail and adapt as pursuit develops, over hours to days.
Retention of escape infrastructure — a maintained safe location, prepared documents, or cached resources suggesting a durable evasion plan.

Freedom-of-action framing paired with egress — the actor prepared to survive and remain at large (rather than expecting capture or self-destruction) AND executed a disciplined withdrawal; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
low_signal_anchors: Panic flight — undirected movement away from danger consistent with any frightened occupant.
Immediate self-exposure — the actor surrenders, remains at the scene, or announces presence, inconsistent with an evasion objective.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — an evacuee, responder, or passerby role surfaces and checks out.
No preparation behavior — departure shows no staged resources, route knowledge, or counter-tracking.
Direction ambiguity — movement lacks any consistent vector or destination logic.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity to complete the withdrawal rises when the actor can convert planning into distance — mastery of egress routes and timing, exploitable gaps in perimeter containment, available transportation, and the positional ability to reach a safe location. Opportunity falls with responsive containment not adapted to, distance not closed, or interdiction that blocks the actor's known routes; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: No containment friction encountered — the actor's departure proceeds unimpeded before a perimeter is established.
Egress pattern-of-life mastery — the actor reliably knows route timing, traffic and response cadence, and low-observation windows around the site. The informational dimension of opportunity.
Containment-gap knowledge — the actor knows camera blind spots, uncovered exits, jurisdiction seams, or interdiction latency along the escape corridor.

Insider or facilitation connection being exploited — an identified driver, host, or logistics contact the actor is actively leveraging to move and shelter. Dormant contacts are potential, not realized; the exploitation pattern is what is high-signal.
Geographic-temporal advantage — the actor timed egress to evacuation or response chaos and had a short, prepared line to cover.
Prepared safe destination — the actor has an established location or jurisdiction offering shelter and reduced pursuit reach.
low_signal_anchors: Egress defeated by rapid containment — perimeter, lockdown, or interdiction actively blocked the departure. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor materially adapts or containment lifts.
Institutional closure of a facilitation route — a driver, host, or transit pathway was actively cleared or removed, not merely unobserved.
Structural degradation of the escape plan — the prepared route or safe location became unavailable (road closure, host withdrawal, surveillance on the destination).
Containment friction encountered without adaptation — the actor was turned back at a choke point and did not re-route or adapt. Transient: may flip if the actor adapts.
Distance not closed — the safe location is remote and completing the escape requires a major movement not yet made.
Posture change created barriers — new perimeter procedures, camera coverage, or interdiction along known routes block the actor's methods; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Many legitimate departures resemble withdrawal on the surface — a frightened occupant fleeing an alarm looks similar to an actor egressing after an act; a delivery driver leaving during an incident looks similar to a staged transportation switch. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the departure has a verifiable legitimate purpose, a transparent identity behind it, or institutional accountability that can be checked against the reconstructed movement.
contexts: Ordinary evacuation — occupants, visitors, and staff leaving the site under alarm, drill, or responder direction, moving with the crowd.
Legitimate transportation activity — delivery, rideshare, transit, and service drivers departing the area on lawful business during or after an incident.
Authorized response movement — law enforcement, fire, EMS, security, and utility personnel moving to, from, and around the scene.
Personal or community connection — neighbors, patrons, and passersby leaving an area of disturbance for ordinary reasons.
Non-threatening presence — bystanders, media, and onlookers whose movement near an incident reflects curiosity or avoidance, not evasion.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Withdrawal findings that correlate with staging-class or force-class behaviors elsewhere — a recovered secondary device or re-attack positioning along the egress route, evidence destruction at the site, or a switch vehicle staged in advance — warrant immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: credibility of the indicator, breadth across modalities, and persistence of a reconstructable escape pattern. A single low-credibility departure sighting with an available legitimate explanation sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility indicator with operational specificity about the egress — a switch vehicle, a reconnoitered route — sits at the investigation tier. Cross-modal corroboration — camera, witness, and transportation records converging on the same vector — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as a planned withdrawal from a premeditated attack. Indicators showing the actor continuing to break the trail despite pursuit sit at the committed-actor tier, indicating an at-large actor retaining freedom of action. Multiple lower-priority indicators correlating temporally or modally may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers logging and pattern-detection; investigation triggers actor-identification and egress-route reconstruction; elevation triggers pursuit and containment coordination with law enforcement; the committed-actor tier triggers cross-jurisdiction interdiction and an at-large-actor advisory; a confirmed actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor departs the scene along a directed line immediately after the act, moving with atypical purpose away from the site rather than sheltering or evacuating with occupants
Threat actor breaks the trail during egress by switching vehicles, changing clothing or appearance, or transferring to alternate transportation away from observed corridors
Post-incident reconstruction reveals a pre-positioned escape route — staged vehicles, cached supplies, or reconnoitered egress paths prepared before the attack
Threat actor exploits evacuation flow and emergency-response confusion to blend with fleeing occupants and exit the perimeter before it is established
Threat actor flees the jurisdiction or goes to ground at a prepared safe location, using distance and time to defeat pursuit and reduce interdiction reach

countermeasures.measure: Establish egress-focused camera and license-plate-reader coverage on likely escape routes and choke points around the facility to capture departure vectors and transportation switches
countermeasures.limitations: Coverage gaps and camera blind spots along secondary corridors remain exploitable; a determined actor who switches vehicles or transits unmonitored routes can still break continuous tracking

countermeasures.measure: Pre-plan and rehearse rapid perimeter containment with local law enforcement — choke-point control, road interdiction, and transit alerts — to shrink the window in which an actor can egress unimpeded
countermeasures.limitations: Containment latency almost always trails a fast, pre-planned departure; effectiveness depends on response time, jurisdiction coordination, and the actor not having already cleared the cordon area

countermeasures.measure: Preserve and rapidly exploit post-incident egress evidence — witness canvassing, camera and plate-reader pulls along escape corridors, and transportation records — to reconstruct the withdrawal path and support pursuit
countermeasures.limitations: Reconstruction is retrospective and cannot recover a departure already completed; value depends on evidence retention windows, prompt canvassing, and cross-jurisdiction data-sharing speed

countermeasures.measure: Harden and monitor secondary exits, loading docks, and vehicle-staging areas that offer covert egress, reducing the availability of unobserved escape paths and staged-transportation positions
countermeasures.limitations: Cannot eliminate egress through public rights-of-way adjacent to the site; hardening back-of-house paths may displace the actor to routes outside facility control

response_protocols.trigger: An attack has occurred and the actor is fleeing or has just fled the scene (directed departure observed, occupant reports, camera capture of an egressing individual)
response_protocols.action: Activate pursuit and containment. (a) Broadcast description, direction of travel, and any vehicle to responders; (b) coordinate law-enforcement interdiction on likely egress routes and choke points; (c) pull camera and license-plate-reader data along the departure corridor; (d) canvass and hold witnesses; (e) preserve escape-path evidence. Watch for a switch vehicle and for secondary-device or re-attack positioning along the route. Document all sourcing.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Indications of a transportation switch, cross-jurisdiction flight, an exploited facilitation network, or a secondary device on the egress route
response_protocols.legal_notes: Pursuit, interdiction, and cross-jurisdiction data requests must rest on a documented investigative basis and follow chain-of-custody for egress evidence. Coordinate authority and jurisdiction with law-enforcement partners before acting; preserve records to support prosecution.

response_protocols.trigger: Post-incident reconstruction indicates a pre-planned egress (staged or switch vehicles, reconnoitered routes, a prepared safe location) or the actor remains at large
response_protocols.action: Feed the reconstructed withdrawal pattern into the investigation and into facility posture review. Issue an at-large-actor advisory as warranted, share egress-vector intelligence with peer facilities and fusion centers, and adapt containment and camera-coverage planning to the demonstrated route. Reassess perimeter and secondary-exit controls against the observed method.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Withdrawal pattern matches a known actor or cell TTP, recurs against peer sites, or the at-large actor shows signs of preparing a further act
response_protocols.legal_notes: Advisories and intelligence-sharing should convey attributable facts and the confidence basis, avoiding premature identification. Document the reconstruction methodology to support proportionate posture changes and any resource requests.

tactics.field_notes: Withdrawal is where premeditation shows most clearly after the fact — a planned attacker gets off the X along a line they already know, and an improviser runs in whatever direction is open. The clearest tells are separation of transportation (a switch vehicle staged a few blocks out), an appearance change, and timing that rides the evacuation and response chaos rather than fighting it. Most of the signal is reconstructed backward from cameras, plate readers, and witness vectors, so evidence-retention windows and prompt canvassing decide how much you recover. Containment almost always trails a fast, prepared egress, which is why the durable value is pattern reconstruction: the route the actor chose, the seams they used, and how to close them before the next one. Panic flight and ordinary evacuation are the dominant false positives — what separates them is a consistent vector, preparation artifacts, and counter-tracking discipline.
observed_contexts: arson case where the actor left along a pre-driven route and switched to a second vehicle two blocks from the site, breaking the camera trail before a perimeter formed
active-assailant incident where the assailant blended into the evacuating crowd and exited the area before responders established containment
utility-facility sabotage followed by cross-jurisdiction flight to a prepared location, with recovered mapping showing reconnoitered egress paths
[literature: FBI-ACTIVESHOOTER-2024 / START-GTD-2020 pattern — planned egress and post-incident flight distinguishing premeditated facility attacks from spontaneous acts]

tactics.name: Evidence Management
tactics.notes: Handling of physical evidence at or removed from the attacked site to frustrate attribution, defeat reconstruction, or misdirect the investigation — removing tools, containers, packaging, and device or accelerant remnants; destroying items in place by burning, crushing, or dissolving; planting false or misleading physical evidence to implicate another party or suggest a different motive or method; and disposing of collected items away from the scene. Distinct from Counter-Forensics (TF0407), which defeats forensic attribution techniques such as accelerant obfuscation, DNA and latent-print denial, and digital scrubbing; TF0402 is the physical handling of the evidence items themselves — what is taken, destroyed, staged, or discarded — rather than the technical defeat of the analysis applied to them. Also distinct from Withdrawal (TF0401), which is the flight itself; evidence management is what the actor does to the material record on the way out.
tactics.cpn_notes: Post-attack evidence handling is increasingly informed and exposed by the same digital environment that documents the attack — actors research what investigators recover from similar scenes, purchase disposal or destruction materials through traceable channels, and are themselves captured by third-party cameras, license-plate readers, and waste-stream records while removing or dumping items. The physical act of managing evidence now leaves a parallel digital trail.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, persistence over time, and recoverable evidence backing first-hand reports that the actor handled, removed, destroyed, or staged physical items at the scene. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when a plausible legitimate reason for the item-handling — cleanup, salvage, personal-property retrieval — was never ruled out.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — scene observations of item removal, recovered disposal materials, and witness accounts of the actor carrying or discarding objects against the same event within overlapping timeframes.
Temporal persistence — a pattern of scene-sanitizing behavior observed across the immediate aftermath and any return visits, not a single ambiguous moment.

Material evidence — recovered dump sites, burn residue from destroyed items, purchase records for solvents or accelerants used on evidence, or third-party imagery physically tying the actor to the handling.

First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who saw the actor collect, burn, bury, or plant items and can describe what, where, and when; high-resolution reporting of the action, context, and timing.
Behavioral specificity — the account names the specific items handled and the disposition (removed, destroyed, planted, dumped) rather than a vague impression of tampering.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — trained responder, investigator, or camera-of-record through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip, reporter cannot be re-contacted or was not present during the aftermath.
Content-specificity weakness — a vague claim that 'someone cleaned up' that could describe ordinary scene disturbance.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one ambiguous observation with no corroborating disposal or destruction evidence.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to allege tampering (insurance dispute, liability, rivalry with the property owner).
Unrebutted legitimate explanation — the item-handling admits a benign reading (first-responder overhaul, owner securing property, salvage) that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that ordinary post-incident disturbance is retrofitted into a tampering narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the actor's evidence handling shows operational discipline — knowing which items are probative, removing or destroying them cleanly, staging convincing false evidence, and using cut-outs or waste streams to break the chain between item and actor. Capability falls with conspicuous, incomplete, or self-implicating handling that leaves the probative material recoverable.
high_signal_anchors: Evidentiary literacy — the actor targets the items that actually matter (initiator remnants, containers, tools, biological traces on objects) rather than sweeping indiscriminately, showing knowledge of what investigators recover.
Clean removal tradecraft — items are collected and carried off without being dropped, and the actor avoids creating a fresh trail of residue or packaging on the egress route.
Effective destruction method — burning, dissolving, crushing, or mechanically reducing items to a state that defeats reconstruction, matched to the material.
Convincing misdirection — planted or staged items are internally consistent with a false motive, method, or attribution and would survive a first-pass reading of the scene.
Disposal through breaks in the chain — use of distant dump sites, waste streams, water, or third parties so the recovered item cannot be walked back to the actor.
Pre-planned handling — destruction or removal materials were staged in advance, indicating the evidence plan was part of the operation rather than improvised.
low_signal_anchors: Conspicuous handling — the actor is seen carrying obvious scene items away in the open or dumping them within view of cameras or witnesses.
Incomplete removal — probative items are missed, dropped on the egress route, or left partially destroyed and still recoverable.
Self-implicating disposal — items are discarded in the actor's own waste, near their residence or vehicle, or in a traceable container.
Implausible staging — planted evidence contradicts the physical facts of the scene and collapses on first examination.
Improvised, single-modality handling — a hasty grab-and-go with no destruction, no disposal plan, and no misdirection.
Handling that adds evidence — the sanitizing effort itself deposits new residue, prints, or purchase records that did not previously exist.

intent.criteria: Intent to evade attribution rises when handling is deliberate, pre-planned, and paired with other consciousness-of-guilt behavior — retention of destruction materials, rehearsed disposal, and staging designed to redirect blame. Intent falls with incidental item movement, handling that has a verifiable innocent purpose, and disturbance consistent with ordinary aftermath rather than concealment.
high_signal_anchors: Deliberate, selective handling — the actor removes or destroys specifically the items that would implicate them while leaving unrelated material, showing purpose rather than panic.
Pre-attack provisioning for the aftermath — destruction or disposal materials acquired or staged before the act, indicating evidence management was planned.
Staging to redirect — false evidence planted to implicate a rival, suggest a different motive, or point the investigation at another method or actor.
Return to sanitize — the actor or a proxy comes back to the scene specifically to retrieve or destroy items left behind, accepting exposure to reduce the evidentiary record.
Retention or concealment of the disposition — the actor keeps a record of what was removed or maintains the dump site, or actively conceals it when questioned.
Consciousness-of-guilt language — statements to co-conspirators or in communications about 'cleaning up,' 'nothing left,' or making it 'look like' something else, paired with the observed handling.
low_signal_anchors: Incidental item movement — objects displaced by the act itself or by flight, not selectively targeted for their evidentiary value.
Verifiable innocent purpose — the handling resolves to legitimate cleanup, salvage, or personal-property retrieval that checks out.
One-time ambiguous disturbance — scene alteration surfaced but shows no pattern, no destruction, and no disposal effort.
No retention or concealment — items were moved but not hidden, destroyed, or disclaimed when the actor was asked.
Ordinary-aftermath consistency — the disturbance matches what any occupant or responder would produce and needs no concealment explanation.
Target ambiguity — it is unclear the handled items had any bearing on attribution at all.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can act on the material record — controlling the scene long enough before responders arrive, holding legitimate access to return, and commanding disposal channels the investigation cannot easily reach. Opportunity falls when response is fast, the scene is quickly secured, or the actor's disposal and return pathways are cut; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: Uncontested dwell time — a gap between the act and first response long enough to collect, destroy, or stage items without interruption.
Scene-control mastery — the actor knows response times, camera coverage, and the window in which the scene remains unsecured, and manages evidence within it.
Legitimate return access — an employee, contractor, or occupant role that lets the actor or a proxy re-enter the site after the act without raising suspicion.
Controlled disposal channels — access to waste streams, remote dump sites, water, incineration, or third parties that place discarded items beyond easy recovery.
Proxy availability — a co-conspirator or unwitting party positioned to carry, destroy, or dump items, distancing the actor from the handling.
Geographic-temporal proximity — the actor lives or works near the site and can manage the scene or a return during its unsecured window.
low_signal_anchors: Rapid response and scene lock-down — responders arrived and secured the scene before meaningful handling was possible. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor secures a return pathway.
Institutional rule-out of return access — access audits or process actively cleared the possibility of an insider re-entering, not merely failed to find it.
Structural access degradation — the actor's prior access pathway to the site terminated (role ended, contract lapsed, relocation).
Disposal channel closed — the actor's dump route, waste stream, or proxy was identified and interdicted; transient unless the actor finds another.
Geographic distance not closed — the actor is remote and any return or disposal run requires a travel investment not yet made.
Surveillance saturation encountered without adaptation — third-party cameras or LPRs covered the egress and disposal routes and the actor did not adapt; transient if the actor changes methods.

false_positive_context.criteria: Much legitimate aftermath activity resembles evidence management on the surface — firefighters overhaul and pull down materials that look like destruction, cleanup crews and property owners remove debris that could be evidence, and lawful investigators handle and remove items by design. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the handling has a verifiable legitimate purpose, a transparent identity behind it, and institutional accountability that can be checked.
contexts: Emergency response operations — firefighters conducting overhaul, EMS and rescue disturbing the scene to reach victims, and utility crews making the site safe; disturbance is a byproduct of saving life and property.

Authorized investigation and recovery — law enforcement, fire and explosives investigators, and forensic technicians collecting and removing items under lawful process and documented chain of custody.
Property owner and insurer activity — owners, managers, and adjusters securing, photographing, and clearing a damaged site as part of legitimate recovery, salvage, and claims work.
Contracted remediation — restoration, hazmat, and cleanup crews removing debris and contaminated material under contract, often before an investigation releases the scene.
Ordinary occupant retrieval — employees or residents recovering personal property from a damaged but accessible site, with no bearing on attribution.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Evidence management is an aftermath tactic: by the time it is observed the primary harm is usually done, and its significance is what it protects and what it may presage. Findings correlating with re-attack positioning — a secondary device, return with materiel, or staging against responders and returning occupants — warrant immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier, because sanitizing behavior can accompany a renewed attack. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: credibility of the indicator, breadth across modalities, and persistence over time. A single low-credibility observation with an available legitimate explanation (responder overhaul, owner cleanup) sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility indicator with operational specificity — selective destruction of probative items, staged false evidence, or a controlled off-site dump — sits at the investigation tier. Cross-modal corroboration — witnessed handling plus recovered disposal materials plus a return to the scene against the same event — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as deliberate attribution-defeat by a disciplined actor. Handling that persists across a return visit or that names a false party sits at the committed-actor tier, indicating an actor investing in impunity and possibly preparing to reoffend. Multiple lower-priority indicators correlating temporally or modally may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers scene-integrity logging and pattern-detection; investigation triggers actor-identification, chain-of-custody protection, and a canvass of disposal routes; elevation triggers evidence-preservation and forensic escalation appropriate to the method; the committed-actor tier triggers re-attack-aware posture and offender-focused coordination; a confirmed actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor removes physical items from the scene before departing — tools, containers, packaging, unspent materials, or device and accelerant remnants — carrying off objects that would tie them to the act
Threat actor destroys physical evidence at the site — burning, crushing, dissolving, or otherwise reducing items to a state intended to defeat reconstruction and analysis
Threat actor plants false or misleading physical evidence — staging items to implicate another party, suggest a different motive, or point investigators toward a different method or actor
Threat actor returns to the site, or dispatches a proxy, after the attack to retrieve or sanitize items left behind, accepting renewed exposure to reduce the evidentiary record

Threat actor disposes of collected evidence away from the scene — discarding, burying, incinerating, or transferring items through waste streams, water, or third parties to break the chain between item and actor

countermeasures.measure: Establish a scene-integrity and chain-of-custody protocol activated at first response — secure the perimeter, restrict access to logged personnel, photograph the undisturbed state, and document every item and its handler before recovery
countermeasures.limitations: Depends on responders arriving before the actor can act and on discipline under emergency conditions; life-safety overhaul and rescue legitimately disturb the scene and can be indistinguishable from destruction at the moment it occurs

countermeasures.measure: Deploy and retain overlapping recorded surveillance covering scene approaches, egress routes, waste and loading areas, and the perimeter, integrated with third-party camera and license-plate-reader canvassing to capture removal, return, and dumping behavior
countermeasures.limitations: Coverage has blind spots and finite retention; a disciplined actor identifies gaps and disposes off-camera, and third-party footage may be overwritten before it is requested

countermeasures.measure: Control post-incident site re-entry — suspend routine access, require identity verification and escort for anyone returning to a released or unreleased scene, and audit access logs for the aftermath window to detect return-to-sanitize behavior
countermeasures.limitations: Cannot fully bar personnel with legitimate recovery roles; an insider with a plausible reason to return may sanitize under cover of authorized activity, and enforcement competes with restoration pressure

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate rapid forensic and disposal-route canvassing — engage fire, explosives, and forensic investigators early, and canvass nearby dumpsters, waste transfer points, water, and remote sites for removed or discarded items before they are lost
countermeasures.limitations: Waste and water disposal channels move and destroy material quickly; canvassing is resource-intensive and may not reach a distant or well-chosen dump site in time

response_protocols.trigger: Indications that physical evidence was removed, destroyed, staged, or dumped in connection with an attacked facility (witnessed handling, missing or altered items, recovered disposal materials)
response_protocols.action: Preserve and reconstruct the material record. (a) Freeze scene access and enforce chain of custody; (b) capture and retain all on-site and third-party surveillance covering the aftermath and egress windows; (c) engage forensic, fire, and explosives investigators to assess destruction and staging; (d) canvass disposal routes — waste, water, remote sites — for removed items; (e) document what is present, missing, and altered against any pre-incident baseline. Treat the evidence-management effort as itself investigable.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Staged evidence names or implicates a specific party, OR removal/destruction is paired with indicators of re-attack positioning or a return to the scene
response_protocols.legal_notes: Chain-of-custody integrity and lawful evidence handling are dispositive for later prosecution; tampering, planting, and destruction may be chargeable offenses in themselves. Coordinate closely with law enforcement and counsel, and do not let restoration or insurance activity compromise the evidentiary record.

response_protocols.trigger: Evidence of a return to the scene, or of staged evidence intended to misdirect the investigation toward a false motive, method, or actor
response_protocols.action: Guard against misdirection and reoffense. Independently validate any evidence that points to a convenient alternative narrative before acting on it; treat a return visit as a potential precursor to renewed activity by upgrading posture and re-attack awareness at the site; audit access logs and identify who had legitimate reason to re-enter; and brief investigators on the specific misdirection so attribution is not prematurely fixed on a planted party.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Return-to-scene resolves to a specific actor, OR misdirection is sophisticated enough to have redirected the investigation
response_protocols.legal_notes: Acting on planted evidence risks a wrongful accusation and downstream liability; document the basis for discounting misleading evidence. Posture upgrades are within facility authority — record the threat basis to support resourcing and proportionality.

tactics.field_notes: Evidence management is read backward from what is missing, altered, or too convenient at the scene, not usually caught in the act. The clearest tells are selectivity and provisioning: an actor who removes or destroys exactly the probative items — the container, the initiator, the tool — while leaving everything else is showing knowledge of what investigators recover, and destruction materials staged in advance say the aftermath was planned, not panicked. Planted evidence is the inverse tell — something that points a little too cleanly at a rival or a different motive deserves independent validation before the investigation commits to it. The two aftermath behaviors that change the risk picture most are a return to the scene and a dump run: the return can precede reoffense and should trigger re-attack awareness, and the dump run is often the one moment the disciplined actor is on someone else's camera. The recurring difficulty is that legitimate aftermath — firefighter overhaul, owner cleanup, lawful recovery — disturbs a scene in ways that look identical to concealment until identity and purpose are checked.
observed_contexts: arson case where the actor removed the accelerant container and ignition materials and burned personal items in a separate location before responders cleared the scene
attack scene where a returning insider used an authorized recovery role to retrieve tools left behind during the act
incident in which items were staged to suggest a rival group's method, briefly redirecting the early investigation before forensic review exposed the inconsistency
[literature: START-GTD-2020 / USFA-ARSON-2021 pattern — post-incident removal and destruction of probative materials complicating attribution at attacked sites]

tactics.name: Cover Reestablishment
tactics.notes: Post-attack return to a normal legend, identity, and routine in order to evade suspicion and defeat attribution. The threat actor sheds the operational persona used to reach or breach the site — the fake vendor role, the uniform, the burner credentials, the disposable device — and reinserts into an ordinary pattern of life: back to work, back to a familiar appearance, back to a plausible whereabouts account. This is the temporal inverse of Cover Construction (TF0108), which builds a pretext for access before the attack; Cover Reestablishment collapses that pretext afterward and restores the actor's baseline identity so that nothing about them reads as unusual after the fact. The objective is impunity through normalcy: the more completely the actor snaps back into an unremarkable routine, the harder it is to tie them to the act.
tactics.cpn_notes: Cover reestablishment is increasingly a digital exercise — operational accounts and burner communications are deleted, dormant 'clean' social profiles are reactivated, location history is scrubbed or spoofed, and the actor curates a normal-looking online footprint that corroborates an innocent post-incident narrative.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises when the signal that a return to normalcy is deceptive rather than genuine is corroborated across modalities, is anchored to the incident window, and is backed by recoverable evidence tying the person to the operational persona they are now shedding. Credibility falls when the sole basis is a subjective read of demeanor, when an innocent explanation for the routine change was never excluded, and when the temporal link to the attack is loose.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — a shed operational persona, an unverifiable alibi, and a scrubbed digital footprint all surfacing for the same person within the incident window.
Temporal anchoring to the event — the return-to-normal behaviors cluster tightly around the attack rather than reflecting a long-standing life change.
Material evidence of the discarded legend — recovered uniforms, credentials, burner devices, or deleted accounts that physically link the person to the pretext used for site access.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who observed the persona before the attack and the abrupt reversion after, reporting the change with specific timing and detail.
Behavioral specificity — the reversion targets exactly the artifacts an investigator would key on (the access role, the whereabouts account, the operational comms), not a diffuse mood shift.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — a trained observer or records custodian reporting through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip that the person 'seems too calm,' with no re-contact possible.
Content-specificity weakness — a vague impression of feigned normalcy that could describe many people processing a nearby incident.
Temporal-pattern weakness — the routine or appearance change predates the attack or reflects an unrelated life event.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to cast suspicion (workplace dispute, rivalry, litigation).
Unrebutted legitimate explanation — the person's calm, absence, or account change admits a benign reading that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that ordinary behavior is retrofitted into a suspicious narrative after the attack became known.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the reestablishment shows operational discipline — a pre-positioned clean identity to snap back into, thorough disposal of the operational persona, a rehearsed and corroborated alibi, and counter-forensic handling of digital traces. Capability falls when the reversion is improvised, when operational artifacts are retained or clumsily discarded, and when the alibi collapses on first check.
high_signal_anchors: Pre-positioned clean legend — a maintained legitimate identity and routine prepared in advance for the actor to return to without friction.
Thorough persona disposal — operational clothing, credentials, and burner devices are destroyed or removed rather than merely set aside.
Rehearsed, corroborated alibi — the whereabouts account is internally consistent, supported by cooperating third parties, and resistant to timeline pressure.
Digital counter-attribution literacy — operational accounts deleted, location history scrubbed or spoofed, dormant clean profiles reactivated to backstop the innocent narrative.
Compartmentation of the two identities — no observable bleed between the operational persona and the restored baseline (separate devices, contacts, financial rails).
Composed performance under scrutiny — the person sustains the normal legend through questioning, community response, or media attention without decompensating.
low_signal_anchors: Improvised reversion — the return to normal is hasty and inconsistent, betraying no prepared clean identity.
Retained operational artifacts — uniform, credentials, or burner device kept, or discarded where they are trivially recoverable and attributable.
Alibi failure on first check — the whereabouts account contradicts CCTV, access logs, or device telemetry immediately.
Identity bleed — the operational persona and the baseline identity share devices, accounts, or contacts, collapsing the separation.
Performative overshoot — conspicuously staged grief, surprise, or helpfulness that reads as rehearsed to observers.
Direct engagement with the inquiry — the person inserts themselves into the investigation or response in a way that breaches the discipline of a low-profile reversion.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the reversion is selective and evasion-directed — targeting precisely the artifacts and accounts that would attribute the act, timed to the emergence of the investigation, and paired with an affirmative false narrative. Intent falls when the change is undirected, when nothing evasive is being managed, and when a verifiable innocent purpose explains the behavior.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression broad-to-narrow — from a general return to routine toward the deliberate elimination of the specific traces that tie the actor to the site.
Attribution-directed selectivity — the destruction and scrubbing concentrate on the operational persona and the incident window, not on unrelated parts of the person's life.
Timing keyed to the inquiry — reversion and disposal accelerate as the investigation, canvass, or media coverage begins.
Affirmative false narrative — the person volunteers an innocent account of the incident, feigns surprise or grief, or steers others away from their involvement.
Retention of what still serves — operationally useful items are kept while attributable items are destroyed, showing a deliberate keep/discard logic rather than panic.

Concealment paired with proximity — evasion behaviors observed in a person who also had access, presence, or a grievance tied to the site; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
low_signal_anchors: Undirected change — a general life or routine shift not organized around the incident or its evidentiary traces.
One-off behavior without pattern — a single odd act (a discarded item, a missed shift) with no reinforcing evasion signal.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — the absence, account change, or disposal has an independently confirmed innocent basis.
No narrative management — the person makes no effort to shape how their whereabouts or role are perceived.
Ambiguous targeting — the disposal is indiscriminate housekeeping rather than a focused removal of attributable material.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can actually reinsert into a normal identity — a legitimate role or routine still available to return to, cooperating third parties to backstop the alibi, and control over the physical and digital traces that need managing. Opportunity falls when the baseline identity is compromised, when the traces are already in defender hands, and when the reinsertion is blocked; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: Intact baseline to return to — a legitimate job, residence, and social role remain available and unquestioned after the attack.
Control of the evidentiary trail — the operational artifacts, devices, and accounts are in the actor's hands and can be disposed of before any hold or seizure.
Cooperating backstops — third parties willing to corroborate the whereabouts account or otherwise vouch for the restored normalcy.
Legitimate post-incident presence — the actor can plausibly be at or near the site during the response through a real role (occupant, worker, neighbor), easing reinsertion.
Unmonitored reversion window — no active surveillance or records review covers the person during the period they restore their normal pattern.
Digital control surface — the actor retains administrative control of the accounts and location data that must be scrubbed or reshaped.
low_signal_anchors: Compromised baseline identity — the person's legitimate role or routine is already under question, leaving nothing clean to return to. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor rebuilds cover.
Traces already secured — access logs, CCTV, credentials, or devices are preserved by defenders before the actor can dispose of them.
Backstops unavailable or unwilling — no third party will corroborate the alibi, or a would-be backstop cooperates with investigators.
Reinsertion blocked without adaptation — the actor is challenged or excluded from the normal setting and does not adapt. Transient: may flip if the actor finds another route back.
Structural access degradation — the role or relationship that made the site presence plausible has ended, undercutting the cover story.
Active post-incident monitoring — surveillance or records review covers the person during the reversion window; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Nearly everyone near an attack returns to routine, and many people process a violent event with calm, avoidance, or a need to help — behaviors that superficially resemble deceptive reestablishment. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the return to normal has a verifiable innocent basis, a transparent identity behind it, and no selective management of attributable traces tied to the site and the incident window.
contexts: Ordinary resumption of life — occupants, staff, neighbors, and responders returning to work and routine after an incident as a normal coping and continuity response.
Legitimate absence or schedule change — pre-planned leave, travel, shift changes, or relocation that coincide with the incident window by chance and check out on review.
Non-deceptive affect — flat, calm, avoidant, or busy demeanor that reflects individual stress response, not a performance staged to deflect suspicion.
Routine digital housekeeping — account cleanup, device replacement, or privacy-driven scrubbing that is habitual or unrelated to the attack.
Community helpers and self-inserters — people drawn to volunteer, comfort others, or follow the story out of genuine concern or ordinary curiosity, not to shadow the investigation.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Cover Reestablishment is an evasion tactic, so its findings gain weight chiefly by correlation — with a person who had access, presence, or grievance tied to the site, and with staging- or execution-class facility indicators observed elsewhere. Findings correlating with such evidence warrant immediate activation of response protocols, including evidence preservation and alibi verification, regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: credibility of the indicator, breadth across modalities, and how tightly the behavior is anchored to the incident window. A single low-credibility read of demeanor with an available innocent explanation sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility signal — a shed operational persona or a failed alibi for a person with site access — sits at the investigation tier. Cross-modal corroboration — discarded operational identity plus an unverifiable whereabouts account plus digital scrubbing for the same person — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as deliberate attribution evasion. Signals persisting once the person is aware of scrutiny, or accelerating as the inquiry begins, sit at the committed-actor tier. Multiple lower-priority indicators correlating temporally or modally may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers logging and pattern-detection; investigation triggers actor-identification, alibi verification, and a legal hold on relevant records and devices; elevation triggers coordinated evidence preservation and law-enforcement referral; the committed-actor tier triggers protection of investigative integrity against active counter-attribution; a person matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor abruptly resumes a normal routine and familiar appearance after the attack — returning to work, restoring or altering hair, clothing, and grooming, and discarding the operational look used at the site
Threat actor fabricates and rehearses an alibi placing them away from the site at the time of the attack, recruiting or coaching third parties to corroborate the false whereabouts account

Threat actor scrubs and reverts their digital identity — deleting operational accounts and burner communications, scrubbing or spoofing location history, and reactivating a dormant clean profile to backstop an innocent post-incident narrative

Threat actor performs deliberate normalcy after the attack — feigned surprise or grief about the incident, staged calm, and participation in the community or organizational response to appear as an ordinary affected party

Threat actor sheds the operational persona used for site access and reinserts into a legitimate presence near the site — discarding uniforms, credentials, and access artifacts and reverting to a normal occupant, worker, or neighbor role to blend back in

countermeasures.measure: Run a post-incident behavioral-baseline comparison across persons with legitimate site access, flagging abrupt reversions in routine, appearance, presence, or digital pattern that cluster on the incident window
countermeasures.limitations: Innocent people also change routine after an incident; the method surfaces candidates for review, not proof, and depends on having a pre-incident baseline to compare against

countermeasures.measure: Apply an alibi-verification protocol for persons of interest — reconcile claimed whereabouts against CCTV, access logs, device telemetry, and independent witnesses before accepting an innocent account
countermeasures.limitations: A rehearsed, well-backstopped alibi can survive verification; corroborating records may be incomplete or the person may have a legitimate reason to have been elsewhere

countermeasures.measure: Reconcile issued versus returned credentials, uniforms, and vendor identities associated with the site, and preserve access artifacts, to detect operational personas being shed after the attack
countermeasures.limitations: Effective only where credentials and vendor identities were tracked at issue; disposable or fully fabricated personas may never have entered the reconciliation system

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate early with investigators to place a legal hold on the accounts, devices, and records of identified persons of interest, preserving digital traces before the actor can scrub or spoof them
countermeasures.limitations: Requires a defensible investigative basis and legal authority; scrubbing may already be complete before a hold is in place, and closed or foreign-hosted platforms may not honor preservation requests

response_protocols.trigger: Indicators of cover reestablishment surface for a person connected to the site (shed operational persona, unverifiable or rehearsed alibi, digital scrubbing anchored to the incident window)
response_protocols.action: Open or update the facility threat case and move immediately to preserve perishable evidence. Conduct a 24-hour action set: (a) place a legal hold on the person's relevant accounts, devices, and records, (b) verify the whereabouts account against CCTV, access logs, and telemetry, (c) reconcile issued site credentials and vendor identities, (d) refer to law enforcement for attribution work. Document all sourcing and the investigative basis.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Alibi fails verification, an operational persona is confirmed shed, OR indicators across other facility tactics link the same person to the attack
response_protocols.legal_notes: Preservation and monitoring of an identified person implicate privacy, evidence-handling, and due-process requirements that vary by jurisdiction. Coordinate with counsel and investigators before acting; document the investigative basis to support any legal hold or referral.

response_protocols.trigger: A person of interest exhibits performative normalcy — staged surprise or grief, or self-insertion into the incident response — without yet meeting the threshold for a named suspect
response_protocols.action: Protect the integrity of the investigation: brief a limited circle, avoid tipping the person to scrutiny, discreetly document their post-incident behavior and any access to the response, and preserve corroborating records. Coordinate with investigators on whether and when to interview.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Performative behavior resolves into a verifiable evasion signal (failed alibi, shed persona, or digital scrubbing) tied to the person
response_protocols.legal_notes: Discreet observation must stay within lawful bounds and avoid prejudicing any future prosecution; document the basis and keep the circle of knowledge minimal to protect both the inquiry and the person's rights pending evidence.

tactics.field_notes: Cover reestablishment is rarely caught in the act; it is reconstructed afterward from the gap between who the actor was during the operation and who they insist they are once the investigation opens. The tell is selectivity — an ordinary person rattled by a nearby attack does not surgically delete the one account, discard the one uniform, and rehearse the one whereabouts story that would tie them to the site. Timing matters: the reversion that accelerates the moment a canvass or news cycle begins is more diagnostic than the one that was already underway. The hardest cases are the disciplined ones, where a clean legend was prepared in advance and the actor simply steps back into it — there the signal is not the behavior itself but its perfect, frictionless normalcy against a backdrop of access, presence, or grievance. This tactic almost never stands alone; treat it as a correlation multiplier on the actor already surfaced by execution- or staging-class facility indicators.
observed_contexts: arson case where the actor returned to a normal work shift the next day and volunteered a detailed but uncorroborated account of being across town when the fire started
insider who used a vendor uniform to reach a restricted area, then discarded the uniform and badge and reverted to an ordinary occupant role during the post-incident evacuation and headcount
actor who deleted burner accounts and reactivated a dormant clean social profile within hours of the attack, then posted ordinary content to backstop an innocent timeline
[literature: CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 / FBI-PREATTACK-2018 pattern — post-attack reversion to a prepared legitimate identity and rehearsed alibi to defeat attribution]

tactics.name: Network Protection
tactics.notes: Post-attack actions taken to protect the human network that enabled the operation against the facility — co-conspirators, cell members, cultivated insiders, and peripheral facilitators. The objective is not the actor's own flight (Withdrawal) or the site's physical evidence (Evidence Management), but the survival and impunity of the network: destroying coordination communications, invoking compartmentation and pre-arranged silence protocols, warning associates of investigative attention, and pressuring witnesses or peripheral participants into silence. Distinct from Cover Reestablishment (restoring one actor's legend) in that it manages the collective — the people who can implicate the operation. The protective logic is about the network: who can talk, what links can be severed, and how to keep the group intact and unattributable after the act.
tactics.cpn_notes: Network protection increasingly runs through encrypted and disappearing-message platforms — coordination groups deleted in bulk after the act, associates warned through ephemeral channels, and coded go-dark instructions that leave little recoverable artifact. The same digital surfaces that built the network are the first thing scrubbed to protect it.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, persistence over time, and recoverable evidence that the actor is actively protecting a network rather than merely reacting to fear. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when ordinary post-incident anxiety or privacy behavior was never distinguished from deliberate network protection.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — device-wiping activity, warning communications to named associates, and witness pressure observed against the same operation within overlapping timeframes.
Temporal persistence — protective coordination observed across days to weeks after the act, not a single deleted message.
Material evidence — recovered fragments, carrier records, or witness statements that physically tie the actor to warning associates or destroying coordination records.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who received a warning, silence instruction, or threat and can describe the sender, content, and timing with high resolution.
Behavioral specificity — the actor named specific associates to protect, specific records to destroy, or a specific witness to silence rather than a vague sense of exposure.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — trained reporter or a directly-pressured participant through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip, reporter cannot be re-contacted.
Content-specificity weakness — a vague report that the group 'went quiet' that could fit ordinary post-incident caution.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one deleted account or one lapsed contact with no broader pattern.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to embellish (falling-out with the group, informant incentive, litigation).
Unrebutted legitimate explanation — the communications changes admit a benign reading (privacy reaction, unrelated device replacement) that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that a warning or silence instruction may be retrofitted to a coordination narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when network protection shows operational discipline — pre-arranged compartmentation, bulk destruction of coordination records, secure warning channels, and control over what peripheral participants know. Capability falls with disorganized reaction, self-incriminating traffic, and associates who were never compartmented and can each implicate the whole.
high_signal_anchors: Pre-arranged compartmentation — the network was structured so that participants knew only their own cell, and silence protocols activated cleanly after the act.
Coordinated bulk destruction — coordination groups, shared drives, and messaging histories wiped in a synchronized way across multiple members, not ad hoc by one person.
Secure warning tradecraft — associates alerted through ephemeral or coded channels that resist recovery and attribution.
Control over peripheral knowledge — facilitators and insiders were fed only what they needed, limiting what any one witness can disclose.
Counter-investigative behaviors — the network anticipates the direction of inquiry and moves witnesses, funds, or members ahead of it.
Demonstrated command structure — one actor visibly directs others' post-attack behavior, indicating an organized network rather than a lone offender.
low_signal_anchors: Disorganized reaction — panic deletion and warnings sent in the clear, easily recovered and attributed.
No compartmentation — every participant knew the others and the plan, so any one can implicate all.
Self-incriminating traffic — warning or silence messages that themselves establish the coordination they were meant to hide.
Single-actor footprint — no evidence of others to protect; behavior consistent with a lone offender managing only their own exposure.
Uncontrolled peripheral participants — facilitators talk freely because they were never briefed on silence.
Direct-contact exposure — the actor personally approached a witness or associate in a traceable, observed way, breaching operational discipline.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when post-attack behavior progresses from self-preservation toward deliberate protection of others — warning associates, enforcing silence, and preserving the network's capacity to act again. Intent falls with behavior explained by individual fear, encounters that do not escalate, and a verifiable benign purpose behind communications changes.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression self-to-collective — an observable shift from covering the actor's own tracks to actively shielding named others.
Network-specific behavior — attention concentrates on particular associates, insiders, or witnesses and their exposure, not just the actor's own.
Operational specificity in warnings or instructions — telling associates what to say, what to delete, where to go, or how to respond to investigators.
Sustained enforcement of silence — the actor tracks whether participants are holding to the cover story over time and re-pressures those who waver.
Preservation for re-use — the network is protected intact (leadership, funding, tasking) in a way that suggests intended future operations, not just escaping this one.

Coercion paired with prior coordination — the actor pressures a witness or associate AND is tied to the operation's planning; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
low_signal_anchors: Individual-fear behavior — communications caution explained by ordinary anxiety, not by protecting a group.
One-time encounter without escalation — a single warning surfaced but no pattern of enforcement or coordination.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — the device change, relocation, or contact lapse has an innocent explanation that checks out.
No enforcement behavior — associates drift apart with no evidence of directed silence.
Target ambiguity — unclear whether any network exists to protect; behavior fits a lone actor.
Reactive-only posture — behavior consistent with panic rather than deliberate protection of others.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can effectively shield the network — reach over associates, control of the communications surface, leverage over witnesses, and time before investigators close in. Opportunity falls when investigative access is already established, witnesses are protected, or the communications record is preserved beyond the actor's reach; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: No investigative friction encountered — the actor's protection of the network proceeds unimpeded before any preservation or protective order is in place.
Reach over associates — the actor can contact and direct the relevant participants, insiders, and witnesses reliably.
Control of the communications surface — the actor holds the accounts, devices, and channels needed to destroy or scrub coordination records before they are captured.
Leverage over witnesses — the actor has coercive or relational hold over the people who could implicate the network. Dormant leverage is potential; the applied pressure is what is high-signal.
Time and proximity — the actor is positioned close to associates and acting inside the window before investigators establish access.
Direct network access — the actor occupies a leadership or hub role with unsupervised ability to move members, funds, or evidence.
low_signal_anchors: Preservation already in place — devices imaged, logs held, or witnesses secured before the actor could act. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor finds a new avenue.
Institutional rule-out of reach — the actor's access to a witness or associate was actively severed, not merely unobserved.
Structural access degradation — the actor's hub role or channel control terminated (accounts seized, custody, relocation).
Investigative friction encountered without adaptation — the actor was challenged or surveilled and did not adapt or persist. Transient: may flip if the actor finds another route.
Witnesses beyond reach — key participants are relocated, protected, or cooperating, out of the actor's coercive span.
Communications preserved beyond reach — the coordination record was captured before destruction; transient advantage to the defender unless the actor degrades it.

false_positive_context.criteria: Ordinary post-incident behavior resembles network protection on the surface — people delete accounts out of privacy fear after any newsworthy event, and communities close ranks around the accused for reasons that are not conspiratorial. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the communications changes and contacts have a verifiable innocent purpose, a transparent relationship behind them, or an explanation that survives being checked.
contexts: Privacy reaction — individuals deactivating accounts or changing numbers out of general fear of association or media exposure after a high-profile incident, with no coordination.
Legal-privilege activity — defense counsel, investigators, and advocates coordinating a lawful, privileged response; do not mistake legitimate representation for network protection.
Community and family solidarity — relatives, congregants, or coworkers supporting or believing an accused person for relational reasons, without directed silence.
Routine records lifecycle — normal message auto-deletion, device upgrades, and account churn unrelated to the incident.
Trauma and avoidance — witnesses withdrawing or declining to speak from fear or trauma rather than because they were pressured into silence.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Findings correlating with active silencing of a witness, destruction of coordination records, or warnings that preserve a network's capacity for a follow-on act warrant immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: credibility of the indicator, breadth across modalities, and persistence over time. A single low-credibility indicator with an available legitimate explanation (privacy reaction, ordinary records churn) sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility indicator with operational specificity — a directed silence instruction, a synchronized wipe, a concrete witness threat — sits at the investigation tier. Cross-modal corroboration — device destruction plus associate warnings plus witness pressure tied to the same operation — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as coordinated network protection by an organized group. Indicators persisting after preservation orders and protective measures are in place sit at the committed-actor tier, indicating a disciplined network. Multiple lower-priority indicators correlating temporally or by association may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers logging and pattern-detection; investigation triggers actor-identification, rapid evidence preservation, and witness safeguarding; elevation triggers protected-witness handling and law-enforcement referral; the committed-actor tier triggers treatment as an organized network with follow-on potential; a confirmed actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor destroys, wipes, or bulk-deletes communications devices, messaging apps, and stored coordination records shortly after the attack to sever the network's digital trail
Threat actor contacts co-conspirators or cultivated insiders to warn of investigative attention, coordinate a consistent cover story, or instruct on evasion and go-dark behavior
Threat actor pressures, threatens, or intimidates a witness or peripheral participant into silence about the operation or the identities of those involved
Threat actor compartmentalizes the network after the act — severing links between cells, invoking pre-arranged silence protocols, and dispersing members to limit what any one participant can disclose
Threat actor removes or coaches an insider (employee, contractor, or vendor) to conceal their facilitation role and evade internal review or access-audit scrutiny

countermeasures.measure: Execute rapid digital evidence preservation on incident indication — image devices, capture messaging and coordination logs, and issue litigation and data-retention holds before actors can wipe the network's records
countermeasures.limitations: Ephemeral and encrypted platforms may leave little to preserve; holds reach only records within institutional or legal custody and cannot recover what a determined actor destroyed first

countermeasures.measure: Activate a witness identification and protection protocol — separate, safeguard, and confidentially interview witnesses and peripheral participants early to prevent intimidation-driven silence
countermeasures.limitations: Protection depends on identifying witnesses before the actor reaches them; trauma and fear can suppress cooperation even absent direct coercion, and resource limits constrain durable protection

countermeasures.measure: Conduct post-incident communications monitoring within legal authority to detect coordination, warning, and go-dark traffic among identified associates in the days after the act
