countermeasures.limitations: Encrypted and closed channels are not visible; monitoring an identified network implicates privacy and surveillance law and requires a documented legal basis before activation

countermeasures.measure: Run an insider-facilitation review — audit access logs, credential use, and internal roles to identify participants concealing a facilitation role and to blunt coached concealment
countermeasures.limitations: Coached insiders may present clean records; the review surfaces anomalies but cannot by itself prove intent, and depends on log integrity that the insider may have influenced

response_protocols.trigger: Indication that post-attack network protection is underway — synchronized device wiping, warnings to associates, or coordination to align a cover story tied to the operation
response_protocols.action: Open or update the network dimension of the facility case. Within the first hours: (a) execute rapid evidence-preservation and retention holds on reachable devices, accounts, and logs, (b) identify co-conspirators, insiders, and witnesses and their exposure, (c) initiate protected handling for at-risk witnesses, (d) refer coordination and destruction indicators to law enforcement. Document all sourcing and legal basis.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Credible witness intimidation, evidence that the network is preserved for a follow-on act, or indicators across other aftermath tactics surface for the same network
response_protocols.legal_notes: Monitoring an identified network implicates privacy, surveillance, and witness-tampering statutes that vary by jurisdiction. Consult counsel before active monitoring; preserve chain of custody on any evidence and document the investigative basis for each action.

response_protocols.trigger: Credible witness intimidation or insider concealment identified — a witness reports being threatened into silence, or an insider is found to be hiding a facilitation role
response_protocols.action: Activate protected-witness handling and separate the witness from the actor's reach. Refer the intimidation or tampering to law enforcement as a distinct offense. Initiate the insider-facilitation review, preserve access records under hold, and restrict the implicated insider's access pending investigation. Coordinate messaging to avoid tipping the network.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Intimidation escalates toward physical harm, or the concealed insider retains active access to sensitive systems or the site
response_protocols.legal_notes: Witness protection and tampering referrals must preserve the witness's safety and the evidentiary record; adverse action against an implicated insider should be coordinated with counsel and HR to withstand review and avoid compromising the criminal case.

tactics.field_notes: Network protection is what tells you a facility attack was a group effort rather than a lone act, and it usually shows up as an absence — accounts that go dark together, a witness who suddenly will not talk, an insider whose story tightens. The clearest tells are synchronization and direction: multiple participants wiping or going quiet in the same window, or one person visibly telling the others what to say and delete. The window is short and it is a race — the same coordination surface that ran the operation is the first thing scrubbed, so preservation has to move in hours, not days. The hardest part is separating deliberate protection from ordinary post-incident fear: people delete accounts and decline interviews after any newsworthy event, and communities close ranks for reasons that are not conspiratorial. What resolves it is specificity and coercion — a directed instruction, a concrete threat, a facilitation role being actively hidden — not the mere fact that the group got quiet.
observed_contexts: cell members deleting a shared coordination channel in a synchronized window within hours of a facility attack, warning each other to go dark
witness to an arson who initially cooperated then withdrew after being contacted and threatened by an associate of the offender
insider who badged an actor into a restricted area coached to present the access as routine and to conceal the relationship during internal review
[literature: CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 / NAF-CLINICVIOLENCE-2024 pattern — networked and issue-motivated offenders protecting co-participants and pressuring witnesses after an attack on a facility]

tactics.name: Financial Disposition
tactics.notes: Post-attack movement, concealment, or laundering of funds tied to the operation against a facility — the money that financed the act, the proceeds of any theft or extortion connected to it, and the disbursements that reward or protect participants. This is disposition after the fact: structuring cash below reporting thresholds, converting funds into cryptocurrency and routing them through mixers, liquidating assets, moving money offshore, and channeling operational money through front businesses or charities. Distinct from Capability Acquisition (which is pre-attack financing of means) and from Network Protection (which shields people rather than money). The financial trail is often the most durable evidentiary residue an operation leaves, which is precisely why the actor works to break it.
tactics.cpn_notes: Financial disposition is increasingly digital and cross-border — peer-to-peer transfers, non-custodial wallets, mixing and chain-hopping services, prepaid instruments, and money-service businesses that let an actor move and obscure operation-linked funds faster than traditional reporting can surface them, while blockchain analytics simultaneously make some of that movement recoverable long after the fact.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises when financial anomalies are corroborated across institutions and record types, are time-aligned with the operation, and rest on recoverable documentary evidence rather than a single unexplained transaction. Credibility falls when the source is a lone flag, the amounts and timing admit an ordinary financial explanation, and a legitimate reason for the movement was never ruled out.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-institution corroboration — the same funds traced across multiple banks, exchanges, or money-service businesses within a timeframe that brackets the attack.
Temporal alignment — disposition activity clusters in the hours to days after the operation, matching the event rather than a routine cycle.
Documentary residue — subpoenaed account records, blockchain transaction graphs, wire confirmations, or seized ledgers that physically tie the money to the actor and the act.
Chain-of-custody fidelity — records obtained through formal financial-intelligence or legal channels with intact provenance, not a secondhand tip about someone's spending.
Behavioral specificity — the movement is structured to evade a specific reporting threshold or attribution method, not merely large or unusual.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — a compliance officer or financial-intelligence unit reporting through a regulated channel, not an aggrieved associate alleging hidden money.
low_signal_anchors: Single unexplained transaction — one flagged transfer with no corroborating pattern across accounts or time.
Ordinary-explanation weakness — amounts and timing fit routine payroll, tax, or business cycles that were never excluded.
Source-quality weakness — an uncorroborated rumor of sudden wealth or hidden cash with no recoverable record behind it.
Temporal-pattern weakness — the movement predates or long postdates the operation without a plausible link.
Source-motivation misalignment — the reporter has a financial dispute, divorce, or business rivalry giving reason to allege laundering.
Reconstructive inference — a delayed narrative that retrofits normal financial behavior into an operation-linked story.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when disposition shows financial tradecraft — layering across instruments, use of cut-outs and nominees, fluency with crypto obfuscation, and access to laundering infrastructure that survives scrutiny. Capability falls when the movement is crude, self-executed, confined to traceable rails, or collapses on first examination by a compliance function.
high_signal_anchors: Layering discipline — funds passed through several instruments and jurisdictions to break the audit trail rather than moved in a single hop.
Nominee and cut-out use — accounts, wallets, or shell entities held by third parties insulate the actor from the money.
Crypto obfuscation fluency — competent use of mixers, chain-hopping, privacy coins, or peel chains rather than a single transparent on-chain transfer.
Access to laundering infrastructure — a relationship with a money-service business, informal value-transfer network, or professional facilitator that can absorb and reissue funds.
Threshold-aware structuring — deposits and withdrawals engineered just under regulatory reporting limits across multiple days or branches.
Operational security in records — the actor controls or destroys the paper and digital residue of the movement, degrading later reconstruction.
low_signal_anchors: Crude single-hop movement — a lump-sum transfer or withdrawal with no layering.
Traceable-rail confinement — all activity stays on regulated, fully attributed accounts the actor plainly controls.
Self-execution without cut-outs — the actor moves the money personally, leaving direct attribution.
Transparent on-chain behavior — crypto sent address-to-address with no mixing, trivially graphed.
Compliance-triggering clumsiness — the pattern immediately generated a suspicious-activity flag on first review.
No infrastructure reach — the actor has no access to laundering services and is limited to personal accounts and cash.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the financial behavior is purpose-built to sever the money from the act — timed to the operation, structured to defeat attribution, and paired with disbursements that reward participants or seed future capability. Intent falls when the movement is explainable as ordinary finance, does not escalate, and has a verifiable legitimate purpose.
high_signal_anchors: Event-timed disposition — the funds begin moving in tight temporal proximity to the attack, indicating the movement is a response to it.
Attribution-defeating structure — the pattern is shaped specifically to break the link between the actor and the money, not merely to move value.
Participant disbursement — payments to co-conspirators, funders, or facilitators consistent with settling accounts on the operation.
Reseeding behavior — proceeds routed toward acquiring new capability or sustaining a network, signaling continuity of purpose.
Concealment escalation — a progression from open accounts toward nominees, crypto, or offshore vehicles as scrutiny rises.

Hostile financial footprint paired with the act — operation-linked spending or laundering observed alongside expressed grievance or claimed responsibility; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way either signal alone is not.
low_signal_anchors: Ordinary-finance behavior — the movement fits routine income, debt, or business activity not pinned to the operation.
No escalation in concealment — funds remain in transparent, attributed accounts without any move toward obfuscation.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — a documented sale, loan, settlement, or business transaction surfaces and checks out.
No participant nexus — disbursements go to unrelated parties with no tie to the act.
Amount-target ambiguity — sums too small or diffuse to plausibly finance or reward an operation.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can actually move and hide the money — controlling usable accounts and wallets, holding relationships that absorb funds, exploiting weak compliance, and operating across jurisdictions that resist tracing. Opportunity falls when financial controls bite, accounts are frozen or fully attributed, and the actor lacks reach beyond monitored rails; when opportunity appears reduced, whether the reduction is durable matters.
high_signal_anchors: Unobstructed financial reach — the actor moves funds without triggering a hold, freeze, or effective review.
Controlled disposition channels — usable accounts, wallets, prepaid instruments, or a cooperating money-service relationship stand ready to receive and reissue funds.
Compliance-gap exploitation — the actor routes through institutions or products with known weak know-your-customer or monitoring practices.
Cross-border positioning — funds reach jurisdictions with limited cooperation or opaque beneficial-ownership regimes.
Facilitator or nominee availability — a professional launderer, willing third party, or shell structure is actively in use, not merely known.
Insider financial access being exploited — an accomplice inside a facility's finance, vendor, or payroll function is moving or masking operation-linked money.
low_signal_anchors: Freeze or seizure imposed — accounts or wallets are frozen and the actor's known channels are blocked. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor opens new rails.
Full attribution of holdings — every relevant account and wallet is identified and monitored, leaving no covert channel.
Compliance friction without adaptation — a suspicious-activity flag or declined transaction stopped the movement and the actor did not re-route.
Jurisdictional reach absent — the actor cannot move value beyond domestic, cooperative, fully traceable institutions.
Facilitator lost — a prior nominee, exchange, or money-service relationship terminated, closing that channel.
Monitoring-driven barrier — heightened financial-intelligence attention has degraded the actor's known methods; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Much legitimate financial activity resembles operation-linked disposition on the surface — a business owner structuring cash flow looks similar to a launderer; a crypto trader using multiple wallets looks similar to obfuscation; an offshore transfer can be a routine remittance. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the movement has a verifiable legitimate purpose, a transparent party behind it, and institutional accountability that survives examination — and whether it is time-linked to any operation at all.
contexts: Legitimate business finance — cash-intensive businesses, real-estate closings, payroll, tax planning, and normal treasury movement across accounts and entities.
Ordinary crypto activity — traders, DeFi users, and privacy-conscious holders using multiple wallets or exchanges for lawful reasons.
Routine cross-border transfers — immigrant remittances, international tuition and property payments, and multinational business flows to and from opaque jurisdictions.
Life-event liquidity — inheritance, divorce settlement, asset sale, insurance payout, or debt repayment producing large or unusual movement.
Regulated professional activity — money-service businesses, accountants, and attorneys handling client funds through lawful, documented channels.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Financial-disposition findings gain priority when they correlate with a facility attack in fact and in time — proceeds or reimbursements moving in the wake of an arson, bombing, sabotage, or extortion against the site — and correlation with claim-of-responsibility or network-protection behavior for the same actor warrants treating the money trail as part of a single operation regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination depends on three factors: credibility of the financial indicator, breadth across institutions and instruments, and persistence over time. A single low-credibility flag with an available ordinary-finance explanation sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility indicator with attribution-defeating structure time-linked to the operation sits at the investigation tier. Corroboration across institutions — structuring plus crypto obfuscation plus participant disbursement tied to the same event — sits at the elevation tier and warrants coordinated financial-intelligence action. Movement persisting despite flags, freezes, or reviews sits at the committed-actor tier, indicating a facilitated laundering capability rather than a one-time act. Multiple lower-priority financial indicators correlating temporally or across instruments may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single transaction warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers transaction logging and pattern-detection; investigation triggers actor-identification, account mapping, and a suspicious-activity referral; elevation triggers financial-intelligence-unit and law-enforcement coordination and preservation of records; the committed-actor tier triggers pursuit of freeze or seizure authority; a confirmed actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement and financial-crimes coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor structures cash movements below reporting thresholds after the operation — sequential deposits or withdrawals just under regulatory limits across multiple days, branches, or accounts
Threat actor converts operation-linked funds into cryptocurrency and routes them through mixers, chain-hopping, privacy coins, or peel chains to break the transaction trail
Threat actor liquidates assets, closes accounts, or moves funds offshore into opaque beneficial-ownership jurisdictions following the operation
Threat actor disburses funds to co-conspirators, funders, or facilitators after the operation — settling accounts, rewarding participants, or repaying operational backing
Threat actor channels operation-linked money through a front business, shell entity, or charitable vehicle to launder proceeds or disguise the source and reseed future capability

countermeasures.measure: Establish financial-intelligence liaison so that suspicious-activity reports, currency-transaction reports, and account anomalies tied to a facility incident are surfaced, aggregated, and reviewed against the case timeline
countermeasures.limitations: Depends on regulated institutions filing and on lawful access to their records; cash, informal value-transfer, and non-cooperative jurisdictions stay largely invisible, and filings lag the movement

countermeasures.measure: Apply blockchain analytics to trace and cluster crypto addresses associated with the incident, flagging mixer, chain-hopping, and exchange cash-out points for follow-on legal process
countermeasures.limitations: Privacy coins, well-run mixers, and off-chain peer-to-peer transfers degrade attribution; tracing establishes flow but still requires exchange cooperation and legal process to reach identity

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with law enforcement and financial institutions to preserve records and pursue freeze or seizure authority over accounts, wallets, and assets linked to the operation before funds fully disperse
countermeasures.limitations: Freeze and seizure require legal predicate and move slower than digital transfers; funds already layered offshore or into crypto may be beyond reach by the time authority is obtained

countermeasures.measure: Audit facility-linked vendor, payroll, and procurement flows for anomalous payments that could mask an insider's role in financing or profiting from an incident, and tighten beneficial-ownership verification for new payees
countermeasures.limitations: Anomaly review catches only movement that touches facility systems; well-separated external laundering leaves no internal trace, and audits can be defeated by falsified documentation

response_protocols.trigger: Financial-disposition indicators surface for an actor linked to a facility incident (structuring, crypto obfuscation, offshore movement, or participant disbursement time-aligned with the attack)
response_protocols.action: Open or update the financial workstream of the facility case. Within 24-48 hours: (a) preserve and request relevant account, wallet, and transaction records through proper legal channels, (b) map identified accounts, instruments, and counterparties, (c) file or coordinate a suspicious-activity referral, (d) build the disposition timeline against the incident timeline. Document sourcing and legal basis throughout.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Funds actively dispersing toward crypto, offshore, or nominee channels, OR financial activity corroborates other aftermath tactics for the same actor
response_protocols.legal_notes: Access to financial records requires appropriate legal process (subpoena, court order, or regulatory authority) and implicates financial-privacy statutes that vary by jurisdiction. Engage counsel and law enforcement before compelling records; document the investigative predicate for every request.

response_protocols.trigger: Traced movement indicates active laundering through mixers, shell entities, or an offshore route while funds remain partially reachable
response_protocols.action: Engage the financial-intelligence unit and blockchain-analytics support to cluster addresses and identify cash-out points, and coordinate with law enforcement to pursue freeze or seizure authority before dispersal completes. Notify affected financial institutions to preserve records and flag related accounts. Reassess reach as tracing resolves.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Analytics resolve funds to an identifiable holder or a cooperating exchange, OR proceeds appear to be reseeding new operational capability
response_protocols.legal_notes: Freeze and seizure require a legal predicate; act on documented probable cause and coordinate cross-border requests through mutual-legal-assistance channels. Preserve chain of custody for any records to support later proceedings.

tactics.field_notes: The money is usually the last thing an operation cleans up and the hardest to fully erase, which is what makes disposition worth watching. The tells are timing and structure more than amount: funds that start moving in the days after an incident, cash broken into sub-threshold pieces, a sudden pivot into crypto and mixers, or a payment to someone with no ordinary reason to be paid. Crypto cuts both ways — actors reach for it to break the trail, but on-chain movement is permanent and increasingly graphable, so a mixer entry often becomes an investigative anchor rather than a dead end. The hard part is separation: sophisticated actors put nominees, shells, and cooperative money-service businesses between themselves and the funds, so the disposition looks like ordinary commerce until the event timeline lines it up. Chase the record before it disperses; a freeze on day two is worth more than a perfect trace on day sixty.
observed_contexts: ideologically motivated arson case where the actor moved reimbursement to two accomplices in sub-threshold cash withdrawals within days of the fire
sabotage matter in which operational proceeds were converted to cryptocurrency and passed through a mixer before an exchange cash-out flagged the pattern
extortion-linked facility incident where demand proceeds were routed through a shell consulting entity presented as legitimate invoicing

[literature: CHAINALYSIS-CCR-2024 / CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 pattern — post-incident laundering via crypto obfuscation and front entities documented across illicit-finance and infrastructure-attack casework]

tactics.name: After-Action Assessment
tactics.notes: The threat actor's own lessons-learned review of a completed facility attack, conducted to improve future operations. The actor studies what worked and what failed — the effectiveness of the method against the structure, the defender's response timeline, the media reach and framing of the event, and the tradecraft errors that created exposure. Distinct from Attribution Declaration (claiming the act publicly) and from Audience Amplification (spreading it for effect): after-action assessment is inward-facing and instrumental, a critique aimed at the next operation rather than at an audience. The signal is the actor treating the completed attack as a case study — collecting coverage, timing the response, and recording what to change — which marks a persistent, learning adversary rather than a spent one.
tactics.cpn_notes: After-action assessment is increasingly conducted through open-source channels — the actor mines published news coverage, released incident timelines, official after-action reports, court filings, and social-media footage of the aftermath to reconstruct the defender response and validate targeting effectiveness without returning to the site.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across modalities, persistence over time, and recoverable evidence that the actor is studying a completed attack to refine future tradecraft. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when a plausible legitimate interest in the incident — journalistic, academic, or community — was never ruled out.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-modal corroboration — archived coverage, recorded critiques of the defender response, and communications soliciting lessons against the same completed attack within overlapping timeframes.
Temporal persistence — sustained study of the event across weeks to months, not a single reaction to the news.
Material evidence — saved media archives, annotated response timelines, debrief notes, or recovered communications that physically tie the actor to reviewing the attack.
First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who heard the actor critique the operation and describe what to change; high-resolution reporting of the statement, context, and timing.
Behavioral specificity — the actor assessed the specific attack, method, and defender response rather than expressing vague satisfaction.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — trained reporter through a formal channel, not an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous tip, reporter cannot be re-contacted.
Content-specificity weakness — a vague expression of interest in the incident that could fit any news consumer.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one-time reaction to coverage with no follow-through.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to embellish (dispute with the actor, rivalry, litigation).
Unrebutted legitimate explanation — the actor's interest in the event admits a benign reading (journalist, researcher, affected community member) that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that details may be retrofitted to a threat narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the actor's review of the attack shows operational discipline — systematic collection of coverage and response data, structured critique of tradecraft, dissemination of lessons to a network, and the technical literacy to draw actionable conclusions. Capability falls with impulsive or purely emotional reaction, OSINT-only reach with no analytic product, and critique that reveals no operational understanding.
high_signal_anchors: Structured after-action tradecraft — the actor maintains an organized debrief with categorized findings rather than scattered reactions.
Multi-modal coordination — media archiving, response-timeline reconstruction, and network solicitation coordinated across overlapping timeframes.
Restricted-material acquisition — the actor obtains non-public incident data such as internal response reviews, investigative detail, or unreleased footage of the aftermath.
Analytic durability — the actor's conclusions translate into concrete tradecraft changes that hold up as operational improvements, not venting.
Counter-attribution discipline in the review itself — the actor studies how forensics and the response identified errors while conducting the assessment covertly.
Demonstrated technical literacy — the actor reasons productively about method effectiveness, structural damage, and response gaps of the specific facility attack.
low_signal_anchors: Impulsive reaction — celebratory or emotional response to coverage with no analytic content.
No-concealment repetition — repeated open discussion of the operation with no operational discipline.
Analytic failure — the actor draws no usable conclusions; the review is expressive, not instrumental.
OSINT-only reach — all incident knowledge is from public sources; no operational reach beyond browser-and-public-records.
Single-modality engagement — only media consumption or only talk; no structured product.
Direct-contact attempts — the actor sought engagement with investigators, victims, or facility staff to gather assessment data, breaching operational discipline about exposure.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the review progresses from reaction toward operationally specific critique aimed at a next attack, when the actor retains and organizes the assessment, and when lessons-learned are paired with statements of continuing intent. Intent falls with generic interest in the aftermath, reaction that does not translate into forward planning, and a verifiable benign purpose.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression reaction-to-refinement — an observable funnel from consuming coverage to producing operational lessons for a future attack.
Operation-specific behavior — attention concentrates on the completed attack's method, response, and errors rather than the event as news.
Operational specificity in critique — assessing what defeated or slowed the operation, which countermeasures worked, and what tradecraft to change; identifying the next facility or method.
Sustained attention to defender learning — the actor tracks how the facility and responders adapted after the attack and plans around it.
Retention of assessment materials — coverage archived, response timelines saved, debrief notes maintained, suggesting later operational use.

Continuing-intent framing paired with critique — the actor has expressed intent to act again AND is observed conducting a structured after-action review; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
low_signal_anchors: Generic-interest behavior — broad interest in the news event, not pinned to refining a future operation.
One-time reaction without escalation — interest surfaced but no forward-looking critique or pattern.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — journalistic, academic, legal, or affected-community relationship surfaces and checks out.
No retention behavior — coverage viewed casually but not saved or organized.
Backward-looking closure — the actor's review reads as processing a finished event with no next-operation orientation.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can convert the assessment into a renewed capability — combining access to incident and response data, a network to disseminate and refine lessons, retained operational infrastructure, and the positional ability to act again. Opportunity falls with a spent posture, a severed network, or loss of the means to reapply the lessons; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: No degradation of operational posture — the actor retains materiel, network, and freedom of action to apply the lessons learned.
Incident-data access — the actor reliably obtains coverage, response timelines, and investigative detail sufficient to draw operational conclusions. The informational dimension of opportunity.
Defender-gap knowledge — the actor's review yields concrete knowledge of response delays, countermeasure failures, or forensic blind spots to exploit next time.

Network connection being exploited — an identified associate community or cell the actor is actively using to disseminate and refine lessons. Dormant contacts are potential, not realized; the exploitation pattern is what is high-signal.
Geographic-temporal proximity — the actor remains near the facility class or operating environment and is positioned to act on the assessment.
Retained means of re-attack — the actor has preserved the capability the review is intended to improve.
low_signal_anchors: Spent posture after action — the actor is in custody, materially degraded, or has lost the means to reapply lessons. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor recovers capability.
Institutional rule-out of network reuse — investigation actively cleared the associate network, not merely failed to find it.
Structural capability degradation — the actor's prior operational pathway terminated (materiel seized, network dismantled, relocation).
Reaction encountered without adaptation — the actor consumed coverage but produced no forward-looking product and did not return to planning. Transient: may flip if the actor resumes.
Geographic distance not closed — the actor is remote from any next target and re-attack requires a major investment not yet made.
Defender posture change created barriers — hardened facilities of the class, changed response protocols, or active attribution pressure blocks the actor's known methods; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Many legitimate activities resemble after-action assessment on the surface — a journalist reconstructing the response timeline looks similar to an actor critiquing it; a security professional studying the attack for lessons looks similar to reconnaissance of defender gaps. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the underlying interest has a verifiable legitimate purpose, a transparent identity behind it, or institutional accountability that can be checked.
contexts: Verified professional purpose — journalists, documentarians, and analysts covering the incident; security professionals and emergency managers conducting authorized after-action reviews of the response.
Legal authority — investigators, prosecutors, defense counsel, and licensed private investigators with lawful basis to review the attack and its response.
Personal or community connection — victims, survivors, employees, and neighbors processing the event or participating in memorials and inquiries.
Non-threatening attention — true-crime hobbyists, incident-response enthusiasts, and commenters following the coverage with non-operational interest.
Academic and research purpose — students and researchers of terrorism, emergency response, or security studying the attack as a case for prevention.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Findings correlating with renewed target-development or staging behaviors elsewhere — assessment lessons feeding fresh site profiling, accelerant or precursor re-acquisition, or a stated next-target selection — warrant immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: credibility of the indicator, breadth across modalities, and persistence over time. A single low-credibility indicator with an available legitimate explanation sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility indicator with operational specificity — a structured critique of the defender response aimed at a next operation — sits at the investigation tier. Cross-modal corroboration — archived coverage plus recorded critique plus network dissemination against the same completed attack — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as active preparation for renewed operations. Indicators persisting despite implemented countermeasures sit at the committed-actor tier, suggesting a learning adversary re-entering the planning cycle. Multiple lower-priority indicators correlating temporally or modally may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers logging and pattern-detection; investigation triggers actor-identification and a re-attack risk assessment; elevation triggers countermeasure activation and defender-gap remediation identified in the actor's own critique; the committed-actor tier triggers a defensive-posture upgrade across the facility class; a confirmed actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor systematically monitors and archives media coverage of the completed attack — news reports, casualty and damage figures, official statements — to gauge the operation's reach and effect
Threat actor documents and critiques the defender response — police and fire arrival times, evacuation behavior, and countermeasures encountered — to identify what to change in a future operation
Threat actor records personal notes, journals, or debrief materials assessing which tradecraft elements succeeded or failed during the operation
Threat actor discusses the operation's outcomes with associates or online communities, soliciting feedback and disseminating lessons for future actors
Threat actor revisits the site or reviews surveillance and bystander footage of the aftermath to assess physical damage and validate targeting effectiveness

countermeasures.measure: Establish OSINT monitoring for post-incident actor behavior — accounts and forums that archive, critique, or solicit lessons about the attack — and correlate with any identified subject
countermeasures.limitations: Coverage is incomplete; encrypted and closed channels are not visible, and instrumental critique aimed at a next operation may be indistinguishable from ordinary post-event commentary

countermeasures.measure: Discipline the public release of after-action detail — response timelines, countermeasure specifics, and forensic methods — so official reporting does not hand a learning adversary a defender-gap roadmap
countermeasures.limitations: Much incident detail is public by law or emerges through litigation and journalism; withholding operational specifics must be balanced against transparency and community-trust obligations

countermeasures.measure: Conduct the facility's own after-action review and rapidly remediate the response gaps a hostile assessment would identify — arrival times, evacuation friction, blind spots — before the actor can exploit them in a follow-on attack
countermeasures.limitations: Remediation competes for resources during recovery and may lag the actor's own learning cycle; some structural gaps cannot be closed quickly

countermeasures.measure: Maintain liaison with fusion centers and peer facilities to share observed post-incident learning behavior and lessons-dissemination patterns, flagging a persistent adversary re-entering the planning cycle
countermeasures.limitations: Depends on peer reporting discipline and fusion-center throughput; dissemination in closed communities may not surface until a lesson is already in reuse

response_protocols.trigger: One or more After-Action Assessment indicators reported for a subject linked to a completed or attempted facility attack (archiving coverage, critiquing the defender response, maintaining debrief notes, disseminating lessons)
response_protocols.action: Open or update the post-incident threat case. Conduct a preliminary assessment: (a) corroborate the observation, (b) review the subject's digital footprint for structured after-action product and next-target orientation, (c) map any associate network receiving disseminated lessons, (d) brief facility security leadership and responders on the specific defender gaps the actor's critique appears to target. Document all sourcing.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Assessment product shows forward-looking target selection or renewed acquisition, OR indicators across other facility tactics surface for the same actor
response_protocols.legal_notes: Monitoring an identified actor's post-incident communications may implicate privacy, First Amendment, and anti-stalking statutes that vary by jurisdiction. Consult counsel before active monitoring; document the investigative basis tying the review behavior to a completed act.

response_protocols.trigger: Evidence that a hostile after-action critique has identified specific, exploitable defender gaps (response delay, evacuation failure, forensic blind spot) at the attacked facility or its class
response_protocols.action: Prioritize remediation of the identified gaps and elevate posture across the affected facility class for the recovery window: adjust response protocols, close the exposed weaknesses, and coordinate with responders and fusion centers on the re-attack risk picture. Reassess as remediation completes.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Gap-focused critique resolves to a specific next target, date, or renewed staging behavior
response_protocols.legal_notes: Posture and remediation decisions are within facility authority; document the threat basis to support resource requests and to defend proportionality of any heightened measures.

tactics.field_notes: After-action assessment is what separates a one-off actor from a program. The tell is instrumental attention to a finished attack — not celebrating it, but taking it apart: how fast the response came, what the countermeasures actually did, where the tradecraft leaked, how the media framed it. Terrorist and state-linked actors are the most disciplined here; they keep debriefs and push lessons to a network so the next cell starts smarter. The defender's advantage is that the same review the actor conducts, the facility can conduct first — and the actor's own critique, if it can be recovered, is a map of exactly which gaps to close. The hard part is that most of the assessment behavior looks like ordinary post-event interest until it pairs with retained capability or a next-target orientation.
observed_contexts: extremist actor maintaining an organized archive of coverage and a written critique of the defender response after a facility arson, circulated within an online community
saboteur debriefing associates on which breaching approach worked and which alarm defeated the plan, framing the notes for a follow-on operation
actor revisiting the site and reviewing bystander footage to validate structural damage against the intended effect
[literature: CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 / START-GTD-2020 pattern — post-incident lessons-learned and tradecraft dissemination feeding iterative campaigns against infrastructure and soft targets]

tactics.name: Counter-Forensics
tactics.notes: Deliberate defeat of the forensic techniques investigators use to reconstruct a facility attack and attribute it to an actor — obscuring accelerant or explosive-residue signatures, scrubbing biological and latent-print evidence, wiping or encrypting digital traces, and staging the scene to frustrate fire and blast cause-and-origin reconstruction. Distinct from Evidence Management (TF0402), which handles specific physical evidence items (removing a weapon, planting an object, disposing of a garment); Counter-Forensics targets the analytic methods themselves — the residue lab, the DNA workup, the burn-pattern read, the device image — so that even a worked scene yields no usable attribution. Detection here is inferential: investigators recognize the pattern of what is missing or manipulated against what the physical act should have left behind.
tactics.cpn_notes: Counter-forensic knowledge is increasingly commoditized online — case write-ups of failed prosecutions, forensic-methodology papers, accelerant-detection thresholds, and anti-forensic software are all publicly discussed, letting an actor pre-plan attribution defeat from open sources before the attack and leaving a discoverable research footprint.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises when the counter-forensic reading is corroborated by trained examiners across multiple evidence vectors, when the absence-or-manipulation pattern is documented rather than impressionistic, and when a benign explanation for the missing evidence was actively excluded. Credibility falls when a single examiner infers scrubbing from one negative result, when the scene condition admits an ordinary cause, and when chain-of-custody or collection gaps could themselves explain the absent signature.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-vector corroboration — residue, biological, latent, and digital examiners independently note evidence defeat converging on the same scene.
Documented absence-against-expectation — the physical act required specific contact or residue that certified analysis affirmatively could not recover, not merely a routine negative.
Material trace of intent — recovered anti-forensic tooling, cleaning-agent purchases, or research into detection thresholds physically ties the actor to attribution defeat.
Examiner fidelity — certified cause-and-origin, explosives, or digital-forensic examiners reporting through formal channels, not a first-responder impression.
Method-specificity — the defeat pattern maps to a named forensic technique (ignitable-liquid-residue analysis, latent development, device imaging) rather than a vague 'clean scene.'
Collection integrity confirmed — sampling and chain of custody were sound, so the negative result reflects the scene, not the workup.
low_signal_anchors: Single-vector inference — scrubbing assumed from one negative residue or print result with no corroboration.
Ordinary-cause ambiguity — the fire, blast, or clean surface admits an accidental or routine-maintenance reading not excluded.
Collection-gap confound — degraded sampling, late scene access, or suppression-water washout could explain the absent signature.
Impressionistic reporting — 'it looked staged' without documented reference to what the act should have left.
Source-motivation misalignment — the report originates in an insurance or liability dispute with a stake in an arson-versus-accident finding.
Reconstructive narrative — the counter-forensic theory was assembled after an attribution failed, retrofitting intent to an unremarkable result.

capability.criteria: Capability rises with demonstrated fluency in how forensic attribution works and the discipline to defeat it consistently across vectors — residue, biology, latents, and digital media handled coherently and covertly. Capability falls with partial or inconsistent defeat, reliance on a single scrubbed vector while others are ignored, and measures that examiners recognize as amateur or that themselves leave signatures.
high_signal_anchors: Multi-vector coherence — residue obfuscation, biological and latent scrubbing, and digital wiping all executed against the same operation, not one vector alone.
Demonstrated forensic literacy — the actor reasons correctly about detection thresholds, persistence of residue, and what examiners can and cannot recover.
Anti-forensic tradecraft — use of validated tooling (device-wiping utilities, encryption, specialized cleaning regimes) applied competently and without leaving obvious counter-traces.
Pre-planned integration — counter-forensic measures were designed into the operation beforehand, evidenced by research and acquisition preceding the act.
Covert execution — the defeat measures themselves left minimal signature; no conspicuous purchase, disposal, or cleanup pattern was observable.
Scene-reconstruction awareness — the actor manipulated burn or blast patterns in a way that reflects understanding of how origin-and-cause is determined.
low_signal_anchors: Single-vector defeat — one evidence type scrubbed while others (digital, latent, residue) were left fully intact.
Amateur measures — cleanup that examiners immediately read as staged or that introduced its own recoverable signature (excess accelerant, cleaning-agent residue).
Threshold errors — the actor misjudged residue persistence or detection sensitivity, leaving recoverable signatures.
Conspicuous acquisition — anti-forensic materials or tooling bought under the actor's own identity with a clear record.
Inconsistent execution — defeat attempted on some surfaces or devices and forgotten on others.
Recognizable-tooling artifacts — anti-forensic software left characteristic wipe or metadata artifacts that examiners flagged.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the evidence-defeat is purposeful, pre-planned, and paired with the attack rather than incidental — research into forensic methods before the act, acquisition of scrubbing means, and manipulation aimed specifically at attribution. Intent falls when the 'defeat' is explicable as ordinary cleaning, fire dynamics, or routine device use, and when no pre-attack counter-forensic behavior is present.
high_signal_anchors: Pre-attack forensic research — the actor studied how investigators attribute fires, blasts, or digital acts before the operation.
Purposive acquisition — cleaning agents, specialized accelerants, gloves, or anti-forensic software obtained in advance and tied to the operation.
Attribution-directed manipulation — measures targeted precisely at what would identify the actor (prints on the ignition point, DNA on tools, device linkage), not general tidying.
Alternate-narrative staging — the scene was arranged to support a specific false cause (accidental ignition, electrical fault) rather than merely cleaned.
Sequenced defeat — counter-forensic steps follow the attack in a planned order (wipe devices, clean tools, obscure residue), indicating rehearsed intent.
Stated anti-attribution aim — the actor discussed avoiding forensic identification or 'leaving nothing to trace' with a third party or in recovered writings.
low_signal_anchors: Ordinary-cleaning explanation — the absent evidence is consistent with normal housekeeping or maintenance, not attribution defeat.
Fire-dynamics explanation — residue or pattern loss is explained by burn intensity, collapse, or suppression rather than deliberate obfuscation.
Routine device hygiene — deletions and encryption fit the actor's ordinary privacy practice, not operation-specific wiping.
No pre-attack footprint — no research, acquisition, or discussion of forensic defeat preceded the act.
Opportunistic tidying — post-act cleanup looks reactive and unfocused, not directed at specific attributive evidence.
Verifiable benign purpose — the acquired materials or software have an established legitimate use in the actor's life.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can actually defeat attribution — unobserved post-attack access to the scene and devices, time to work before responders arrive, and knowledge of which vectors matter. Opportunity falls when responder speed, surveillance, immutable logging, or preserved off-site records deny the actor the access or time needed; when opportunity appears reduced, whether the reduction is durable matters.
high_signal_anchors: Unobserved post-attack window — the actor had time at the scene, or with tools and devices, before detection or response closed it.
Scene and evidence control — the actor could reach the ignition point, tools, garments, and media without observation to work them.
Vector knowledge — the actor knew which evidence types investigators prioritize and where they collect, and could act on that.
Device and account control — the actor held the credentials and physical access needed to wipe or encrypt the linking digital record.
Absent independent record — no off-site logging, CCTV, or witness existed to preserve what the actor scrubbed at the scene.
Delayed discovery — the attack was not detected until after residue, biological traces, or volatile digital evidence had degraded or been removed.
low_signal_anchors: Rapid response closed the window — responders reached the scene before the actor could work it, preserving evidence. Durable unless response tempo drops.
Immutable off-site record survived — logging or backups outside the actor's reach preserved the digital linkage despite device wiping.
Surveillance captured the aftermath — CCTV or witnesses recorded the actor's post-attack presence, converting cleanup into evidence.
No unobserved access — the actor could not return to the scene or reach the devices without exposure. Transient if access is later regained.
Preserved collateral evidence — third-party records (vendor logs, cloud accounts, financial trails) outside the scene remained recoverable.
Forensic hardening in place — early scene preservation and specialized examiner tasking blocked the actor's known defeat methods; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Many innocent conditions mimic counter-forensics — a fire that destroys its own residue, a routinely cleaned workspace, a habitually encrypted phone. What separates a false positive is whether the absent or altered evidence has an ordinary physical or behavioral explanation, whether collection quality could account for it, and whether any pre-attack forensic-defeat footprint exists at all.
contexts: Fire and blast dynamics — high-intensity combustion, structural collapse, or suppression-water washout that destroys residue and patterns without any human obfuscation.
Routine cleaning and maintenance — janitorial, industrial, or personal cleaning that removes biological and latent evidence as an ordinary byproduct.
Normal digital hygiene — habitual encryption, auto-deletion, privacy tooling, or device turnover consistent with the actor's established practice.
Collection and custody limits — degraded sampling, late scene access, contamination, or lab sensitivity limits that produce negatives unrelated to actor conduct.
Legitimate anti-forensic professions — security researchers, penetration testers, digital-privacy practitioners, and remediation contractors whose lawful work involves the same tools and techniques.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Counter-forensic findings are most decisive when read together with the attack they follow and with any pre-attack forensic-defeat footprint, not in isolation. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: the credibility of the defeat reading across examiners, its breadth across evidence vectors, and whether a pre-planned intent footprint exists. A single-vector negative with an available ordinary-cause explanation sits at the monitoring tier. A documented absence-against-expectation confirmed by a certified examiner, or recovered anti-forensic tooling, sits at the investigation tier. Multi-vector defeat corroborated across residue, biological, latent, and digital examiners — or defeat paired with pre-attack forensic research and acquisition — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating the case as a deliberate attribution-defeat operation. Counter-forensic activity continuing to frustrate a worked case despite specialized examiner tasking sits at the committed-actor tier and argues for expanded collection aperture, third-party record preservation, and inter-agency lab coordination. Because counter-forensics is designed to shrink the evidentiary picture, multiple weak or single-vector findings that correlate temporally or by method may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any one warrants; triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers documentation and preservation; investigation triggers specialized-examiner tasking and a scene- and device-preservation order; elevation triggers expanded multi-vector collection and third-party record preservation; the committed-actor tier triggers inter-agency forensic coordination; an identified actor matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Certified examiners document a facility fire or blast scene that yields no recoverable ignitable-liquid or explosive-residue signature despite physical evidence that an accelerant or charge was used, consistent with deliberate obfuscation of the residue analysis rather than an accidental cause

Investigators recover a scene notable for the absence of expected biological or latent-print evidence — surfaces wiped, cleaning agents applied, or gloves indicated — inconsistent with the physical contact the attack required, with anti-forensic cleaning materials traceable in procurement or financial records

Threat actor wipes, encrypts, or destroys the digital traces linking them to the facility or the operation — purged search history, wiped or reset devices, deleted cloud accounts, or anti-forensic software artifacts discovered on recovered media

Threat actor researches or discusses how fire, blast, or digital investigators reconstruct scenes and attribute acts — studying residue-detection thresholds, evidence-recovery methods, or failed-prosecution case write-ups — indicating pre-planned counter-forensic intent tied to a facility operation

Threat actor manipulates the post-attack facility scene to defeat cause-and-origin reconstruction — staging an alternate accidental narrative, introducing misleading ignition sources, or disrupting the burn or blast patterns examiners rely on to determine origin

countermeasures.measure: Task certified cause-and-origin, explosives, and forensic examiners to work facility attack scenes with full multi-vector capture — ignitable-liquid residue, biological, latent, and trace — so that single-vector scrubbing cannot defeat attribution and absence-against-expectation is documented deliberately
countermeasures.limitations: Specialized examiner capacity is limited and often external; high-intensity fire or collapse can destroy residue independent of any obfuscation, and negatives remain ambiguous without corroboration

countermeasures.measure: Maintain immutable, off-site and redundant logging of facility access, network, and security telemetry so that device wiping or on-scene destruction cannot erase the digital record that links an actor to the operation
countermeasures.limitations: Off-site logging preserves only what was already captured; gaps in coverage, short retention windows, and encrypted actor-owned devices outside the facility remain beyond reach

countermeasures.measure: During investigation, cross-reference procurement, retail, and financial records for anti-forensic materials — specialized accelerants, cleaning agents, gloves, and anti-forensic software — to recover the acquisition footprint that on-scene scrubbing was meant to hide
countermeasures.limitations: Cash purchases, common dual-use materials, and third-party or cut-out acquisition defeat record-matching; results require legal process and are retrospective

countermeasures.measure: Train first responders and investigators to recognize counter-forensic staging and absence-of-evidence patterns, to preserve the scene and chain of custody aggressively, and to escalate suspected attribution defeat to specialized examiners rather than accepting an accidental-cause narrative at face value
countermeasures.limitations: Recognition depends on responder experience and scene tempo; over-reading absence as obfuscation risks false positives against fire dynamics and routine cleaning, so it informs escalation rather than conclusion

response_protocols.trigger: Scene indicators of counter-forensic activity at a facility attack — documented absence of expected residue, biological, or latent evidence; signs of scrubbing; or manipulation of burn or blast patterns inconsistent with an accidental cause
response_protocols.action: Preserve the scene and hold the accidental-cause narrative open. Task certified cause-and-origin, explosives, and forensic examiners for full multi-vector capture. Order preservation of facility logs, CCTV, and any recoverable devices. Document the absence-against-expectation reasoning and the collection integrity supporting it.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Multi-vector defeat corroborated across examiners, OR discovery of pre-attack forensic research or anti-forensic tooling tied to an identified actor
response_protocols.legal_notes: Scene preservation, sampling, and any device seizure must follow warrant and chain-of-custody requirements; an arson-versus-accident determination carries insurance and liability implications, so document the forensic basis carefully. Consult counsel before compelled record production.

response_protocols.trigger: Discovery of anti-forensic research, tooling, or acquisition — device-wiping utilities, encryption, cleaning-agent or specialized-accelerant purchases, or study of forensic-defeat methods — tied to an identified actor or the operation
response_protocols.action: Forensically image recovered media before any further access. Preserve and, through legal process, subpoena third-party and off-site records (cloud accounts, procurement, retail, financial) that on-scene scrubbing could not reach. Coordinate with digital-forensic and lab units to reconstruct the linkage the actor attempted to defeat.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Recovered evidence establishes a pre-planned, multi-vector attribution-defeat effort, OR the actor matches a known threat-actor profile
response_protocols.legal_notes: Digital imaging, account preservation, and third-party subpoenas require proper legal authority and documented investigative basis; anti-forensic tools have lawful uses, so tie possession to the operation before drawing conclusions. Preserve original media integrity to withstand challenge.

tactics.field_notes: Counter-forensics is almost never caught in the act — it is inferred from the gap between what the attack physically required and what the scene will give up. The tell is absence against expectation: a fire that clearly involved an accelerant but yields no ignitable-liquid residue, an ignition point that should carry prints or DNA but is wiped, a suspect whose devices are scrubbed clean the day of the act. Distinguish this from Evidence Management, which is about removing or planting specific items; counter-forensics attacks the analysis itself, so a fully worked scene still comes back empty. The discipline is not to over-read absence — high-intensity fire, suppression washout, and routine cleaning all destroy evidence innocently — but to treat a documented, method-specific, multi-vector absence, especially when paired with a pre-attack forensic-research footprint, as deliberate attribution defeat. The most recoverable signal is usually off-scene: what the actor bought, searched, or could not wipe because it lived on someone else's server.
observed_contexts: arson case where certified examiners documented a multi-point origin consistent with accelerant use yet recovered no ignitable-liquid residue, with cleaning-agent purchases surfacing in later record checks
facility bombing in which the actor's recovered devices had been wiped and encrypted the day of the attack while off-site network logs preserved the linking access record
sabotage scene staged to present as an electrical fault, with misleading ignition sources introduced to defeat cause-and-origin reconstruction
[literature: USFA-ARSON-2021 / NFPA-INTENTIONAL-2021 pattern — intentional-fire scenes engineered to frustrate ignitable-liquid-residue analysis and origin determination]

tactics.name: Secondary Device / Re-attack Positioning
tactics.notes: Emplacement of a secondary device, or physical positioning for a renewed attack, timed to the response that follows an initial attack on the facility — deliberately aimed at arriving responders, evacuating and returning occupants, and the personnel who converge on the scene. This tactic captures the re-attack as a defender observes it: a second device positioned along the expected responder approach, at the command post, at a casualty-collection or muster point, or at the reunification site; an actor who withdraws to an overwatch vantage over the response rather than fleeing; or leakage that a follow-on strike is intended. Distinct from Withdrawal (TF0401), where the actor's objective is escape; here the actor's objective is a second wave of harm directed at the people the first attack drew into the open. Because the secondary threat is placed where responders and occupants mass, contact with it applies direct physical force to those persons — the highest-severity behavior in the aftermath phase.
tactics.cpn_notes: Re-attack positioning is increasingly informed by publicly exposed emergency-response detail — published evacuation and reunification plans, fixed muster points and assembly areas, predictable first-responder staging and command-post locations, and hospital-approach routing that let an actor anticipate exactly where responders and occupants will converge and place a secondary device or overwatch accordingly.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with physical evidence of a second device or emplaced object at a point the response will occupy, corroboration across modalities that an actor remained or re-positioned rather than fled, and recoverable reporting that ties the actor to the re-attack posture. Credibility falls when the signal is a single uncorroborated report, when an unattended object at a chaotic scene admits an innocent lost-property explanation, and when no path from the observed behavior to a massing of persons was established.
high_signal_anchors: Physical evidence of a secondary threat — a second device, suspicious package, or emplaced object recovered along a responder approach route, at the command post, or at a casualty-collection, muster, or reunification point that the response will occupy.
Cross-modal corroboration — an emplaced object, an actor placed on CCTV lingering or re-positioning after the attack, and post-attack leakage of a second-wave intent within overlapping timeframes.
Withdrawal-then-overwatch pattern — the actor is observed leaving the immediate scene and taking up a vantage over the assembling response rather than continuing to escape.

First-hand witness fidelity — a named witness who saw the actor place an object at a staging point, or remain in an overwatch position, and reported it through a formal channel with time and location.

Behavioral specificity — the observed positioning concentrates on where responders and evacuees will actually mass (the known approach, the reunification site, the occupied assembly area) rather than a vague post-attack presence.
Sequencing consistent with a planned second wave — the timing of the object or the re-positioning is keyed to the arrival of the response, not to escape.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — single anonymous report of 'a bag left behind' that cannot be re-contacted or corroborated against any other signal.
Lost-property ambiguity — an unattended item at an evacuation route or assembly point that plausibly belongs to a fleeing occupant and was never assessed as a device.
No path to massing persons — the observed behavior does not connect to any location the response or the returning occupants will occupy.
Bystander-presence ambiguity — a person lingering near the scene who is plausibly an onlooker, a witness, or a returning occupant rather than a re-positioned actor.
Temporal-pattern weakness — a one-time presence near the perimeter with no accompanying object, leakage, or overwatch behavior.
Reconstructive memory — a reporting delay during which an ordinary evacuation artifact or onlooker was retrofitted to a secondary-device narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the actor demonstrates the means to place a second harmful effect where the response will converge — a functioning secondary device, a defensible overwatch position with reach onto the assembly area, and understanding of how responders and occupants will move after the first attack. Capability falls with no functioning secondary means, conspicuous behavior that is recognized before the response arrives, and positioning that does not actually cover where persons will mass.
high_signal_anchors: Functioning secondary means — evidence the actor possesses or has emplaced a genuinely hazardous second device rather than an inert or abandoned object.
Overwatch with reach — the actor occupies a vantage that genuinely covers the responder approach, command post, or assembly area, not a position without a line to where persons gather.

Response-pattern literacy — the actor reasons correctly about where first responders stage, where casualties are collected, and where occupants reunify, and positions the secondary threat accordingly.
Covert emplacement tradecraft — the second device or the re-positioning is concealed within the disorder of the evacuation so it survives the initial scene sweep undetected.
Timing discipline keyed to the response — the secondary effect is set to the predictable arrival window of responders rather than triggered prematurely.

Insider or prior-reconnaissance advantage — the actor exploits known staging doctrine, muster points, or approach routes obtained through an insider role or earlier surveillance of the facility's emergency plan.
low_signal_anchors: No functioning secondary means — the recovered object is inert, abandoned, or poses no real hazard to the response.
Position without reach — the actor's location does not actually cover any point where responders or occupants will mass.
No response-pattern literacy — the chosen point misjudges how the response will move, revealing a misunderstanding of responder and evacuation behavior.
Conspicuous posture recognized early — obvious loitering, an obviously placed package, or overwatch behavior spotted and cleared before the response converged.
Single clumsy attempt — one uncoordinated re-approach with no concealment and no timing to the response.
Positioning defeated at first contact — perimeter control, a scene sweep, or law-enforcement observation removed the actor or the object before persons were exposed.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the actor's behavior moves from escaping the scene toward covering the response, when the secondary threat is placed and timed to strike responders and returning occupants specifically, and when the positioning pairs with a stated intent to inflict a second wave or with grievance against responders or the institution. Intent falls with behavior explained by ordinary escape or bystander presence, positioning that does not reach persons, and a verifiable legitimate purpose for remaining near the scene.
high_signal_anchors: Escape-to-re-attack progression — an observable shift from fleeing to positioning over, or emplacing a device at, the point the response will occupy.

Response-timed emplacement or presence — the secondary object or the overwatch is keyed to the arrival of responders and the assembly of evacuees, revealing exposure of the response itself as the objective.
Concentration on where persons converge — attention fixed on the responder approach, casualty-collection point, or reunification site rather than on the primary scene.

Hostile attribution toward the response paired with positioning — the actor has voiced grievance against first responders, law enforcement, or the institution AND is observed emplacing a secondary threat or taking an overwatch over the response; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way no single indicator captures.
Concealment aimed at surviving the sweep — steps taken so the secondary threat outlasts the initial scene search imply intent to strike the response as it builds.
Second-wave leakage — post-attack statements, claims, or communications referencing a follow-on device or a renewed strike on those who respond.
low_signal_anchors: Escape-consistent behavior — the actor's movement is fully explained by fleeing the scene, with no coverage of the response.
Bystander-consistent presence — remaining near the scene is explained by witness, onlooker, or returning-occupant status that checks out.
Positioning without reach to persons — the observed location cannot expose any responder or occupant.
One-time perimeter presence without escalation — presence surfaced but no object, leakage, or overwatch pattern followed.
Verifiable legitimate purpose — off-duty responder, credentialed press, or accountable-occupant status surfaces and is confirmed.
Abandoned rather than emplaced — the object is discarded in flight, not positioned to cover the response.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the response is forced into predictable, pre-surveilled locations the actor can cover, when the initial scene sweep is incomplete, and when the actor retains reach onto the assembly of persons through position, timing, or insider knowledge of the emergency plan. Opportunity falls when responder staging is varied and unpredictable, when disciplined secondary-sweep doctrine denies the actor a survivable emplacement, and when perimeter control removes the actor's line to where persons mass; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: Predictable response geography — responders, command post, casualty collection, and reunification default to fixed, publicly known locations the actor could anticipate and cover.
Incomplete scene sweep — the response occupies ground before a secondary-device search cleared it, leaving an emplaced threat live among persons.
Retained overwatch reach — the actor holds a vantage over the assembling response that has not been observed, challenged, or denied.
Insider knowledge of the emergency plan — the actor knows the facility's evacuation routes, muster points, and staging doctrine through a role or prior reconnaissance and exploits them.
Timing advantage over the response — the secondary threat is set to a responder-arrival window the defenders have not varied or protected.
Uncontrolled perimeter — no cordon or observation denies the actor the ability to remain within reach of where persons converge.
low_signal_anchors: Varied, unpredictable staging — responder approach, command post, and assembly points are changed from the pre-surveilled defaults, denying the actor a fixed target. Durable signal if made routine.
Disciplined secondary sweep completed — a systematic search cleared the response ground before occupancy, actively removing the emplacement opportunity rather than failing to find it.
Overwatch denied by observation — counter-observation or a cordon identified and blocked the vantage the actor needed. Transient unless sustained through the response.
Institutional rule-out of insider knowledge — the emergency plan's staging detail is compartmented or was confirmed not exposed, not merely presumed secure.
Perimeter control closed the reach — an enforced cordon put the actor beyond any line to where persons mass; sticky unless the actor adapts or the cordon drops.
Response completed before re-attack window — the assembly dispersed before the actor could set or trigger a secondary effect.

false_positive_context.criteria: The disorder of a post-attack scene produces many behaviors that resemble re-attack positioning on the surface — an evacuee's dropped bag looks like an emplaced device; an onlooker or returning occupant looks like a re-positioned actor; press at a vantage looks like overwatch. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the object has an accountable owner, whether the person has a verifiable reason to be near the scene, and whether any actual reach to a massing of persons exists.
contexts: Evacuation artifacts — bags, containers, and personal property abandoned by fleeing occupants and staff during the initial evacuation, later recovered as lost property.
Legitimate scene presence — off-duty and mutual-aid responders self-deploying, credentialed press at an established vantage, and utility or facilities staff supporting the response.
Returning and reunifying occupants — evacuated occupants moving back toward the building for belongings, pets, or family members and gathering at the reunification point.
Onlookers and witnesses — bystanders drawn to the scene, and witnesses remaining to give statements, who linger at the perimeter without any operational reach.
Ordinary deliveries and vehicles — parked or delivery vehicles near the scene with a routine business purpose that predates the attack and are not positioned to cover the response.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Any indication of a secondary device or a re-positioned actor at a scene under response is treated as an active, imminent threat to life and warrants immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier — the standing assumption for a post-attack scene is that a second threat may be present. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: the credibility of the secondary-threat indicator, its reach to where responders and occupants will mass, and its timing to the arrival of the response. A single low-credibility signal with an available lost-property or bystander explanation and no reach to persons sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility indicator — an emplaced object at a staging point, or an actor in overwatch over the assembly — sits immediately at the elevation tier because force-on-person is imminent, not at a lower investigative tier. Cross-modal corroboration — an emplaced object, an actor observed re-positioning, and second-wave leakage against the same response — sits at the committed-actor tier and warrants treating the scene as an ongoing coordinated attack. Multiple lower-confidence signals correlating temporally at the points where persons converge may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers a secondary-device sweep and logging; elevation triggers a halt to responder ingress, standoff cordon, and relocation of casualty-collection and command elements beyond blast radius; the committed-actor tier triggers a defensive-posture upgrade across the response and urgent law-enforcement and EOD coordination; a confirmed device or a confirmed re-positioned actor at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement action to protect the response.

indicators.behavior: A secondary device or suspicious emplaced object is discovered positioned along the expected first-responder approach route, at the command-post location, or at a casualty-collection point serving the scene, consistent with an intent to strike arriving responders

Threat actor is observed withdrawing from the immediate scene and taking up an overwatch position with a vantage over the assembling response or the occupant muster point, consistent with positioning for a renewed direct attack on responders and returning occupants
Post-attack communication, claim, or leakage references a follow-on device or a renewed strike aimed at those who respond, warning of a second wave against responders or returning occupants

An unattended package, container, or vehicle is found positioned at an evacuation route, occupant assembly area, or reunification point where displaced occupants gather, before any render-safe or scene sweep has cleared it

Threat actor delays egress or re-approaches the scene during the response phase, timing movement to responder arrival in a pattern consistent with observing, triggering, or re-engaging a secondary effect rather than escaping

countermeasures.measure: Adopt standing secondary-device doctrine that treats every post-attack scene as potentially containing a second threat: stage responders short of the scene, control ingress along swept routes, and systematically search command-post, casualty-collection, and muster points before they are occupied
