countermeasures.limitations: Depends on responder discipline under pressure; a determined actor may conceal a device to survive a rushed sweep, and the doctrine slows life-saving response to reduce secondary exposure

countermeasures.measure: Vary and pre-plan multiple responder staging, command-post, casualty-collection, and reunification locations so the response does not default to fixed, publicly known points an actor could pre-surveil and cover
countermeasures.limitations: Alternate sites must still be reachable and functional; published emergency plans and habitual practice can re-expose the defaults, and coordination overhead grows with the number of options

countermeasures.measure: Post overwatch and perimeter observation during the response to detect a re-positioned actor holding a vantage over the assembling response, and integrate scene-camera review to identify anyone lingering or returning against the flow of evacuation
countermeasures.limitations: Requires trained observers and camera coverage of vantage points and approaches; a disciplined actor may blend with onlookers or press, and overwatch competes for resources during a mass-casualty response

countermeasures.measure: Establish standoff cordons and pre-arranged EOD and bomb-squad liaison so a discovered secondary device is isolated, personnel are held beyond blast radius, and reoccupation is withheld until render-safe and a full sweep are complete
countermeasures.limitations: EOD response and cordon enforcement take time and personnel; standoff distances conflict with the urgency of casualty care, and reoccupation delay carries its own operational cost

response_protocols.trigger: A secondary device, suspicious emplaced object, or a re-positioned actor is indicated at a scene already under response (device found on an approach route, at a staging point, or at a muster or reunification location, or an actor observed in overwatch)
response_protocols.action: Treat the scene as an active, ongoing attack. Halt or hold responder ingress, establish a standoff cordon, and relocate the command post, casualty-collection point, and assembly areas beyond blast radius. Initiate a systematic secondary-device sweep of all ground the response will occupy, request EOD and law-enforcement support, and account for the actor. Withhold reoccupation until render-safe and sweep are complete. Document all sourcing and timing.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: A secondary device is confirmed, the actor is confirmed in an overwatch or re-engagement posture, or a second effect is initiated against the response
response_protocols.legal_notes: Render-safe, cordon enforcement, and scene control are law-enforcement and EOD functions; facility action supports and does not substitute for them. Preserve the scene for investigation to the extent life-safety allows, and document the threat basis for reoccupation-delay decisions.

response_protocols.trigger: Post-attack leakage, a claim, or communications reference a follow-on device or a renewed strike on responders or returning occupants, without a device yet located
response_protocols.action: Maintain the scene as active. Extend and hold the cordon, brief responders on the second-wave indicator, and coordinate law-enforcement overwatch of the approaches and assembly areas. Delay reoccupation and reunification until a full sweep is complete, and message occupants and staff to remain clear of the scene and assembly points.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: The referenced device is located, the actor re-engages, or corroborating physical or CCTV indicators of re-attack positioning surface
response_protocols.legal_notes: Public messaging during an active scene should be coordinated with law enforcement to avoid compromising the response or the investigation; document the threat basis for extended cordon and reoccupation-delay decisions to support proportionality.

tactics.field_notes: Secondary devices and re-attack positioning are aimed at the response itself — the people the first attack pulls into the open: responders on a predictable approach, a command post at the usual spot, families at the reunification point. The clearest tell is anything that seems designed to invite a crowd into a fixed location, or an actor who does not behave like someone escaping — who withdraws to a vantage over the scene, delays leaving, or re-approaches as responders arrive. The hardest problem is the disorder of the scene: dropped bags, onlookers, returning occupants, and press all look like the thing you fear, so the discipline is to assume a second threat is present until a sweep clears the ground the response will occupy, and to vary the staging so there is no predictable crowd to strike.
observed_contexts: bombing case in which a second device was placed along the expected first-responder approach and near the command-post location to strike arriving personnel
attack where the actor withdrew to an elevated overwatch and re-engaged responders and evacuees as they assembled at the muster point
incident in which an unattended package left at the occupant reunification site forced a second evacuation before it could be rendered safe
[literature: ATF-EIR-2024 / START-GTD-2020 pattern — secondary devices and re-attack positioning directed at responders and returning occupants following an initial facility attack]

tactics.name: Attribution Declaration
tactics.notes: After an attack on the facility, the threat actor claims responsibility and signs the act — asserting authorship publicly through a communique, manifesto release, social-media claim, media contact, or physical signature left at the site. Distinct from Audience Amplification (which spreads and publicizes the attack for reach) and from Symbolic Messaging (which encodes ideological meaning into the act); Attribution Declaration is specifically about ownership — who did this and on whose behalf. Claiming converts an anonymous act into an attributable one, trading operational anonymity for the intimidation, recruitment, and campaign-signaling value of a named authorship. The declaration may be spontaneous or pre-staged, released by the individual actor or routed through an organizational channel, and can precede detonation in drafted form while surfacing only in the aftermath.
tactics.cpn_notes: Attribution is increasingly staged and delivered online — pre-written manifestos scheduled for automatic release at the moment of attack, communiques posted to movement forums and encrypted channels, and dedicated media wings that authenticate and distribute claims. The digital claim often reaches an audience before the physical scene is processed, and pre-staged attribution materials recovered from devices can tie an actor to the act independent of the public claim.

credibility.criteria: Credibility of an attribution claim rises when the claim carries proof of genuine authorship — non-public hold-back detail only the perpetrator would know, forensic corroboration, signature markers matching a known actor, and a single authoritative channel with timing consistent with the act. Credibility falls when the claim is generic, opportunistic, anonymous, contradicted by forensics, or one of several competing claims for the same event.
high_signal_anchors: Hold-back knowledge — the claim contains operational detail (device placement, entry method, timing, target-specific facts) that was not publicly released and only the perpetrator would possess.
Forensic corroboration — physical, digital, or signature evidence at the site independently supports the claimant's account of the act.
Signature continuity — tags, symbols, phrasing, or tradecraft in the claim match a previously attributed actor or group's established pattern.
Single authoritative channel — the claim issues from one established, verifiable outlet or account rather than scattered anonymous posts.
Temporal consistency — the claim surfaces on a timeline consistent with genuine authorship, not lagging behind open reporting it could have copied.
Recovered pre-staged materials — a drafted manifesto, recorded statement, or prepared communique found on the actor's devices matches the public claim.
low_signal_anchors: Detail-poverty — the claim recites only facts already in press coverage, with no non-public specificity.
Opportunistic bandwagon claim — a group or individual claims a high-profile attack to gain reflected notoriety without evidence of involvement.
Competing-claim environment — multiple actors claim the same act, none corroborated.
Anonymity without proof — the claim is fully anonymous and offers no verifiable authorship marker.
Forensic contradiction — the claimant's account conflicts with established facts of the scene.
Reconstructive timing — the claim appears only after extensive public reporting, consistent with a copy rather than authorship.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the attribution apparatus is disciplined and effective — professional communique production, an established distribution network, embedded proof-of-authorship, and operational security that lets the actor claim while preserving anonymity or acceptable exposure. Capability falls with crude, unproofed, self-incriminating, or low-reach claims that fail to land or to be believed.
high_signal_anchors: Production quality — the claim is a structured, edited communique or manifesto rather than an off-hand remark, indicating deliberate messaging capacity.
Established distribution reach — the actor commands or accesses a channel (media wing, forum, follower network) that carries the claim to a real audience.
Embedded proof-of-authorship — the claim is built to be verified, incorporating hold-back detail or signature markers deliberately.
Claim-time operational security — the actor asserts authorship while managing exposure (anonymized release, controlled channel) rather than incidentally self-incriminating.
Multi-platform or multi-language release — the claim is prepared for cross-platform propagation, showing an amplification-aware apparatus.
Coordination with an attribution organ — the claim is authenticated and released through a group's designated media or claims process.
low_signal_anchors: Crude claim — an unstructured boast with no framing, proof, or distribution plan.
No proof offered — the claim asserts authorship but supplies nothing verifiable.
Single low-reach platform — the claim sits on one account with no propagation path.
Uncontrolled self-incrimination — the actor exposes identity carelessly with no deliberate anonymity design, indicating no apparatus.
No organizational backing — no media wing, spokesperson, or authentication process stands behind the claim.
Failed propagation — the claim is deplatformed, ignored, or fails to reach any meaningful audience.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the declaration is instrumental — claiming to intimidate an audience, recruit, signal an ongoing campaign, coerce a target, or inspire emulation, especially with future-directed language. Intent falls when the claim is purely expressive, personal, notoriety-only, and carries no audience-directed or forward-looking aim.
high_signal_anchors: Campaign framing — the claim positions the attack as one act in an ongoing series and signals or calls for more.
Audience-directed intimidation — the declaration explicitly addresses a target population or class to instill fear.
Recruitment or call-to-action content — the claim solicits others to act, join, or emulate.
Named future targets — the declaration names or categorizes further facilities or classes as intended targets.
Propaganda-of-the-deed framing — the claim treats the attack as a communicative act meant to inspire, not merely to report.
Ideological future-orientation — grievance is tied to a forward-looking program, not a closed personal grievance.
low_signal_anchors: Purely expressive claim — an assertion of authorship with no audience-directed or forward aim.
Notoriety-only motivation — the claim seeks personal fame with no campaign, cause, or call to action.
Closed personal grievance — the stated motive is a settled individual dispute with no forward orientation.
No audience targeting — the declaration addresses no population and issues no threat.
One-off framing — the claim explicitly presents the act as finished and singular.
Absence of emulation cues — nothing in the claim invites or models further action.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can make the claim land — a ready audience, an uncontested distribution channel, a high-attention news window, and a media ecosystem that will carry or amplify the declaration. Opportunity falls when the actor lacks audience, channels are denied or deplatformed, the news cycle is contested, or the claim is buried; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: Ready audience — the actor has an existing following or movement primed to receive and spread the claim.
Uncontested channel — the actor controls or reliably accesses a distribution path not subject to takedown.
High-attention window — the claim lands during a peak news cycle that maximizes reach and effect.
Sympathetic ecosystem — a media or online environment predisposed to carry, translate, or valorize the claim.
Platform amplification — algorithmic or network dynamics propagate the claim beyond the actor's own reach.
Verification-ready posture — the actor can supply proof on demand, sustaining media and follower interest in the claim.
low_signal_anchors: No audience — the actor has no following and no path to one; the claim reaches almost no one.
Channel denial — platforms deplatform or remove the claim faster than it can spread. Durable if enforcement is sustained.
Contested news cycle — a larger competing story buries the claim.
Hostile ecosystem — the surrounding media environment refuses to carry or actively debunks the claim.
No verification capacity — the actor cannot substantiate authorship, so interest decays. Transient if proof later surfaces.
Attribution suppression agreement — responsible-reporting or no-amplification practices deny the claim oxygen; transient unless sustained across outlets.

false_positive_context.criteria: Many communications resemble a genuine attribution declaration without being one — false claimants seeking reflected notoriety, hoaxers, researchers and journalists quoting or reposting a claim, and simple misattribution. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the claim carries verifiable authorship, whether the speaker is the perpetrator or merely relaying, and whether institutional accountability behind the account can be checked.
contexts: Opportunistic false claimants — individuals or groups claiming a high-profile attack for notoriety or recruitment leverage without any involvement.
Hoax and prank claims — fabricated communiques or boasts issued for attention, disruption, or to misdirect investigators.
Journalistic and research relay — reporters, analysts, and OSINT researchers quoting, archiving, or reposting a claim in the course of legitimate work.
Automated and bot reposting — accounts amplifying or duplicating a claim without originating it, inflating apparent claim volume.
Parody, satire, and misattribution — commentary or error that surfaces as an apparent claim without any authorship behind it.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: An attribution claim is triaged first on credibility, then on what the claim signals forward. A claim reciting only public facts, offered anonymously with no proof, sits at the monitoring tier pending verification and should not drive attribution decisions on its own. A claim carrying non-public hold-back detail, forensic corroboration, or signature continuity with a known actor sits at the investigation tier and warrants formal attribution analysis and law-enforcement coordination. A verified claim that frames the attack as part of a campaign, names or categorizes further targets, or issues a call to emulate sits at the elevation tier — it indicates continuing intent and elevated copycat and re-attack risk, and should trigger a follow-on-threat assessment and protective-posture review for the facility class. A claim routed through an established organizational channel or media wing, or corroborated by recovered pre-staged attribution materials, sits at the committed-actor tier and warrants urgent law-enforcement and fusion-center coordination for cross-incident linkage. Multiple weak or competing claims for the same act may still compose to an actionable picture when signature or forensic threads converge on one authorship; consumer triage tooling should make this composition explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers claim logging and channel watch; investigation triggers attribution analysis and evidence preservation; elevation triggers a follow-on-threat and copycat assessment plus responsible-reporting coordination; the committed-actor tier triggers law-enforcement referral and cross-incident linkage.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor publicly claims responsibility for the attack on the facility — a communique, social-media post, or message to media naming the site and asserting authorship
Threat actor releases a manifesto or ideological statement tied to the attack, explaining motive and framing the targeted facility as a symbolic objective
Threat actor signs the act — leaving graffiti, tags, symbols, or an organizational name at the site or in the claim to attribute the attack to a person or group

Threat actor routes the claim through an organizational channel or media outlet — formal communique distribution, press contact, or authenticated forum posting — to establish authoritative attribution
Threat actor drafts and stages attribution materials in advance — a pre-written claim, recorded statement, or prepared manifesto scheduled or held for release at the time of the attack

countermeasures.measure: Monitor extremist forums, social-media channels, encrypted platforms, and media inboxes for attribution claims and communiques following any incident at the facility or its peer class
countermeasures.limitations: Coverage is incomplete; claims on closed or encrypted channels are not visible, and genuine claims may be indistinguishable from opportunistic ones without corroboration

countermeasures.measure: Establish a claim-verification protocol that authenticates or refutes attribution claims — matching hold-back detail, signature markers, and forensic corroboration — before any public attribution is made
countermeasures.limitations: Verification depends on preserved hold-back detail and forensic quality; sophisticated false claims and deliberate misdirection can defeat rapid authentication

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with platforms, media, and fusion partners on responsible-reporting and no-amplification practices that deny the actor the audience and propaganda payoff of a claim
countermeasures.limitations: No-amplification depends on voluntary media and platform cooperation; a determined claim can still propagate through sympathetic or uncontrolled channels

countermeasures.measure: Preserve and catalog signature evidence — tags, symbols, communique language, and claim metadata — for attribution and cross-incident linkage, feeding it to fusion centers and forensic databases
countermeasures.limitations: Linkage value depends on shared repositories and reporting discipline across jurisdictions; novel actors with no prior signature yield no immediate match

response_protocols.trigger: An attribution claim, communique, manifesto, or signature marker surfaces in connection with an attack on the facility
response_protocols.action: Activate the claim-verification and attribution workflow. Within the first operational period: (a) capture and preserve the claim and any signature evidence, (b) test the claim against non-public hold-back detail and scene forensics, (c) check signature continuity against known-actor and cross-incident databases, (d) refer to law enforcement and coordinate no public attribution until authenticated. Document sourcing and chain of custody.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Claim authenticates against hold-back detail or forensic corroboration, OR the claim is routed through a known organizational channel, OR pre-staged attribution materials are recovered
response_protocols.legal_notes: Public attribution carries defamation, prejudicial-publicity, and investigative-integrity risks; make no formal attribution before authentication and coordinate messaging with counsel and law enforcement.

response_protocols.trigger: A verified claim or manifesto frames the attack as part of a campaign, names further targets, or issues a call to emulate
response_protocols.action: Elevate to a follow-on-threat and copycat assessment. Brief facility and peer-class security leadership, raise protective posture for the exposure window, coordinate with fusion centers and law enforcement on campaign and re-attack risk, and manage public messaging with responsible-reporting partners to limit amplification. Reassess as the news window closes.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Campaign framing resolves to a specific named next target or a date-certain follow-on threat
response_protocols.legal_notes: Posture changes and public communications must be documented against the threat basis to support proportionality; coordinate cross-jurisdiction sharing consistent with information-handling rules.

tactics.field_notes: The claim is where an anonymous act becomes an attributable one, and the actor trades operational cover for the payoff of authorship — intimidation, recruitment, standing within a movement. The strongest early signal is not the loudest claim but the one carrying detail no one outside the act could know; opportunistic and hoax claims cluster around high-profile attacks and recite only what the press already published. Pre-staged material matters disproportionately: a manifesto scheduled to auto-publish, or a recorded statement recovered from a device, ties an actor to the act independent of the public claim and often reveals campaign intent before investigators would otherwise see it. Treat the forward-looking content of a verified claim — campaign framing, named next targets, calls to emulate — as the operational half of the signal; that is where a finished attack turns into a warning about the next one.
observed_contexts: extremist actor posting a communique to a movement forum within hours of an arson at a clinic, claiming the act and framing it ideologically
attacker's pre-recorded manifesto auto-published to social platforms at the moment of a facility attack, recovered later from the actor's devices
spray-painted organizational symbol and slogan left at a firebombed site to signal authorship and movement affiliation
[literature: CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 / FBI-HATECRIME-2024 pattern — post-attack claims and manifestos used to attribute, intimidate, and inspire emulation]

tactics.name: Audience Amplification
tactics.notes: Deliberate spreading and publicizing of a completed facility attack to maximize its reach, reaction, and downstream effect — releasing self-recorded footage or livestream, running hashtag and meme campaigns, distributing propaganda packages, mirroring content to defeat takedowns, and seeding imitation among sympathizers. Distinct from Attribution Declaration (TF0409), which claims and signs the act, and from Symbolic Messaging (TF0411), which encodes the ideological meaning of the act; Audience Amplification is about the propagation itself — the volume, velocity, and virality of the aftermath, and the copycat and contagion effect that a widely circulated attack produces. The harm here is not the original strike but its multiplication: reach that terrorizes a wider population, recruits, and lowers the threshold for the next actor.
tactics.cpn_notes: Amplification is now overwhelmingly a networked-media phenomenon — attack footage is staged for livestream and short-form platforms, media kits are pre-positioned on file-hosts and channels, and sympathizer networks re-upload and translate content faster than any single platform can remove it. The public-facing nature of amplification makes the behavior visible, but attribution of the amplifying network and interdiction of mirrored copies remain hard.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises with corroboration across platforms, persistence of the amplification pattern over time, and recoverable artifacts that tie the spreading activity to the attack and to an identifiable actor or network. Credibility falls when the source, the content, or the temporal pattern is thin, and when an organic news or bystander reaction was never distinguished from actor-driven amplification.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-platform corroboration — the same attack media, framing, and hashtags appear in coordinated form across multiple platforms within overlapping timeframes.
Temporal persistence — amplification sustained across days to weeks through re-uploads and mirrors, not a single viral spike.
Material evidence — recovered upload logs, prepared media kits, account clusters, or communications that physically tie the spreading activity to the attack and its author.
First-hand attribution fidelity — the amplifying accounts demonstrably originate with the actor or a known sympathizer network rather than unaffiliated commentators.
Behavioral specificity — the content packages the specific attack (named facility, dated footage, actor-produced narrative) rather than generic reaction.
Source motivation aligned with accuracy — platform trust-and-safety telemetry or law-enforcement referral rather than an informal tip with a competing agenda.
low_signal_anchors: Source-quality weakness — a single screenshot of virality with no provenance for the accounts driving it.
Content-specificity weakness — generic outrage or news reposting that could attach to any incident.
Temporal-pattern weakness — one viral moment with no sustained re-upload or mirroring behavior.
Source-motivation misalignment — reporter has a structural reason to inflate the reach (platform rivalry, advocacy framing, litigation).
Unrebutted organic explanation — the spread admits a benign reading as ordinary news coverage or bystander sharing that investigation did not exclude.
Reconstructive memory — reporting delay long enough that account behavior may be retrofitted to a coordinated-amplification narrative.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the amplification shows operational discipline — pre-staged media, resilient distribution across redundant channels, evasion of takedown and moderation, and the reach of an organized sympathizer network. Capability falls with improvised single-account posting, no takedown resilience, and content that fails to propagate beyond a closed circle.
high_signal_anchors: Pre-staged media production — helmet-cam or livestream captured and edited for release, media kits and manifestos packaged before the attack for immediate distribution.
Multi-channel resilience — content seeded simultaneously across platforms, file-hosts, and encrypted channels so takedown of one node does not stop the spread.
Takedown evasion tradecraft — re-uploads with altered hashes, mirrored copies, translation and re-cutting to defeat automated moderation.
Network reach — an organized sympathizer or propaganda network with existing audience amplifies on cue rather than an isolated actor.
Platform literacy — the actor exploits recommendation mechanics, trending tags, and short-form formats to maximize algorithmic reach.
Demonstrated media competence — production and framing show prior practice at making content that travels.
low_signal_anchors: Improvised single-account posting — one account, no redundancy, no preparation.
No takedown resilience — content removed once and not re-uploaded or mirrored.
Closed-circle reach — material stays within a small private group and never propagates outward.
Low production competence — content is unwatchable, mislabeled, or fails to convey the intended narrative.
Single-platform engagement — activity confined to one platform with no cross-posting.
Direct-exposure posting — the actor amplifies under an attributable personal identity, breaching operational discipline about exposure of the network.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the spreading is engineered for reach and effect rather than incidental — pre-planned release, explicit calls to circulate or imitate, framing tuned to terrorize or recruit, and celebration of engagement metrics. Intent falls with incidental sharing, activity that does not seek wider audience, and a verifiable non-amplifying purpose.
high_signal_anchors: Behavioral progression private-to-public — an observable shift from documenting the act to actively pushing it toward the widest possible audience.
Reach-maximizing behavior — deliberate use of trending tags, cross-posting, and re-uploads whose only function is to extend circulation.
Operational specificity in the call — explicit instructions to share, mirror, translate, or imitate the attack; copycat seeding aimed at the next actor.
Sustained attention to reach — the actor or network tracks views, shares, and takedowns and adapts to keep content circulating.
Retention and re-release of assets — master copies preserved and re-released after removals, indicating a durable amplification objective.

Terror-or-recruit framing paired with spread — content framed to maximize fear in a wider population or to recruit, AND actively propagated; the combination is intent-diagnostic in a way neither alone is.
low_signal_anchors: Incidental sharing — a single repost with no effort to extend reach.
One-time posting without escalation — content surfaced but no push, mirroring, or follow-through.
Verifiable non-amplifying purpose — journalistic, evidentiary, or counter-speech sharing that surfaces and checks out.
No retention behavior — content posted casually and not preserved or re-released after removal.
Audience ambiguity — sharing within an audience that has no plausible amplification or recruitment function.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can propagate freely — control of resilient distribution channels, an existing audience primed to amplify, weak or slow platform moderation, and a live news cycle that carries the content further. Opportunity falls with rapid coordinated takedown, deplatforming of the network, and audience saturation that the actor cannot overcome; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: No moderation friction encountered — content spreads unimpeded despite platform policies against it.
Distribution-channel control — the actor or network owns resilient channels (file-hosts, mirrors, encrypted broadcast) that survive takedowns. The infrastructural dimension of opportunity.
Moderation-gap knowledge — the actor knows which platforms, formats, or hashing gaps let content persist, and routes around enforcement.

Primed audience being exploited — an identified sympathizer network with existing reach is actively re-circulating the content. Dormant sympathy is potential; the active re-circulation is what is high-signal.
News-cycle proximity — the attack lands amid a live news or anniversary window that carries the content to a mass audience the actor could not reach alone.
Direct broadcast reach — the actor holds an established large-audience account or channel that pushes content instantly.
low_signal_anchors: Spread defeated by coordinated takedown — cross-platform enforcement actively removed and hash-blocked the content. Durable signal: sticky unless the network materially adapts.
Institutional rule-out of network reach — platform analysis actively cleared the presence of an organized amplifying network, not merely failed to find it.
Structural reach degradation — the actor's or network's primary channels were deplatformed and audiences dispersed.
Moderation friction encountered without adaptation — content removed and the actor did not re-upload, mirror, or re-cut. Transient: may flip if the actor adapts.
Audience saturation not overcome — the message failed to break out of a closed circle and the actor cannot expand reach.
Enforcement-posture change created barriers — new hashing, tag suppression, or account takedowns block the actor's known methods; transient unless sustained.

false_positive_context.criteria: Much legitimate activity resembles audience amplification on the surface — a journalist circulating attack footage looks similar to an actor releasing it; a researcher archiving propaganda looks similar to a sympathizer mirroring it. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the sharing has a verifiable legitimate purpose, a transparent identity behind it, or institutional accountability that can be checked.
contexts: Verified journalistic purpose — reporters, wire services, and news outlets covering the attack with editorial context and attribution.
Legal and evidentiary authority — law enforcement, courts, and litigants preserving or circulating content for investigation or prosecution; platform trust-and-safety preserving evidence.
Academic and research purpose — terrorism researchers, archivists, and analysts collecting and studying propaganda under institutional review.
Counter-speech and prevention — civil-society groups, survivors, and P/CVE practitioners resharing to rebut or contextualize, not to amplify the actor's aims.
Bystander and community reaction — ordinary users sharing news, expressing shock, or checking on others without intent to extend the attacker's reach.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Findings correlating with an active or renewed threat — a secondary-device or re-attack signal, an explicit call to imitate naming a facility or class, or an amplification surge timed to an anniversary or ongoing campaign — warrant immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: credibility of the amplification signal, breadth across platforms and networks, and persistence over time. A single low-credibility viral moment with an available organic explanation sits at the monitoring tier. A single high-credibility, actor-attributable release with reach-maximizing framing sits at the investigation tier. Cross-platform corroboration — coordinated re-uploads, mirroring, and network re-circulation of the same package — sits at the elevation tier and warrants treating as an organized amplification campaign. Amplification persisting despite coordinated takedowns sits at the committed-network tier, suggesting durable propaganda capability and elevated copycat risk. Multiple lower-priority signals correlating temporally or across platforms may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers logging and reach tracking; investigation triggers network-identification and copycat-risk assessment; elevation triggers coordinated takedown and counter-messaging appropriate to the audience; the committed-network tier triggers referral for network disruption; a confirmed actor or network matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor releases self-recorded footage, livestream, or photographs of the completed facility attack to public platforms to reach a mass audience
Threat actor or sympathizer network runs a coordinated hashtag, meme, or trending-tag campaign to push the attack toward the widest possible audience
Threat actor distributes a propaganda or manifesto package alongside attack media, framed to inspire imitation and seed copycat attacks against similar facilities
Investigators recover a pre-staged media kit or pre-positioned release channels, indicating the amplification of the attack was planned before it was carried out
Threat actor or supporters re-upload, mirror, translate, and re-cut attack content to defeat takedowns and sustain reach, celebrating engagement metrics

countermeasures.measure: Stand up cross-platform monitoring and hashing to detect attack media and its variants early, and pursue coordinated rapid takedown across platforms and file-hosts before content saturates
countermeasures.limitations: Re-uploads with altered hashes, translation, and re-cutting defeat automated matching; encrypted and closed channels are not visible, and takedown on one platform can drive spread to less-cooperative hosts

countermeasures.measure: Adopt a responsible-communication protocol with news media and staff — withhold the attacker's produced media, name, and manifesto, and deny the reach the amplification seeks (no-notoriety framing)
countermeasures.limitations: Depends on voluntary media cooperation and cannot control organic sharing; the news value of a major facility attack creates pressure to publish detail

countermeasures.measure: Prepare and deploy counter-messaging and authoritative-information response to contest the actor's narrative, reassure the affected population, and reduce copycat contagion
countermeasures.limitations: Counter-messaging can inadvertently extend reach if it re-shares the original; effectiveness is hard to measure and lags the initial viral spike

countermeasures.measure: Establish liaison with platform trust-and-safety, fusion centers, and peer facilities to share indicators of amplifying networks and to flag elevated copycat risk against the facility class
countermeasures.limitations: Depends on platform responsiveness and cross-jurisdiction information-sharing discipline; network-level indicators may not resolve to a specific next target

response_protocols.trigger: Attack media, manifesto, or a coordinated amplification campaign tied to the facility attack is detected circulating on public platforms
response_protocols.action: Activate the aftermath communications and takedown cell. Within hours: (a) preserve evidentiary copies of the content and originating accounts, (b) refer to platform trust-and-safety for coordinated cross-platform takedown and hashing, (c) assess reach, network structure, and copycat-seeding language, (d) brief leadership and adopt no-notoriety framing for all outward communication. Document all sourcing.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Content contains an explicit call to imitate naming a facility or class, resolves to an organized amplifying network, OR correlates with a secondary-device or renewed-threat signal
response_protocols.legal_notes: Preservation and referral must follow evidence-handling and platform legal-process requirements; counter-messaging must avoid re-publishing the actor's produced media. Consult counsel on takedown demands and cross-jurisdiction requests.

response_protocols.trigger: Amplification persists or resurges despite takedowns, or copycat-seeding content raises the threat to the facility class
response_protocols.action: Elevate to a network-disruption and prevention posture: coordinate sustained cross-platform enforcement, deploy authoritative counter-messaging to the affected audience, issue a copycat-risk warning to peer facilities and fusion centers, and reassess protective posture for the exposure window. Reassess at window close.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Amplification is linked to an active mobilization or a specific date-certain follow-on threat
response_protocols.legal_notes: Warnings and posture changes are within facility and law-enforcement authority; document the threat basis to support resource requests and defend proportionality. Coordinate public statements with counsel and investigators.

tactics.field_notes: Amplification is where a single facility attack becomes a template. The tell is not that the attack was recorded — it is that the recording was engineered to travel: pre-staged media, a manifesto packaged for release, hashtags and re-uploads that keep it alive after the first takedown. The copycat effect is the real harm; a widely circulated attack lowers the threshold for the next actor and terrorizes a population far larger than the people in the building. The hard part for defenders is that most of the amplification looks like ordinary sharing and protected speech until it pairs with reach-maximizing tradecraft or an explicit call to imitate — and every takedown, counter-message, or news story risks handing the actor more of exactly the reach they wanted. No-notoriety discipline and fast, coordinated hashing beat arguing with the content.
observed_contexts: extremist attacker livestreaming an assault on a facility and releasing a pre-written manifesto packaged for immediate distribution across multiple platforms
sympathizer network re-uploading and translating banned attack footage faster than platforms could hash and remove it
arson case where the actor filmed the fire and pushed the clip with grievance hashtags to seed imitation against similar clinics
[literature: CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 / FBI-HATECRIME-2024 pattern — post-attack propaganda circulation and copycat contagion following facility attacks]

tactics.name: Symbolic Messaging
tactics.notes: Encoding ideological or symbolic meaning into the completed attack and the communication surrounding it, so the act reads as a statement rather than a discrete event. Expressed through chosen date and location symbolism, iconography and slogans left at the site or in released materials, coded in-group references, and messaging aimed at a specific community to intimidate. Distinct from Attribution Declaration (TF0409), which simply claims authorship, and from Audience Amplification (TF0410), which is the raw spread and reach of the act. Symbolic Messaging is the meaning-encoding layer: what the attack is made to signify, to whom, and toward what intended effect. The place was chosen and struck; this tactic governs what its destruction is engineered to communicate.
tactics.cpn_notes: Symbolic payloads are increasingly composed for online circulation before or at the moment of attack — pre-staged manifestos, hashtags, iconography optimized for screenshot and reshare, and date choices legible to online subcultures. The symbolic meaning is often authored in networked spaces and only revealed at the site, so digital-forensic recovery of pre-attack composition materials is central to reading intent.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises when the symbolic content is corroborated across the physical scene, released communications, and the actor's prior expressive record, and when the encoded meaning is specific and internally consistent rather than retrofitted by observers. Credibility falls when the reading of symbolism rests on a single ambiguous artifact, when a benign or coincidental explanation for a date or emblem was never excluded, and when the attribution of meaning originates with commentators rather than the actor.
high_signal_anchors: Cross-artifact consistency — the same ideological frame appears at the scene, in released statements, and in the actor's pre-attack expressive record.
Author-originated meaning — the symbolic reading traces to the actor's own words or emplaced materials, not to third-party interpretation after the fact.
Specific encoding — a named cause, dated anniversary, or precise emblem rather than a generic grievance gesture.
Recoverable composition evidence — pre-staged manifesto drafts, saved iconography, or version history that physically ties the actor to the message.
Temporal coherence — the symbolism was composed before the act and revealed on schedule, not improvised after capture.
First-hand fidelity — a named witness or recovered device documents the actor asserting the intended meaning, with high-resolution reporting of content and timing.
low_signal_anchors: Single-artifact inference — the entire symbolic reading rests on one ambiguous mark, object, or date.
Observer-supplied meaning — analysts or media assigned the symbolism; the actor never asserted it.
Coincidence not excluded — the date or location has an ordinary explanation (routine occupancy, opportunistic timing) that investigation did not rule out.
Retrofit narrative — meaning surfaced only after arrest or notoriety, plausibly reconstructed to fit a movement.
Source-quality weakness — the symbolic content comes through a single unverifiable channel that cannot be re-examined.
Generic emblem — a widely shared symbol with no specific tie to this actor or act.

capability.criteria: Capability rises when the actor commands a sophisticated messaging apparatus — pre-staged materials, fluency in a movement's visual and rhetorical grammar, control of distribution channels, and the discipline to time the reveal for maximum legibility. Capability falls when the symbolism is crude, self-produced without reach, misfires on its intended audience, or is assembled ad hoc after the act.
high_signal_anchors: Pre-staged message package — manifesto, imagery, and slogans prepared in advance and released on a deliberate schedule.
Subcultural fluency — accurate command of a movement's iconography, numerology, and coded language, legible to insiders.
Distribution control — the actor commands or has cultivated channels (accounts, forums, sympathetic amplifiers) that carry the message intact.
Production quality — materials engineered for reshare: framed imagery, quotable lines, screenshot-durable formatting.
Timed reveal discipline — the symbolic payload surfaces synchronized to the act rather than leaking early or arriving late.
Cross-incident craft — the messaging borrows recognized templates from prior attacks, showing study of what propagates.
low_signal_anchors: Crude self-production — disjointed or illegible materials with no evident audience design.
No distribution reach — the message exists but never leaves the actor's immediate ambit.
Audience misfire — the intended in-group does not recognize or claim the symbolism.
Post-hoc assembly — the ideological frame was improvised after the act, not composed for it.
Emblem error — misused symbols or garbled references that insiders read as inauthentic.
Single-channel fragility — the message depends on one account or venue that is easily removed, collapsing its reach.

intent.criteria: Intent rises when the encoding is deliberate and directed — a named cause, an audience selected to be intimidated, and a stated or implied program the attack is meant to advance. Intent falls when the symbolism is incidental, expressively vague, or better explained as notoriety-seeking than as message-delivery to a target community.
high_signal_anchors: Directed intimidation — the messaging names or unmistakably targets a specific community, congregation, or demographic to instill fear.
Programmatic framing — the act is presented as a step toward a stated objective, not an end in itself.
Deliberate date or site symbolism — the timing or location was chosen to carry meaning, and the actor acknowledges or the evidence shows the choice was intentional.
Exemplary framing — the actor presents the attack as a model for others to emulate, with instructional or invitational language.
Consistency of cause — the same ideological target recurs across the actor's statements, materials, and target choice.
Encoded call-to-action — the message pairs the act with an appeal for further action against the same community or category, making message-delivery the diagnostic purpose.
low_signal_anchors: Incidental symbolism — a date or emblem present but not shown to be chosen for meaning.
Notoriety over message — the communication centers the actor's fame rather than any cause or audience.
Expressive vagueness — grievance language too diffuse to identify a targeted community or program.
No audience selection — nothing indicates a specific community was meant to receive or fear the message.
Borrowed frame without commitment — the actor invokes a cause superficially with no supporting record.
Contradictory signaling — symbolic claims that conflict across artifacts, suggesting improvisation rather than intent.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor can deliver the symbolic message to its intended audience and have it land — media and platform reach, proximity or standing within the targeted community, and an information environment primed to carry the meaning. Opportunity falls when channels are denied or degraded, when the targeted audience is insulated from the message, or when responders control the narrative frame; when opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: Unobstructed reach — the message circulates freely through platforms or press without friction or takedown.
Audience proximity — the actor stands close enough to the targeted community (geographically, socially, or online) that the intimidation is felt directly.
Primed information environment — an anniversary, news cycle, or active campaign amplifies the symbolic meaning the actor intends.
Sympathetic amplifiers — aligned accounts or outlets propagate and interpret the message on the actor's terms.
Iconography durability — the symbolic artifacts persist at the site or online despite removal efforts.
Narrative uncontested — no authoritative counter-frame competes with the actor's intended meaning during the exposure window.
low_signal_anchors: Channels denied — platforms and press decline to carry or actively suppress the symbolic content. Durable signal: sticky unless the actor opens new channels.
Audience insulated — the targeted community does not encounter the message or is effectively reassured, blunting the intimidation.
Counter-frame established — responders and community leaders set an authoritative narrative that displaces the actor's intended meaning.
Artifact removal sustained — symbolic materials are catalogued and removed and do not reappear.
Reach not achieved — the message exists but never attains circulation; transient if the actor finds new amplification.
Environment not primed — no anniversary, campaign, or news context to carry the symbolism; the meaning falls flat.

false_positive_context.criteria: Many legitimate activities resemble symbolic messaging in the aftermath of an attack — a community memorial reproduces the very symbols the attacker used; journalism reporting the event reproduces its iconography; a date coincidence looks chosen when it was opportunistic. What distinguishes a false positive is whether the symbolic content originates with the actor and is directed at a community, versus originating with observers, mourners, or reporters processing the event.
contexts: Memorial and mourning expression — vigils, tributes, and community responses that reproduce or reclaim symbols associated with the attack.
Journalistic and academic reproduction — reporters, researchers, and analysts documenting and interpreting the act's iconography and timing.
Coincidental timing — an attack date or location with an ordinary operational explanation later read as symbolic without basis.
Protest and advocacy speech — lawful activism near the event that shares vocabulary or emblems with the actor's cause but is expressive, not attack-linked.
Artistic and commemorative works — art, murals, or writing engaging the event's meaning without endorsing or continuing the actor's message.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: Symbolic messaging that pairs with any live operational signal — a community-directed threat of further action, secondary-device or re-attack positioning, or an active emulation call drawing responses — warrants immediate activation of response protocols regardless of this tactic's internal tier. Tier-determination for this tactic's findings depends on three factors: credibility that the symbolism originates with the actor, whether the message is directed at an identifiable community, and the reach the message has attained. A single ambiguous artifact with an available benign explanation sits at the monitoring tier. Author-originated symbolism with specific encoding but no directed audience sits at the investigation tier. Symbolic messaging directed at a named community to intimidate, or framed to invite emulation, sits at the elevation tier and warrants coordinated community-protection and narrative response. Messaging that continues to circulate and draw aligned responses despite removal efforts sits at the committed-movement tier, suggesting the act is being adopted as a template. Multiple lower-priority indicators correlating temporally or across artifacts may compose to a higher aggregate tier than any single finding warrants; consumer triage tooling should make this composition rule explicit. Tier-triggered actions: monitoring triggers logging and cross-incident pattern-detection; investigation triggers attribution analysis and actor-identification; elevation triggers community-protection liaison and a coordinated counter-narrative; the committed-movement tier triggers cross-jurisdictional coordination against emulation; a confirmed actor or movement matching a known threat-actor profile at any tier warrants urgent law-enforcement coordination.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor times or locates the attack to a symbolically significant date, anniversary, or site so the act itself carries encoded meaning legible to a movement
Threat actor leaves iconography, slogans, emblems, or manifesto materials at the scene or in released communications to signal ideological affiliation and encode the act's meaning
Threat actor directs messaging at a specific community, congregation, or demographic to intimidate, framing the attack as a warning to that population
Threat actor frames the attack as exemplary or instructional, presenting the act as a model and inviting emulation against similar facilities or communities
Threat actor incorporates numerology, coded language, or in-group references legible to a subculture to claim the act within a movement's symbolic grammar

countermeasures.measure: Stand up a symbolic-attribution analysis capability that decodes date, location, iconography, and coded-language choices to identify the movement, the intended audience, and the encoded meaning, and links the artifacts across incidents with fusion partners
countermeasures.limitations: Decoding is interpretive and can over-read coincidence or under-read novel symbolism; coded in-group references may be illegible without subcultural expertise, and analysis lags the message's initial circulation

countermeasures.measure: Execute a measured communications response that denies the actor the intended symbolic payoff — avoid gratuitous reproduction of iconography or manifesto content, decline to name the actor where policy allows, and establish an authoritative counter-frame during the exposure window
countermeasures.limitations: Cannot control independent media or platform amplification; over-suppression can itself become a story, and a counter-frame competes with a message often engineered for faster spread

countermeasures.measure: Activate protective liaison with the targeted community — reassurance outreach, dedicated reporting channels, and elevated posture at facilities associated with that community — to blunt the intimidation the messaging is engineered to produce
countermeasures.limitations: Reassurance cannot fully offset a message that has already reached the community; outreach requires pre-existing trust that may be absent, and elevated posture is resource-limited over time

countermeasures.measure: Preserve, catalog, and cross-reference symbolic artifacts — scene graffiti, emplaced objects, released materials, and coded references — into a shared repository so emulation and template-borrowing across incidents can be detected early
countermeasures.limitations: Cross-incident matching depends on reporting discipline and repository participation; novel symbolism has no prior match, and cataloguing does not by itself suppress circulation

response_protocols.trigger: Symbolic messaging identified in the aftermath of a facility attack — emplaced iconography, a chosen symbolic date or site, coded in-group references, or released manifesto materials
response_protocols.action: Activate symbolic-attribution analysis. Within 24 hours: (a) preserve and catalog all symbolic artifacts, (b) decode the encoded meaning and intended audience, (c) attribute to a movement or actor profile where evidence supports it, (d) brief law enforcement and set a measured communications posture that denies the actor the intended symbolic payoff. Document all sourcing and interpretive basis.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Messaging directed at a named community to intimidate, framed to invite emulation, or paired with a follow-on operational threat
response_protocols.legal_notes: Attribution of ideological meaning must rest on evidence, not inference, to withstand challenge; reproduction of manifesto content may implicate distribution restrictions, and community-monitoring may implicate civil-rights and privacy protections. Consult counsel before public attribution.

response_protocols.trigger: Symbolic messaging directed at a specific community to intimidate, or an exemplary/emulation frame drawing aligned responses
response_protocols.action: Activate community-protection liaison: reassurance outreach, dedicated reporting channels, and elevated posture at associated facilities for the exposure window. Establish an authoritative counter-narrative, monitor for emulation and copycat signaling across incidents, and coordinate with fusion partners and platforms on artifact removal. Reassess at window close.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Emulation signaling resolves to a specific actor or plot, or the intimidation is paired with a date-certain follow-on threat
response_protocols.legal_notes: Community outreach and posture changes are within facility and protective authority; document the threat basis to support resource requests and defend proportionality. Coordinate content-removal requests with counsel to respect lawful-speech boundaries.

tactics.field_notes: Symbolic messaging is what separates an attack from a statement. The act is over; the meaning is the point, and the actor engineers it — a date that lands on an anniversary, an emblem left where responders will photograph it, a line addressed to a community that is meant to read it and be afraid. The clearest tell that messaging is deliberate rather than incidental is pre-staging: materials composed before the act and revealed on schedule, not improvised after capture. The two findings that should move fastest are messaging pointed at a named community to intimidate and framing that presents the attack as a model for others, because both reach past this incident — one into a population's sense of safety, the other toward the next actor. The hard part is discipline on the defender side: memorials reproduce the same symbols, reporters reproduce the same iconography, and the response itself can hand the actor the amplification the messaging was built to earn.
observed_contexts: attack on a place of worship timed to a movement's anniversary, with an emblem left at the entrance and a manifesto released to aligned online channels within the hour
clinic arson followed by messaging addressed directly to the community the facility served, framed as a warning that more would follow
attacker's released materials presenting the act as a template — instructional framing and coded references inviting emulation against similar sites
[literature: FBI-HATECRIME-2024 / CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 pattern — ideological iconography and community-directed intimidation encoded into facility attacks and their communications]

tactics.name: Coercive Demand
tactics.notes: Issuing demands, ultimatums, or conditional threats that leverage a completed attack on the facility to compel payment, policy change, release, withdrawal, or other concession — the 'pay or comply, or more follows' communication. Distinct from Attribution Declaration (which merely claims responsibility) and Symbolic Messaging (which encodes ideological meaning): the defining feature here is instrumental coercion tied to a stated or implied follow-on consequence. The completed attack functions as proof-of-capability that gives the demand its teeth. A credible follow-on threat — a further device claimed emplaced, a renewed strike promised, a deadline attached — converts the aftermath of one attack into the leverage for the next, and raises the blast picture accordingly.
tactics.cpn_notes: Coercive demands increasingly arrive through online and pseudonymous channels — encrypted messengers, anonymous email, social-media broadcast, or extremist forums — and route payment through cryptocurrency wallets and drop instructions that let an actor extort a facility while masking identity and location.

credibility.criteria: Credibility rises when the demand can be tied to the actor who conducted the attack — private hold-back details, matching signatures, or a communication channel established before the strike — and when any follow-on threat is corroborated by physical or acquisition evidence. Credibility falls when the demand is a bandwagon claim, when it recites only publicly reported facts, and when the follow-on threat has no material backing.
high_signal_anchors: Hold-back knowledge — the demand references non-public details of the attack (device placement, ignition method, timing) known only to the perpetrator.
Pre-established channel — the demand arrives through a contact method the actor set up or signaled before the attack, linking claimant to perpetrator.
Corroborated follow-on — the threat of 'more to come' is backed by a recovered secondary device, an acquisition trail, or an emplacement observed on scene.
Signature consistency — phrasing, symbology, or a claimed name matches prior communications or the physical scene.
Temporal tightness — the demand surfaces within the window when only the perpetrator could compose it, ahead of full public reporting.
Operational specificity in the demand — a concrete sum, account, deadline, and mechanism, not a vague grievance.
low_signal_anchors: Public-facts-only content — the demand recites only what news coverage already carried; no hold-back detail.
Bandwagon claim — a group or individual asserts leverage over an attack investigators cannot tie to them.
Unbacked follow-on — 'more will follow' with no device, acquisition, or positioning evidence to support it.
Channel mismatch — the demand arrives through a channel with no link to the attack and cannot be authenticated.
Reconstructive timing — the demand appears only after saturation coverage, when anyone could assemble it.
Source-motivation misalignment — a claimant with a reason to attach itself to the event (notoriety, fundraising, rival framing).

capability.criteria: Capability rises when evidence shows the actor can actually make good on the follow-on threat — a demonstrated attack just completed, retained or additional materiel, an intact cell, and secure means to receive a concession. Capability falls when the demand outruns any observed means, when the just-completed attack exhausted the actor's resources, and when the payment or compliance mechanism is unworkable.
high_signal_anchors: Demonstrated method — the completed attack itself proves the actor can inflict the harm the demand threatens to repeat.
Retained materiel — evidence of additional accelerant, precursors, devices, or weapons beyond what the first attack consumed.
Intact network — co-conspirators or an insider remain in place and able to act on the follow-on threat.
Secure receipt mechanism — a functioning cryptocurrency wallet, laundering path, or drop that could actually collect an extortion payment.
Operational security in the demand channel — anonymized, encrypted, or cut-out communications that survive scrutiny.
Evidence of pre-planned coercion — the demand mechanism was prepared before the attack, indicating a deliberate extortion campaign rather than an afterthought.
low_signal_anchors: Means-exhausting attack — the strike consumed the actor's apparent capability with nothing observed in reserve.
Empty follow-on — the threat of renewed attack has no acquisition, device, or positioning evidence behind it.
Unworkable mechanism — the demanded payment path is technically broken, monitored, or trivially traceable.
Lone-actor exposure — the actor is identified or in custody, degrading ability to execute a follow-on.
Conspicuous demand channel — the communication exposes the actor's identity or location, undercutting sustained coercion.
Recycled threat language — the follow-on wording is copied from prior incidents with no operational tailoring to this facility.

intent.criteria: Intent to coerce rises when the demand is instrumental and structured — a concrete objective, a deadline, an escalation ladder, and evidence the actor intends to act on non-compliance. Intent falls when the communication is purely expressive with no achievable ask, when it lacks any consequence, and when it reads as catharsis rather than leverage.
high_signal_anchors: Concrete achievable ask — a specific sum, policy reversal, release, or withdrawal the target could actually grant.
Explicit conditional structure — 'if you do not X by Y, then Z,' a genuine ultimatum rather than a grievance.
Stated escalation ladder — the actor describes graduated consequences for continued non-compliance.
Deadline discipline — a date-certain or countdown attached to the demand, with follow-through signaling.
Instrumental framing — the attack is presented as the first move in a campaign to force the concession, not an end in itself.
Consequence follow-through — a prior deadline lapsed and the actor executed or advanced the threatened consequence.
low_signal_anchors: Expressive-only communication — venting or triumphalism with no ask the target can act on.
No stated consequence — a claim or grievance without a conditional threat attached.
Unmeetable demand — the ask is impossible, absurd, or addressed to no one who could grant it.
One-off statement — a single message with no deadline, no follow-up, and no escalation structure.
Cathartic register — the language reads as closure or self-justification rather than leverage.
Target ambiguity — the demand is broadcast generally without a recipient positioned to comply.

opportunity.criteria: Opportunity rises when the actor retains the positional and informational means to press the demand — an unimpeded channel to the target, a live follow-on capability the facility cannot yet neutralize, and pressure points (occupants, operations, reputation) the actor can credibly hold at risk. Opportunity falls when the channel is closed, when the follow-on capability is contained, and when the facility's response removes the leverage; where opportunity appears reduced, the durability of that reduction matters.
high_signal_anchors: Open communication channel — the actor can reliably reach decision-makers with demands and updates unimpeded.
Live follow-on capability — a claimed or evidenced secondary device or renewed-attack posture the facility has not yet cleared.
Held-at-risk population — occupants, responders, or returning staff the actor can credibly threaten to compel compliance.
Operational leverage — the facility's continuity (production, services, events) is disrupted in a way the actor can prolong.
Untraceable receipt path — a payment or compliance mechanism the actor can use without exposure.
Time pressure controlled by the actor — a deadline the actor sets and the target cannot easily outlast.
low_signal_anchors: Channel closed — the demand pathway is identified and shut, cutting the actor off from the target. Durable if the actor cannot re-establish contact.
Follow-on contained — the site has been swept and cleared, or the claimed capability disproven, removing the renewed-attack leverage.
Actor identified or in custody — attribution or arrest strips positional ability to press the demand. Durable signal.
Payment path neutralized — the demanded mechanism is frozen, monitored, or traced, denying a clean concession.
Population secured — occupants evacuated or protected, dissolving the held-at-risk leverage. Transient if the actor shifts targets.
Deadline outlasted without consequence — a stated deadline passed and no follow-on materialized, degrading the threat's credibility. May flip if the actor then acts.

false_positive_context.criteria: Some post-incident communications resemble coercive demands without being one — a labor action with an ultimatum, an advocacy campaign timed to an event, or a hoax rider on real news. What distinguishes a genuine coercive demand is an authenticated link to the attack perpetrator, an instrumental and achievable ask backed by a real or evidenced follow-on capability, and a consequence the actor is positioned to deliver.
contexts: Legitimate labor or advocacy action — unions, protest organizers, or campaigners issuing lawful demands or ultimatums unconnected to any attack.
Opportunistic hoax — a bandwagon caller or emailer attaching a demand to a real incident they had no part in, with no hold-back detail.
Media or research inquiry — journalists, analysts, or researchers pressing an organization about an incident, mistaken for a coercive contact.
Insurance, legal, or regulatory pressure — legitimate claims, litigation, or compliance demands arriving in the aftermath that carry conditional language.
Internal grievance escalation — an aggrieved employee or stakeholder issuing conditional complaints in temporal proximity to an unrelated incident.

assessment_guidance.threshold_guidance: A coercive demand tied to a completed facility attack is treated as an active-threat matter, not a routine claim, because it asserts continuing leverage over the site and its people. Tier-determination depends on three factors: the credibility of the link between claimant and perpetrator, the credibility and specificity of any follow-on threat, and the actor's demonstrated willingness to execute consequences. A demand reciting only public facts with an unbacked follow-on sits at the monitoring tier pending authentication. A demand carrying hold-back knowledge or a concrete ultimatum sits at the investigation tier and warrants immediate law-enforcement referral and forensic preservation. A demand backed by a credible follow-on — a claimed or recovered secondary device, an acquisition trail, or a positioning consistent with re-attack — sits at the elevation tier and triggers active-threat response including sweep and protective measures for occupants and responders, coordinated with the Secondary Device / Re-attack Positioning protocols. A demand where a prior deadline lapsed and the actor executed the threatened consequence sits at the committed-actor tier. Never negotiate or concede unilaterally; route all demand communications to counsel and law enforcement, preserve them without alteration, and deny the actor the coercive leverage of public panic through pre-planned crisis communications.

indicators.behavior: Threat actor issues an explicit demand referencing the completed attack — payment, policy change, release, or withdrawal — coupled with a stated consequence for non-compliance
Threat actor attaches a deadline or countdown to the demand, signaling a date-certain point after which the threatened consequence follows
Threat actor claims a live follow-on capability against the facility — a further device emplaced, a renewed strike promised — to give the demand credible teeth
Threat actor specifies a payment or compliance mechanism — cryptocurrency wallet, drop instructions, or account — through which the extortion concession is to be delivered
Threat actor broadcasts the demand to press, public, or authorities to amplify pressure and compel the target toward compliance

countermeasures.measure: Establish a demand-handling protocol before an incident — a do-not-negotiate-unilaterally posture, a single trained point of contact, evidence-preservation steps, and pre-authorized law-enforcement referral for any post-attack extortion communication
countermeasures.limitations: A protocol governs the facility's response but cannot stop an actor from issuing a demand; effectiveness depends on staff training and disciplined adherence under pressure

countermeasures.measure: Forensically preserve all demand communications without alteration — headers, metadata, wallet addresses, timestamps, and channel artifacts — and route them intact to law enforcement to support authentication and attribution
countermeasures.limitations: Preservation supports investigation but does not neutralize the threat; anonymized and encrypted channels may yield limited attribution even when captured cleanly

countermeasures.measure: Coordinate with financial institutions, payment processors, and blockchain-analytics partners to flag, trace, and where possible freeze the demanded payment channels
countermeasures.limitations: Tracing depends on the actor using a traceable path; sophisticated laundering, mixers, or off-ramp discipline can defeat attribution and recovery

countermeasures.measure: Pre-establish a crisis-communications plan that denies the actor coercive leverage over public and staff — controlled messaging, rumor management, and stakeholder briefing — to prevent panic-driven concession and reputational pressure
countermeasures.limitations: Messaging discipline reduces the actor's psychological leverage but cannot address a genuine follow-on capability, which requires operational response

response_protocols.trigger: A demand, ultimatum, or conditional threat referencing the completed attack is received through any channel
response_protocols.action: Activate the demand-handling protocol. Do not negotiate or concede unilaterally. (a) Preserve the communication forensically without alteration; (b) refer immediately to law enforcement and counsel; (c) attempt to authenticate the link to the perpetrator via hold-back detail; (d) assess the credibility of any follow-on threat; (e) brief executive leadership and route external messaging through the crisis-communications plan.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: The demand carries a credible follow-on threat — claimed secondary device, evidenced renewed-attack capability, or a lapsed-deadline consequence executed
response_protocols.legal_notes: Extortion and terroristic-threat communications are evidence; preserve chain of custody and avoid altering originals. Any decision touching payment, concession, or negotiation must involve counsel and law enforcement. Ransom or payment may carry independent legal exposure under sanctions and anti-terrorism-financing regimes.

response_protocols.trigger: The demand is backed by a credible claim of a further device or a renewed attack against the facility, its occupants, or responders
response_protocols.action: Treat as an active threat. Initiate protective measures for occupants and responders — evacuation or shelter as appropriate, controlled re-entry, and a systematic sweep coordinated with EOD and law enforcement. Do not let the demand's deadline drive an unsafe concession. Maintain protective posture until the follow-on capability is cleared or disproven, coordinating with Secondary Device / Re-attack Positioning response.
response_protocols.escalation_trigger: Physical confirmation of a secondary device or an in-progress renewed attack
response_protocols.legal_notes: Protective and evacuation decisions are within facility authority; document the threat basis to defend proportionality. Coordinate closely with EOD and law enforcement, who hold primacy over any confirmed device.

tactics.field_notes: Coercive demand is where an attack stops being an end and becomes leverage. The tell is instrumental structure: a concrete ask, a deadline, and a consequence, rather than the venting or triumphalism of a bare claim. The first authentication question is always whether the claimant is the perpetrator — hold-back detail settles it faster than anything, which is why investigators guard a few facts from public release specifically to test post-incident communications. The dangerous variant is the demand backed by a live follow-on: 'there is a second device, and there will be more.' That claim has to be treated as true until a sweep clears it, because the whole point of a secondary is to catch responders and returning occupants. Do not let the actor's deadline set the tempo of your response. The counterintuitive part is that many coercive demands are working from a spent hand — the attack consumed the capability — but you cannot assume that from the message alone, and the cost of guessing wrong is measured in lives.
observed_contexts: extortion note left after an arson attack demanding payment to a cryptocurrency wallet with a threat of a second fire
ideologically motivated actor broadcasting a demand to reverse a facility's function, claiming a further device was already emplaced
bomb-threat campaign following an initial detonation, using a deadline and a claimed secondary to pressure evacuation and concession
[literature: CTC-INFRATERROR-2026 / CISA-BOMBTHREAT-2023 pattern — post-attack demand paired with a claimed follow-on device used to coerce a target facility]

facility.scope: Tactics centered on a physical venue, structure, or built environment as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is damage, destruction, denial, or symbolic action against the place itself. Incidental human harm in an unoccupied facility does not move the tactic to People.

organization.scope: Tactics centered on an institution, mission, brand, or operational continuity as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is disruption, delegitimization, infiltration, or coercion of what the organization does or represents, distinct from its facilities or its individuals.

infrastructure.scope: Tactics centered on infrastructure or technical systems as the primary target. The adversary's primary objective is disruption, degradation, or compromise of the system's function — physical infrastructure, cyber-physical systems, or critical service delivery. Cyber-Physical Nexus tactics are tagged via the cpn field on tactic.

actor_profiles.name: Fixated Individual
actor_profiles.description: Psychologically-driven actor with obsessive focus on a specific named target. The fixation is the defining characteristic — this actor's threat is organized entirely around one person. Motivation is personal, delusional, or grievance-rooted. Follows a slow-building predatory pathway that may span months to years. Clinical anchor: WAVR-21, PATH model, Threat Assessment in Schools.
behavioral_markers: Sustained surveillance or contact attempts directed at one specific named target
Leakage of fixation content to third parties — friends, family, online platforms
Escalating attempts to communicate with or approach the target despite rejection
Acquisition of the target's personal information, schedule, and location patterns
Grievance documentation — letters, journals, social media posts referencing the target

actor_profiles.name: Domestic / Intimate Partner
actor_profiles.description: Actor in or formerly in an intimate, family, or cohabiting relationship with the target. The prior relationship is both the access vector and the motivational anchor.
